B.  ULTIMATE FACTS INCLUDING THE 
EVIDENCE   
 
The allegations of the complaint must be 
based on the ultimate facts, including the 
evidence on which the party pleading relies 
for their claims or defenses, which must be 
attached to the complaint. (Sec. 1, Rule 8, 
Rules of Court, as amended) 
Note: It is a basic rule that the allegations of 
the complaint—not the prayer—determine 
the basis of the plaintiff’s relief. Similarly, the 
prayer will not be construed as enlarging the 
complaint to include a cause of action not 
pleaded 
therein. 
(Republic 
v. 
Capital 
Resources 
Corp., 
G.R. 
No. 
217210, 
November 7, 2016) 
 
C.  ALTERNATIVE CAUSES OF ACTION 
OR DEFENSES   
 
Under Section 2, Rule 8 of the Rules of 
Court, a party may state two or more causes 
of action or defenses in the alternative or 
hypothetically, 
regardless 
of 
their 
consistency, provided that such causes or 
defenses are sufficiently substantiated by 
the allegations in the pleading. 
 
D.  CONDITIONS PRECEDENT  
 
Pursuant to Section 3, Rule 8 of the Rules of 
Court, compliance with any conditions 
precedent must be specifically alleged in 
the pleading.  
 
A condition precedent refers to an act or 
event that must occur before a claim or 
cause of action can arise. Failure to comply 
with these conditions can result in the 
dismissal of the case for lack of a valid cause 
of action.  
 
Ex. In cases where barangay conciliation is 
required 
under 
the 
Katarungang 
Pambarangay Law, the plaintiff must allege 
such compliance in the complaint. 
 
E.  CAPACITY TO SUE OR BE SUED   
 
Under Section 4, Rule 8 of the Rules of 
Court, the legal capacity of a party to sue or 
be sued must be affirmatively stated in the 
pleadings if it is required to establish the 
party’s standing in the case. If the party is 
suing in a representative capacity (e.g., as a 
guardian or trustee), such capacity must also 
be specifically pleaded.  
 


<!-- PAGE 68 -->

 
 
56 
This ensures that the court has jurisdiction 
over the proper parties and that the plaintiff 
or defendant is capable of participating in the 
litigation. 
 
F.  FRAUD, MISTAKE, MALICE, INTENT, 
KNOWLEDGE, AND OTHER CONDITION 
OF THE MIND, JUDGMENTS, OFFICIAL 
DOCUMENTS OR ACTS   
 
Under Section 5, Rule 8 of the Rules of 
Court, allegations of fraud, mistake, malice, 
intent, or knowledge must be stated with 
particularity. However, the mental condition 
of a party may be averred generally.  
 
This ensures that a party making such 
serious claims provides enough detail to give 
the opposing party fair notice of the issues to 
be addressed. Similarly, official documents, 
acts, and judgments must be specifically 
pleaded if relied upon, providing sufficient 
context for the court and opposing parties. 
 
G. 
 
PLEADING 
A 
JUDGMENT 
OR 
DECISION   
 
In pleading a judgment or decision of a 
domestic or foreign court, judicial or quasi-
judicial tribunal, or of a board or officer, it is 
sufficient to aver the judgment or 
decision without setting forth matter 
showing jurisdiction to render it. 
 
H. 
 
PLEADING 
AN 
ACTIONABLE 
DOCUMENT   
 
Whenever an action or defense is based 
upon a written instrument or document:  
 
(a) The substance of such document shall 
be set forth in the pleading, and  
(b) The original or a copy thereof shall be 
attached to the pleading as an exhibit, 
which shall form part of the pleading. 
(Rule 8, Sec. 7) 
 
The plaintiff may file a reply only if the 
defending party attaches an actionable 
document to his or her answer (Sec. 10, 
Rule 6). 
Contesting an actionable document

a. The adverse party does not appear to

b. Compliance with an order for an 
inspection of the original instrument is 
refused. Rule 8, Sec. 8) 
 
 
I.  SPECIFIC DENIALS   
 
How to specifically deny 
 
1. By specifically denying the allegation and 
setting forth the substance upon which one 
relies his denial. 
 
2. By specifically denying some part of the 
allegation and admitting the rest. 
 
3. By specifically denying the allegation for 
lack of knowledge sufficient to form a belief 
as to the truth or falsity of the allegation. 
 
When a specific denial requires an oath  
 
GR: Specific denial under oath is required for 
the denial of the genuineness and due 
execution of an actionable document

57 
Meaning 
of 
‘genuineness 
and 
due 
execution’ 
 
Genuineness and due execution of the 
instrument means that the instrument is 
not spurious, counterfeit, or of different 
import on its face from the one executed. 
 
XPNs (when oath is not necessary to 
make a specific denial): 
 
1) when the adverse party does not appear 
to be a party to the instrument or  
2) when compliance with an order for 
inspection of the original instrument is 
refused. 
 
Effect of failure to make specific denials 
 
Failure to comply with the prescribed 
procedure results in the admission of the 
genuineness and due execution of the 
actionable document. (Rule 8, Sec. 8) 
 
GR: Material averments in a pleading 
asserting a claim shall be deemed admitted 
when not specifically denied. (Rule 8, Sec. 
11). 
 
In simpler terms, failure to specifically 
deny results in the admission of the 
opposing party’s allegations. 
 
XPN: The following averments in the 
complaint are not deemed admitted even if 
not specifically denied:  
 
1. Amount of unliquidated damages (Rule 
8, Sec. 11)  
2. Conclusions in a pleading, because it is 
for a court to make conclusions, and  
3. Non-material allegations or averments, 
because the rules provide that only 
material allegations have to be denied.  
 
Claim 
of 
“ignorance 
or 
lack 
of 
information” by the defendant is an 
IMPLIED ADMISSION 
 
 
 
When the defendant alleges having no 
knowledge or information sufficient to form a 
belief as to the truth of the allegations of the 
other party but such matters are plainly and 
necessarily within defendant’s knowledge, a 
claim of “ignorance or lack of information” will 
not be considered a specific denial, hence, 
implied admission (Acquintey vs. Tibong, 
515 SCRA 414, 433; Camitan vs. CA, 511 
SCRA 364, 373). 
 
In simpler terms, mere claim of ignorance or 
lack of information of the allegation will result 
in an implied admission. However, such 
implied admission is deemed waived if the 
party asserting the same has allowed the 
adverse party to present evidence contrary to 
the contents of such document without 
objection (Central Surety vs. Hodges, G.R. 
No. L-28633, March 30, 1971). 
 
Note: A general denial does not become 
specific by the use of the word "specifically” 
A denial is not made specific simply because 
it is so qualified by the defendant.

J. 
 
AFFIRMATIVE 
DEFENSES 
IN 
RELATION TO SEC. 5(B), RULE 6, AND 
SEC. 12, RULE 8   
 
Affirmative defenses are those defenses 
that do not simply deny the allegations of the 
plaintiff’s complaint but INTRODUCE NEW 
FACTS OR MATTERS that, if true, would 
defeat the plaintiff’s claim.  
 
Under Section 5(b), Rule 6 of the Rules of 
Court, affirmative defenses include, but are 
not limited to: 
 
Fraud, statute of limitations, payment, 
waiver, release, res judicata, prescription, or 
any other matter that would bar the plaintiff's 
recovery. 
These 
defenses 
must 
be 
specifically pleaded in the answer, as 
required by Section 12, Rule 8 of the Rules 
of Court, to ensure that the opposing party 
has fair notice of the issues and an 
opportunity to respond. 
 
For example, in a breach of contract, the 
defendant may allege as an affirmative 
defense that the plaintiff has already been 
paid in full. By doing so, the defendant 
introduces a new fact (payment) that, if 
proven, would absolve them of liability under 
the contract.

Effect of Amended Pleading   
 
(1) It Supersedes the pleading that it 
amends;  
 
(2) Admissions in superseded pleadings may 
be Offered in evidence against the pleader; 
and  
 
(3) Claims and defenses therein not 
incorporated in the amended pleading shall 
be deemed Waived (Rule 10, Sec. 8)        
 
No Amendments Necessary to Conform 
to or Authorize Presentation of Evidence   
 
When issues not raised by the pleadings are 
tried with the express or implied consent of 
the parties, they shall be treated in all 
respects as if they had been raised in the 
pleadings. No amendment of such pleadings 
deemed amended is necessary to cause 
them to conform to the evidence. (Rule 10, 
Section 5).

SUPPLEMENTAL PLEADINGS   
 
A supplemental pleading is one which sets 
forth transactions, occurrences, or events 
which have happened since the date of the 
pleading sought to be supplemented. (Rule 
10, Sec. 6) 
 
Purpose of supplemental pleading 
 
To bring into the records new facts which will 
enlarge or change the kind of relief to which 
the plaintiff is entitled (Ada v. Baylon, G.R. 
No. 182435 (2012).   
 
How made 
 
Upon motion of a party, the court may 
(discretionary), upon reasonable notice and 
upon such terms as just permit him or her to 
serve a supplemental pleading.   
 
Note: The supplemental complaint must be 
based on matters arising subsequent to the 
original complaint related to the claim or 
defense presented therein, and founded on 
the same cause of action. When the cause of 
action stated in the supplemental complaint 
is different from the cause of action 
mentioned in the original complaint, the court 
should 
not 
admit 
the 
supplemental 
complaint. It cannot be used to try a new 
matter or a new cause of action. (Leobrera 
vs. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 80001 
February 27, 1989

Motion to extend time to file an answer 
 
The Rules allow for a motion to extend time 
to file an answer, as long as it is for 
meritorious reasons. Such may only be 
availed of by the defendant once and may 
not exceed 30 calendar days (Sec. 1, Rule 
11). 
 
 
7. BILL OF PARTICULARS – RULE 
12 
 
Purpose and When Applied  
 
Before responding to a pleading, a party 
may move for a definite statement or for a bill 
of particulars of any matter, which is not 
averred 
with 
sufficient 
definiteness 
or 
particularity to enable him or her properly 
to prepare his or her responsive pleading. 
 
If the pleading is a reply, the motion must be 
filed within ten (10) calendar days from 
service thereof. Such motion shall point out 
the defects complained of, the paragraphs 
wherein they are contained, and the details 
desired. 
 
Actions of the Court   
 
Upon the filing of the motion, the clerk of 
court must immediately bring it to the 
attention of the court, which may either deny 
or grant it outright, or allow the parties the 
opportunity to be heard. 
 
Compliance with the order 
 
If the motion is granted, either in whole or in 
part, the compliance therewith must be 
effected within ten (10) calendar days from 
notice of the order, unless a different period 
is fixed by the court. The bill of particulars or 
a more definite statement ordered by the 
court may be filed either in a separate or in 
an amended pleading, serving a copy thereof 
on the adverse party. 
 
Effect of Non-Compliance 
 
If the order is not obeyed, or in case of 
insufficient compliance therewith, the court 
may order the striking out of the pleading or 
the portions thereof to which the order was 
directed, or make such other order as it 
deems just. 
 
 
8. FILING AND SERVICE OF 
PLEADINGS – RULE 13 
 
Rule 13 shall govern the filing of all 
pleadings, motions, and other court 
submissions, as well as the service 
thereof, except those for which a different 
mode of service is prescribed.  
 
Filing is the act of submitting the pleading 
or other paper to the court. 
 


<!-- PAGE 75 -->

 
 
63 
Service is the act of providing a party with 
a copy of the pleading or any other court 
submission. 
 
 If the party has appeared by counsel, 
service upon such party shall be made 
upon his or her counsel, unless service 
upon the party AND the party’s counsel 
is ordered by the court. 
 Where one counsel appears for several 
parties, such counsel shall only be 
entitled to one copy of any paper served 
by the opposite side. 
 Where several counsels appear for one 
party, such party shall be entitled to only 
one copy of any pleading or paper to be 
served upon the lead counsel if one is 
designated, or upon anyone of them if 
there is no designation of a lead 
counsel.

1. Pleadings; and  
2. Other court submissions. (Sec. 3, Rule 13, 
ROC, as amended)

Adverse Party 
 
1. Pleadings;  
2. Motions;

4. Orders;

6. Other court submissions (Sec. 5, Rule 13,

The filing of pleadings and other court 
submissions shall be made by: 
 
(a) Submitting 
personally

In the first case, the clerk of court shall

In the fourth case, the date of electronic 
transmission shall be considered as the date 
of filing.

(g) Substituted Service; When allowed 
 
When service cannot be made personally or

2. With proof of failure of both personal

substituted service  
 
1. Pleadings

3. Notices

5. Other papers 
 
Judgments, final orders, or resolutions 
cannot be served by substituted service. 
 
Service of judgments, final orders, or 
resolutions shall be served either: 
 
1. Personally 
 
2. By registered mail 
 
3. By accredited courier, upon ex parte 
motion of any party 
 
4. By publication, when a party summoned 
by publication has failed to appear in the 
action. Expenses of publication must be 
borne by the prevailing party (Sec. 13, Rule 
13). 
 
Jurisprudential Example: 
 
In one case, the CSC Decision was snet via 
registered mail and the registry return receipt 
bore the notation “refused to accept 06-14-
16.” Petitioner claimed she never received 
this decision and only learned of it on March 
8, 2017 when the COA furnished her a copy 
attached to a Notice of Suspension. On 
March 16, 2017, she filed an appeal before 
the CSC. The CSC dismissed her appeal as 
out of time, reckoning the 15-day period from 
June 14, 2016.  
 
The Supreme Court ruled that petitioner’s 
appeal was not filed out of time. The registry 
return receipt alone is insufficient proof 
of service by registered mail under Rule 
13, Section 13 of the Rules of Court. Both the 
registry receipt and the affidavit of the 
mailing officer or postmaster are required to 
establish valid service. While disputable 
presumptions exist that official duty has been 
regularly performed and that a mailed letter 
was received in the ordinary course of mail, 
these 
presumptions 
yield 
to 
contrary 
evidence. (★Labastida v. Quires, G.R. No. 
251903, January 27, 2025, as penned by J. 
Gaerlan) 
 
 
a. Efficient Use of Paper Rule – A.M. 
No. 11-9-4-SC 
 
Prescribed Format 
 
Single space with one and-a-half space 
between 
paragraphs, 
using 
an 
easily 
readable font style of the party’s choice, of 
14-size font, and on a 13-inch by 8.5- inch 
white bond paper.   
 
Coverage of Format Requirement 
 
1. All pleadings, motions and similar papers 
intended for the court and quasi-judicial 
body’s consideration and action;  
 
2. All decisions, resolutions and orders 
issued by courts and quasi-judicial bodies 
under the administrative supervision of the 
Supreme Court;  
 
3. Reports submitted to the courts and 
transcripts of stenographic notes (Sec. 3, 
A.M. No. 11-9-4-SC).

Margins and Prints  
 
The parties shall maintain the following 
margins on all court-bound papers: a left 
hand margin of 1.5 inches from the edge; an 
upper margin of 1.2 inches from the edge; a 
right hand margin of 1.0 inch from the edge; 
and a lower margin of 1.0 inch from the edge. 
Every page must be consecutively numbered  
(Sec. 4, A.M. No. 11-9-4-SC). 
 
b. Electronic Filing and Service – A.M. 
No. 10-3-7-SC; A.M. No. 11-9-4-SC 
 
Electronic Service 
 
May be done only in addition to the four 
modes of service in the case of judgments, 
final orders, and resolutions as dictated by 
Sec. 13, Rule 13.  
 
Electronic service cannot replace these 
modes of service, and may only supplement 
the same. 
 
 
F. SUMMONS – RULE 14 
 
The writ by which the defendant is notified of 
the action brought against him or her 
(Republic vs. Domingo, G.R. No. 175299, 
September 14, 2011) 
 
Two-fold purpose 
 
1. To acquire jurisdiction over the person of 
the defendant and 
 
2. To notify the defendant that an action has 
been commenced so that he may be given 
an opportunity to be heard on the claim 
against him. (Borlongan vs. Banco De 
Oro, G.R. No. 217617, April 5, 2017) 
1. ISSUANCE; CONTENTS 
 
Upon the filing of the complaint and the 
payment of the requisite legal fees, the clerk 
of 
court 
shall 
forthwith 
ISSUE 
the 
corresponding summons to the defendants.  
 
Contents 
 
The summons shall be directed to the 
defendant, signed by the clerk of court under 
seal and contain: 
 
(a) the name of the court and the names of 
the parties to the action;  
 
(b) a direction that the defendant answer 
within the time fixed by these Rules;  
 
c) a notice that unless the defendant so 
answers plaintiff will take judgment by default 
and may be granted the relief applied for. 
 
A copy of the complaint and order for 
appointment of guardian ad litem if any, shall 
be attached to the original and each copy of 
the summons. 
 
a. By Whom Issued 
 
Clerk of court issues the summons 
 
Unless the complaint is on its face 
dismissible under Section 1, Rule 9 of the 
Rules of Court, the court shall, within 5 
calendar days from receipt of the initiatory 
pleading and proof of payment of the 
requisite legal fees, direct the clerk of court 
to issue the corresponding summons to the 
defendants. 
 
b. Purpose in Relation to Actions In 
Personam, In Rem, and Quasi In Rem 
 
In personam 
In rem and quasi in 
rem

over the person of the

process.

2. SERVICE 
 
a. By Whom Made 
 
1. The sheriff 
2. His or her deputy 
3. Other proper court officer, or  
4. The plaintiff together with the sheriff 
 
GR: The list above is EXCLUSIVE 
 
XPN: Counsel may be deputized by the 
court to serve summons on his client where: 
 
a) Summons is improperly served, and 
b) A lawyer makes a special appearance 
on behalf of the defendant to question 
the validity of service of summons. 
 
b. Modes 
 
i. Personal 
 
1. Handing in person - By handing a copy 
to the defendant in person and informing the 
defendant that he or she is being served, or 
 
2. Tender - If he or she refuses to receive 
and sign for it, by leaving the summons within 
the view and in the presence of the 
defendant 
 
The sheriff must still inform the defendant 
that he or she is being served. If he refused 
to receive the summon, the sheriff shall leave 
the summons within the view and in the 
presence of the defendant. (Rule 14, Sec. 5) 
 
ii. Substituted 
 
Substituted service may be availed of when 
for justifiable reasons, the defendant 
cannot be served personally after at least 3 
attempts on 2 different dates (Manotoc v. 
CA, 499 SCRA 21 (2006). 
 


<!-- PAGE 81 -->

 
 
69 
Note: The attempts must be done within the 
30 calendar day period provided for the 
completion of service of summons. (Sec. 20, 
Rule 14) 
 
1. By leaving copies of the summons at the 
defendant's residence to a person at least 
eighteen (18) years of age and of sufficient 
discretion residing therein; 
 
To be of sufficient discretion, a person 
must know how to read and understand 
English to comprehend the import of the 
summons, and fully realize the need to 
deliver the summons and complaint to 
the defendant at the earliest possible 
time for the person to take appropriate 
action. 
 
2. By leaving copies of the summons at the 
defendant's office or regular place of 
business with some competent person in 
charge thereof.  
 
A competent person includes, but is not 
limited to, one who customarily receives 
correspondences for the defendant;  
 
Examples: President or manager; such 
individual 
must 
have 
sufficient 
knowledge to understand the obligation 
of the defendant in the summons, its 
importance, and the prejudicial effects 
arising from inaction on the summons 
(Prudential Bank v. Magdamit, G.R. No. 
183795 (2014).  
 
3. By leaving copies of the summons, if 
refused entry upon making his or her 
authority and purpose known, with any of the 
officers of the homeowners' association or 
condominium 
corporation, 
or 
its 
chief 
security officer in charge of the community or 
the building where the defendant may be 
found  
 
If the defendant voluntarily prevented the 
service of summons, it is deemed served.  
 
In the case of Remelita Robinson vs. 
Celita Miralles, G.R. No. 163584 (2006), 
the security guard was instructed to 
prevent the Sheriff from entering Alabang 
Hills twice. It was then impossible for the 
Sheriff to effect personal or substituted 
service of summons. Considering her 
strict instruction to the security guard, 
she must bear its consequences. Thus, it 
was held that the summons has been 
properly served upon and that it has 
acquired jurisdiction over her. 
 
4. By sending an electronic mail to the 
defendant's electronic mail address, if 
allowed by the court.

iii. Extraterritorial 
 
Extraterritorial Service; When allowed 
 
1. When the defendant does not reside and 
is not found in the Philippines, AND  
 
2. The action: 
 
a. Affects the personal status of the 
plaintiff, OR 
b. Relates to, or the subject of which is, 
property within the Philippines, in which 
the defendant has or claims a lien or 
interest, actual or contingent, or  
c. In which the relief demanded consists, 
wholly or in part, in excluding the 
defendant from any interest therein, 
OR  
d. The property of the defendant has been 
attached within the Philippines (Sec. 
17, Rule 14). 
 
As a rule, when the defendant does not 
reside and is not found in the Philippines, 
Philippine courts cannot try any case 
against 
him/her 
because 
of 
the 
impossibility of acquiring jurisdiction 
over 
his/her 
person 
unless 
such 
defendant voluntarily appears in court. 
But when the case is one of actions in rem or 
quasi in rem enumerated in Section 15, Rule 
14 of the Rules of Court, Philippine courts 
have jurisdiction to hear and decide the case. 
In such actions, Philippine courts have 
jurisdiction over the res, and jurisdiction over 
the person of the non-resident defendant is 
not essential, although summons must still 
be served upon the defendant in order to 
satisfy the due process requirements. In 
such instance, extraterritorial service of 
summons 
can 
be 
made 
upon 
the 
defendant. (★Solis v. Laynes, G.R. No. 
235099, March 29, 2023, as penned by J. 
Gaerlan) 
 
 
(a) 
Hague 
Service 
Convention; 
Administrative Order [A.O.] No. 251-
2020 
 
Scope of guidelines 
 
The guidelines govern the operation and 
implementation of the Hague Service 
Convention in the Philippines, insofar as 
they concern judicial documents in civil or 
commercial matters. 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 83 -->

 
 
71 
Application 
of 
Hague 
Service 
Convention 
 
The Hague Service Convention shall 
apply in the Philippines, provided the 
following conditions are present: 
 
a. A document is to be transmitted from 
one State Party for service to another 
State Party; 
 
b. The address of the intended recipient in 
the receiving State Party is known; 
 
c. The document to be served is a judicial 
document; and 
 
d. The document to be served relates to a 
civil or commercial matter. 
 
Grounds for objecting requests 
 
The Office of the Court Administrator may 
decline the request for service if it does 
not comply with the provisions of the 
Hague Service Convention, or when 
compliance with the request would 
infringe upon its sovereignty or security. 
 
Requests for Extraterritorial Service of 
Judicial Documents from Philippines 
to Other State Parties (Outbound 
Requests for Service) 
 
Upon motion for leave of court of a party 
in a civil or commercial proceeding, the 
court 
shall 
determine 
whether 
extraterritorial service through the Hague 
Service Convention is necessary, in 
accordance with Rules 13 and 14 of the 
Rules of Court, as amended. The motion 
shall be accompanied, in duplicate, by the 
following documents: 
 
a. A copy of the Model Form, including the 
Request, 
Certificate, 
Summary 
of 
Documents to be Served, and Warning; 
 
b. The original documents to be served or 
certified true copies thereof, including all 
annexes; 
 
c. Certified translations of the Model Form 
and all accompanying documents, where 
necessary; 
 
d. An undertaking to pay in full any fees 
associated with the service of the 
documents; and 
 
e. 
Any 
other 
requirements 
of 
the 
Requested State, taking into account its 
reservations, 
declarations 
and 
notifications, which may be found in the 
HCCH website. 
 
Court’s action on the request for 
extraterritorial service 
 
If the court finds that extraterritorial 
service 
under 
the 
Hague 
Service 
Convention is warranted, it shall issue an 
Order to that effect. The Order shall 
include a directive to the requesting party 
to procure and submit a prepaid courier 
pouch which shall be used for the 
transmission of documents from the court 
to the Central Authority of the Requested 
State. 
 
The Judge, in the case of lower courts, or 
the Justice or the Clerk of Court, in the 
case of collegiate courts, as forwarding 
authorities, shall accomplish and sign the 
Request using the Model Form, check the 
completeness of documents, and ensure 
compliance with the requirements of the 
Hague Service Convention and that of the 
Requested State. 
 
Transmission of documents abroad 
 
Once all the requirements are submitted 
by the party requesting the extraterritorial 
service through the Hague Service 
Convention, the court shall coordinate 
with 
the 
Central 
Authority 
of 
the 
Requested 
State 
and 
transmit 
the

3. VOLUNTARY APPEARANCE 
 
 
 
 
GR: A trial court acquires jurisdiction over the 
person of the defendant by service of 
summons.

defendant shall be deemed a voluntary 
appearance (Sec. 23, Rule 14). 
 
Note: Despite Sec. 23, Rule 14 mentioning

motion to dismiss, such still remains to be a 
prohibited motion under Sec. 12, Rule 15, 
as the ONLY allowable grounds for a motion 
to dismiss are lack of jurisdiction over the 
subject matter, litis pendencia, res judicata, 
and prescription.

G. MOTIONS – RULE 15 
 
A motion is any application for relief other 
than by a pleading (Sec. 1, Rule 15).   
 
Form of Motions 
 
GR: In writing  
 
The rules applicable to pleadings shall apply 
to written motions so far as concerns caption, 
designation, signature, and other matters of 
form (Sec. 11, Rule 15).  
 
XPNs: Oral Motions made in:  
 
1. Open court or  
 
2. The course of a hearing or trial  
 
Such 
motions 
should 
be 
immediately 
resolved in open court, after the adverse 
party is given the opportunity to argue his or 
her opposition. However, when the motion is 
based on facts not appearing on record, the 
court may conduct a hearing to:  
 
a. Hear 
the 
matter 
on 
affidavits 
or 
depositions presented by the parties, or  
b. The court may direct that the matter be 
heard wholly or partly on oral testimony 
or depositions (Sec. 2, Rule 15).   
 
Motion for leave 
 
A motion for leave to file a pleading or motion 
shall be accompanied by the pleading or 
motion sought to be admitted  (Sec. 10, Rule 
15) 
 
Contents of Motions  
 
a. Relief sought to be obtained  
 
b. Grounds upon which it is based, and  
 
c. With supporting affidavits and other papers 
if: 
 
i. Required by the ROC, or  
ii. Necessary to prove facts alleged therein 
(Sec. 3, Rule 15).

PLEADINGS

other than by a

Sec. 1).

Its purpose is to

not included in the

Its purpose is to submit 
a claim or defense for

2. LITIGIOUS AND NON-
LITIGIOUS MOTIONS 
 
Litigious 
Non-litigious 
One which requires 
the parties to be 
heard 
before 
a 
ruling on the motion 
is made by the court  
Motions which the court 
may act upon without 
prejudicing the rights of 
adverse parties. Such 
motions shall not be set 
for hearing and the court 
shall resolve the motion 
within 5 calendar days 
from 
receipt 
of 
the

LITIGIOUS MOTIONS 
 
a. Motion for bill of particulars;  
 
b. Motion to dismiss;  
 
Note: A Motion to Dismiss should be 
resolved within 15 calendar days from the 
filing of the opposition to the motion to 
dismiss (Sec. 5(c), Rule 15). Therefore, 
this clearly repeals Secs. 2 and 3, Rule 16 
of the old Rules of Court on hearing and 
resolution of a motion to dismiss.  
 
c. Motion for new trial;  
 
d. Motion for reconsideration;  
 
e. Motion for execution pending appeal; 
 
Period to file an opposition 
 
The period to file an opposition would be 5 
calendar days from the receipt of the litigious 
motion. The court shall then resolve the 
motion within 15 calendar days from receipt 
of the opposition or upon expiration of the 
period to file such opposition.  
 
No other submissions, other than the 
opposition, shall be considered by the court 
in resolving the motion (Sec. 5(c), Rule 15).  
 
Hearing on Litigious Motions 
 
The court may call for a hearing if deemed 
necessary for the motion’s resolution and 
send notice to all parties concerned, 
specifying the time and date of the hearing. 
(Sec. 6, Rule 15)  
 
The allowance for hearing only applies to 
litigious motions, since non-litigious motions 
cannot be set for hearing (Sec. 4, Rule 15). 
 
NON-LITIGIOUS MOTIONS 
 
a. Motion for issuance of an alias summons;  
 
b. Motion for extension to file an answer;  
 
c. Motion for postponement;  
 
d. Motion for the issuance of a writ of 
execution;  
 
e. Motion for the issuance of an alias writ of 
execution  
 
f. Motion for the issuance of a writ of 
possession;  
g. Motion for the issuance of an order 
directing the sheriff to execute the final 
certificate of sale; and  
 
h. Other smilar motions (Sec. 4, Rule 15).

H. DISMISSAL AND DEFAULT 
 
1. DISMISSAL UPON NOTICE BY 
PLAINTIFF; TWO-DISMISSAL 
RULE – RULE 17, SEC. 1 
 
GR: Dismissal is WITHOUT prejudice 
XPNs: Otherwise stated in the notice  
 
A notice operates as an adjudication upon 
the merits when filed by a plaintiff who has 
once dismissed in a competent court an 
action based on or including the same claim 
(Sec. 1, Rule 17).   
 
A complaint may be dismissed by the plaintiff 
by filing a notice of dismissal at any time 
BEFORE SERVICE of: 
 
a. The answer, or  
 
b. A motion for summary judgment Upon 
such notice being filed, the court shall 
issue an order confirming the dismissal 
(Sec. 1, Rule 17). 
 
Note: A court order is required to confirm a 
dismissal, hence, it is not automatic. 
Moreover, it is not the order confirming the 
dismissal which operates to dismiss the 
complaint. It merely confirms the dismissal 
already effected by the filing of the notice. 
 
 
2. DISMISSAL UPON MOTION BY 
PLAINTIFF; EFFECT ON EXISTING 
COUNTERCLAIM – RULE 17, SEC. 
2 
 
GR: Dismissal is WITHOUT prejudice 
XPNs: Otherwise specified in the order (Sec. 
2, Rule 17) 


<!-- PAGE 90 -->

 
 
78 
 
Effect of the dismissal on the defendant’s 
counterclaim 
 
Dismissal is without prejudice to the right of 
the defendant to prosecute his counterclaim 
in the same or in a separate action (Sec. 3, 
Rule 17). 
 
The counterclaim is not dismissed, whether it 
is a compulsory or a permissive counterclaim 
because the rule makes no distinction. 
 
Dismissal which have an effect of an 
adjudication on the merits  
 
Two-dismissal Rule 
 
The notice of dismissal operates as an 
adjudication upon the merits (Sec. 1, Rule 
17). 
 
Applies when the plaintiff has: 
 
1. A twice dismissed action 
2. Based on or including the same claim 
3. In a court of competent jurisdiction 
 
To simplify, under the Two-Dismissal Rule, 
when a plaintiff voluntarily dismisses the 
same claim TWICE, the second dismissal 
operates as an adjudication upon the 
merits.This means the dismissal is now with 
prejudice, and Juan cannot refile the case a 
third time. 
 
 
3. DISMISSAL DUE TO FAULT OF 
PLAINTIFF – RULE 17, SEC. 3 
 
 
GR: Dismissal is WITH prejudice 
 
XPN:  Otherwise declared by the court (Sec. 
3, Rule 17).  
 
The complaint may be dismissed upon 
motion of the defendant or upon the court’s 
own motion if, for no justifiable cause, the 
plaintiff:  
 
1. Fails to appear on the date of the 
presentation of his evidence in chief on the 
complaint 
 
2. Fails to prosecute his action for an 
unreasonable length of time, also called as 
non-prosequitur. 
 
3. Fails to comply with the ROC or any court 
order (Sec. 3, Rule 17).   
 
Note on No. 3: The plaintiff’s failure to comply 
with the order of the court to serve summons 
shall cause the dismissal of the initiatory 
pleading without prejudice. This rule is an 
exception to the general rule that dismissal 
due to failure to comply with the order of the 
court shall cause dismissal with prejudice. 
 
Effect of the dismissal on the defendant’s 
counterclaim 
 
Dismissal is without prejudice to the right of 
the defendant to prosecute his counterclaim 
in the same or in a separate action (Sec. 3, 
Rule 17). 
 
The counterclaim is not dismissed, whether it 
is a compulsory or a permissive counterclaim 
because the rule makes no distinction.

5. DEFAULT 
 
Nature of default 
 
Default is a procedural concept that occurs 
when the defending party fails to file his 
answer within the reglementary period. A 
declaration or order of default is issued as a 
punishment for unnecessary delay in joining 
issues. 
 
Instances when a party may be declared 
in default 
 
1) Defendant who fails to answer a 
complaint within the reglementary period 
XPNs: 
 
(a) In an amended complaint – an answer 
earlier filed may serve as the answer 
to the amended complaint if no new 
answer is filed (Rule 11, Sec. 3) 
(b) In a supplemental complaint – an 
answer to the complaint shall serve as 
the answer to the supplemental 
complaint if no new or supplemental 
answer is filed (Rule 11, Sec. 7) 
 
2) Defendant who fails to answer a 
compulsory counterclaim 
 
XPNs: 
 
(a) A counterclaim need not be answered 
where the answer would be a 
repetition of the allegations in the 
complaint 
(b) Where the issues raised in the 
counterclaim are inseparable from 
those 
posed 
in 
the 
complaint 
(Sarmiento v. Juan, G.R. No. L-56605 
January 28, 1983) or where the issues 
raised in the counterclaim are deemed 
automatically joined by the allegations 
in the complaint 
 
3) Defendant who fails to answer a 
permissive 
counterclaim 
within 
the 
reglementary period 
 
4) Defendant who fails to answer a cross-
claim within the reglementary period 
 
5) Defendant who fails to answer third 
(fourth, etc) party complaint within the 
reglementary period. 
 
Requisites for a declaration of a default 
 
(1) The court has validly Acquired jurisdiction 
over the person of the defending party either 
by service of summons or voluntary 
appearance (Sablas vs. Sablas, G.R. No. 
144568, July 3, 2007); 
 
(2) The defending party Fails to answer 
within the time allowed (Rule 9, Sec. 3); 
 
(3) The plaintiff or claiming party must file a 
Motion to declare the defendant in default 
(Rule 9, Sec. 3) 
 
(4) There must be Notice to the defending 
party of such motion (Rule 9, Sec. 3); 
 
(5) The claiming party must Prove that the 
defending party has failed to answer within 
the period provided by the Rules of Court 
(Sablas vs. Sablas, G.R. No. 144568, July 3, 
2007); and 
 


<!-- PAGE 92 -->

 
 
80 
(6) There must be a Hearing set on the 
motion to declare the defending party in 
default (Spouses de los Santos vs. Carpio, 
G.R. No. 153696, September 11, 2006) 
 
No Motu Propio Declaration of Default 
 
The rule on default requires the filing of a 
motion and notice of such motion to the 
defending party. It is not enough that the 
defendant fails to answer the complaint 
within the reglementary period. The trial court 
cannot motu proprio declare a defendant in 
default as the rules leave it up to the claiming 
party to protect his or its interests. (Sablas 
vs. Sablas, G.R. No. 144568, July 3, 2007) 
 
Dual Stages of Default: 
 
(1) Order of Default 
 
(2) Judgment by Default 
 
Order of Default 
 
It is an Order issued by the court granting the 
plaintiff’s motion at the start of the 
proceedings for failure of the defendant to file 
his 
responsive 
pleading 
within 
the 
reglementary period. 
 
Effect of Order of Default 
 
 To the Party in Default 
 
A party in default shall not take part in the 
trial; thus, he CANNOT: 
 
(a) Participate in the proceedings; 
(b) Present his defenses; 
(c) Adduce evidence on his behalf 
(d) Cross-examine the witnesses of the 
plaintiff; and 
(e) Object or refute evidence or motions filed 
against him 
 
Note: Nevertheless, the party in default is still 
entitled 
to 
notices 
of 
subsequent 
proceedings (Rule 9, Sec. 3[a]) 
 
A party in default may be cited as a witness 
by his co-defendants who have the standing 
and the right to present evidence which the 
former may provide. (Cavilivs. Florendo, 
G.R. No. 73039, October 9, 1987) 
 
 To the Claiming Party 
 
The court shall either: 
 
a. proceed to render judgment granting the 
claimant such relief as his pleading may 
warrant; OR,  
 
b. in its discretion, shall require the claimant 
to submit evidence. The reception of 
evidence may be delegated to the clerk of 
court (Rule 9, Sec. 3, 1st paragraph) 
 
Remedies of the Defaulting Party from an 
Order of Default 
 
1. File Verified Motion to Set Aside Order 
of Default [VMSAOD] (Sec. 3(b), Rule 9) at 
any time after notice of the Order and before 
the judgment 
 
The defaulting party must show: 
 
a) That his or her failure to answer was 
due to (FAMEN): 
(i) Fraud; 
(ii) Accident; 
(iii) Mistake; or 
(iv) Excusable Negligence; and 
 
b) That he or she has a meritorious 
defense 
 
Meritorious defense is a statement of 
the 
evidence 
which 
defendant 
intends to present if the motion is 
granted and which will warrant a 
reasonable belief that the result 
would probably be different if new trial 
is granted (Velayo-Fong vs. Sps. 
Velayo, G.R. No. 155488, December 
6, 2006). 
 
2. In case the VMSAOD is denied, file a 
motion for reconsideration 


<!-- PAGE 93 -->

 
 
81 
 
3. If MR is denied, file a petition for 
certiorari under Rule 65 if the trial court 
improperly declared a party in default, or 
even if the trial court properly declared a 
party in default, if grave abuse of discretion 
attended such declaration 
 
Note: the defaulting party cannot appeal from 
the Order of Default because such order is 
interlocutory in nature (Sitchon vs. Provincial 
Sheriff of Occidental Negros G.R. No. L- 
1853, February 27, 1948) 
 
Judgment of Default 
 
It is a judgment rendered by the court on the 
case after the defendant was declared in 
default. Such judgment is based on the 
plaintiff’s 
complaint 
or 
after 
receiving 
plaintiff’s evidence. (Rule 9, Sec. 3) 
 
GR: There can be no judgment by default it 
there is no order of default triggered by the 
failure of the defending party to file the 
Answer 
 
XPNs: 
 
a) If a disobedient party refuses to obey an 
order requiring him to comply with the 
various modes of discovery (Rule 29, Sec. 
3[c]); 
 
(b) If a party or officer or managing agent of 
a party willfully fails to appear before the 
officer who is to take his deposition, or a party 
fails to serve answers to interrogatories

I. PRE-TRIAL – RULE 18 AND A.M. NO. 
03-1-09-SC 
 
Pre-trial is a procedural device intended to 
clarify and limit the basic issues between the 
parties and to take the trial of cases out of the 
realm of surprise and maneuvering. (Zaldivar 
vs. People, G.R. No. 197056, March 02, 
2016) 
 
 
    1.  WHEN CONDUCTED   
 
After the last pleading has been served and 
filed, if shall be the duty of the plaintiff to 
promptly move ex parte that the case be set 
for pre-trial. (Sec 1, Rule 18) 
 
 
    2.  NATURE AND PURPOSE   
 
Civil Cases. Pre-trial is mandatory and 
should be terminated promptly (Sec. 2, Rule 
18).  
 
Criminal Cases. Pre-trial is mandatory in 
cases cognizable by: 
 
a) Sandiganbayan 
 
b) Regional Trial Courts (RTC) 
 
c) Metropolitan Trial Courts (MeTC), 
Municipal 
Trial 
Courts 
in 
Cities 
(MTCC), Municipal Trial Courts (MTC), 
and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts 
(MCTC). 
 
Pre-trial is also mandatory in both criminal 
and civil cases under the Rule on Summary 
Procedure. 
 
Scope of Court’s Authority 
 
The court's authority during pre-trial is 
confined to determining whether judgment 
on the pleadings or a summary judgment is 
proper. (M. De Leon, Remedial Law 
Reviewer Primer, 2021 Edition, p. 175) 
 
Purpose of Pre-trial: AI(SA) Wit CP 
 
 
 
1. Possibility of an amicable settlement or of 
a submission to alternative modes of dispute 
resolution  
 
2. Simplification of the issues  
 
3. Possibility of obtaining stipulations or

    3.  NOTICE OF PRE-TRIAL 
 
After the last responsive pleading has been 
served and filed, the branch clerk of court 
shall issue a Notice of Pre-Trial within five (5) 
calendar days from filing. (Rule 18, Sec. 1)

5.  PRE-TRIAL BRIEF; EFFECTS OF 
FAILURE TO FILE   
 
Filing of Pre-Trial Brief 
 
The parties shall file with the court and serve 
on the adverse party their respective pre-trial 
briefs in such a manner as to ensure receipt 
at least three (3) calendar days before the 
date of the pre-trial. (Rule 18, Sec. 6) 
 
Contents of a Pre-Trial Brief 
 
1. A concise statement of the case and the 
reliefs prayed for. 
2. A summary of admitted facts and 
proposed stipulation of facts. 
3. The main factual and legal issues to be 
tried or resolved. 
4. The propriety of referral of factual issues 
to commissioners. 
5. The documents or other object evidence 
to be marked, stating the purpose 
thereof. 
6. The names of the witnesses and the 
summary of their respective testimonies. 
7. A brief statement of points of law and 
citation of authorities. (Rule 18, Sec. 6) 
 
Effect of Failure to File a Pre-Trial Brief 
 
Failure to file a pre-trial brief has the same 
effect as failure to appear at the pre-trial. 
(Eubanas v. Chuanico, G.R. No. 218772 
[Notice], March 29, 2022) 
 
Consequences 
 
 No documentary evidence shall be 
presented or offered during the trial other 
than those identified and pre-marked 
during the pre-trial, unless allowed by the 
court for good cause. 
 "Good 
cause" 
is 
defined 
as 
any 
substantial reason that affords a legal 
excuse.

Precedent 
 
The appearance of counsel at the pre-trial 
conference, without a pre-trial brief and 
supported only by bare allegations of 
representation, is insufficient. The trial court 
may reject such an appearance and proceed 
to allow the opposing party to present 
evidence ex parte.

1. COURT-ANNEXED MEDIATION 
(CAM) 
 
After pre-trial and, after issues are joined, the 
court shall refer the parties for mandatory 
court annexed mediation. The period for

If no settlement was reached in CAM, the 
case may further be referred to undergo JDR 
if the judge of the court to which the case was 
originally raffled is convinced that settlement 
is still possible. (Rule 18, Sec. 9)

The JDR shall be conducted within a non

J. INTERVENTION – RULE 19 
 
A proceeding in a suit or an action by which 
a third person is permitted by the court to 
make himself a party, either:  
 
1. Joining plaintiff in claiming what is sought 
by the complaint 
 
2. Uniting with defendant in resisting the 
claims of the plaintiff, or  
 
3. Demanding something adverse to both of 
them (Gutierrez v. Villegas, G.R. No. L-
11848, 1962) 
 
It is never an independent action, but is 
ancillary and supplemental to the existing 
action. 
 
Purpose 
 
To enable a third party to protect or preserve 
his/her right or interest which may be 
affected by such proceedings. (Asia's 
Emerging Dragon Corporation vs. DOTC, 
G.R. No. 169914, 2008) It cannot alter the 
nature of the action and the issues already 
joined (Castro v. David, 100 Phil 454, 1956). 
 
When filed 
 
A motion for leave to intervene filed at any 
time before rendition of judgment by the trial 
court (Sec. 2, Rule 19). 
 
As a litigious motion, the court shall resolve 
the motion within 15 calendar days from 
receipt of the opposition or upon expiration of 
the period to file such opposition. The period 
to file an opposition would be 5 calendar 
days from the receipt of such opposition 
(Sec. 5, Rule 19). 
 
Requisites 
 
1. A motion for leave to intervene filed at any 
time before rendition of judgment by the trial 
court [Sec. 2, Rule 19]. 
 
2. A legal interest:  
 
a. In the matter in litigation;  
b. In the success of either of the parties;  
c. An interest against both; or  
d. So situated as to be adversely affected 
by a distribution or other disposition of 
property in the custody of the court or 
of an officer thereof.  
 
3. Intervention will not unduly delay or 
prejudice the adjudication of rights of the 
original parties.  
 
4. Intervenor’s rights may not be fully 
protected in a separate proceeding (Sec. 1, 
Rule 19) 
 
Remedy if the Motion for Intervention is 
denied 
 
1. Appeal 
 


<!-- PAGE 99 -->

 
 
87 
2. Mandamus (If there is grave abuse of 
discretion and there is no other plain, speedy 
and adequate remedy) 
 
Remedy if the Motion for Intervention is 
granted 
 
Certiorari and Prohibition in case of improper 
granting of Motion for Intervention. 
 
 
K. CALENDAR OF CASES – RULE 20 
 
The clerk of court, under the direct 
supervision of the judge, shall keep a 
calendar of cases for pre-trial, for trial, those 
whose trials were adjourned or postponed, 
and those with motions to set for hearing. 
Preference shall be given to habeas corpus 
cases, election cases, special civil actions, 
and those so required by law. 
 
 
L. SUBPOENA – RULE 21 
 
Subpoena is a process directed to a person 
requiring him or her to attend and to testify at 
the hearing or the trial of an action, or at any 
investigation 
conducted 
by 
competent 
authority, or for the taking of his deposition 
(Rule 21, Sec. 1). 
 
It must be made so as to allow the witness a 
reasonable time for preparation and travel to 
the place of attendance (Sec. 6, Rule 21). 
 
1. Subpoena Ad Testificandum 
 
A process directed to a person requiring him 
to attend and to testify at the hearing or the 
trial of an action, or at any investigation 
conducted by competent authority or for the 
taking of his deposition (Sec. 1, Rule 21) 
 
2. Subpoena Duces Tecum  
 
A process directed to a person requiring him 
to bring with him books, documents, or other 
things under his control (Sec. 1, Rule 21).  
 
The subpoena duces tecum is, in all 
respects, like the ordinary subpoena ad 
testificandum, with the exception that it 
concludes with an injunction that the witness 
shall bring with him and produce at the 
examination the books, documents, or things 
described in the subpoena (see Sec. 1, Rule 
21). 
 
Service of Subpoena 
 
Service of a subpoena shall be made in the 
same manner as personal or substituted 
service of summons (Sec. 6, Rule 21) 
 
Effect of Failure to Obey Subpoena 
 
Any person who fails, without adequate 
cause, to obey a subpoena served upon him 
or her:  
 
a. Contempt of court who issued the 
subpoena, or ; 
 
b. Punishment in accordance with the 
applicable law or rule if the subpoena 
was not issued by a court (Sec. 9, Rule 
21).

M. COMPUTATION OF TIME – RULE 22 
 
Manner of Computing Time 
 
In computing any period of time prescribed 
or allowed by these Rules, or by order of the 
court, or by any applicable statute, the 
following rule shall be observed: 
 
(1) The day of the act or event from which the 
designated period of time begins to run is to 
be excluded and the date of performance 
included. 
 
(2) If the last day of the period falls on 
Saturday, a Sunday, or a legal holiday in the 
place where the court sits, the time shall not 
run until the next working day (Rule 22, Sec. 
1). 
 
Article 13 of the Civil Code Applicable 
 
When the law speaks of years, months, 
days or nights, it shall be understood that: 
 
 Years are of 365 days each; 
 Months are of 30 days; 
 Days are of 24 hours; and 
 Nights are from sunset to sunrise. 
 
If months are designated by their name, they 
shall be computed by the number of days 
which they respectively have. 
 
 
 
Clarification provided in A.M. 00-2-14-SC; 
Where the due date falls on a Saturday, 
Sunday or Holiday 
 
The clarification provided in A.M. 00-2-14-C 
actually covers a situation where the due 
date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or holiday. 
Precisely, what such clarification wanted to 
address is the erroneous claim that “the 
period of extention” in such a case “is to be 
reckoned from the next working day and not 
from the original expiration of the period.” 
 
The 
correct 
rule, 
according 
to 
the 
clarification, is that “any extension of time to 
file the required pleading should be counted 
from the expiration of the period regardless 
of the fact that said due date is a Saturday, 
Sunday, or holiday.” 
 
For example, if a pleading is due on August 
10 and this happens to be a Saturday, the 
time for filing it shall not run, applying Section 
1 of Rule 21, on August 10 (Saturday) nor on 
July 11 (Sunday) but will resume to run on 
the next working day, which is August 12 
(Monday). The pleading will then be due on 
the latter date. If the period is extended by 10 
days, such 10 days will be counted, not from 
August 12 (Monday) but from the original due 
date, August 10 (Saturday) "regardless of the 
fact that said due date is a Saturday." 
Consequently, the new due date will be 10 
days from July 10 or precisely on July 20. 
(Reinier Pacific International Shipping, Inc. v. 
Guevarra, G.R. No. 157020, June 19, 2013) 
 
 
N. MODES OF DISCOVERY – RULES 23-29 
 
Different modes of discovery under the 
Rules of Court 
 
1. Depositions pending action (Rule 23) 
2. Depositions before action or pending 
appeal (Rule 24) 
3. Interrogatories to parties (Rule 25) 
4. Admission by adverse party (Rule 26) 


<!-- PAGE 101 -->

 
 
89 
5. Production or inspection of documents, 
or things (Rule 27)  
6. Physical and mental examination of 
persons (Rule 28) 
 
Note: Rule 29 is the Refusal to Comply with 
the Modes of Discovery 
 
Application 
 
The application of the rules on modes of 
discovery rests upon the sound discretion of 
the court. In the same vein, the determination 
of the sanction to be imposed upon a party 
who fails to comply with the modes of 
discovery rests on the same sound judicial 
discretion. It is the duty of the courts to 
examine thoroughly the circumstances of 
each case and to determine the applicability 
of the modes of discovery, bearing always in 
mind the aim to attain an expeditious 
administration of justice (Lanada vs. CA, 
G.R. No. 102390, February 1, 2002, 375 
SCRA 543;; Limos vs. Spouses Odones, 
G.R. No. 186979, August 11, 2010) 
 
DEPOSITIONS 
 
It is the taking of testimony of any person, 
whether he be a party or not, but at the 
instance of a party to the action. This 
testimony is taken out of court.  
 
Deposition de benne esse and 
Deposition in perpetuam rei memoriam.

Against whom depositions may be used 
 
1. Against any part who was present 
2. Against a party who was present but 
notified 
 
Scope of examination of the deponent 
 
A deponent may be examined regarding 
any matter which is: 
 
1. Relevant to the subject of the pending 
action 
2. Not privileged (Sec. 2, Rule 23) 
3. Not restricted by an order of the court to 
protect the parties and deponents or to 
limit the examination (Secs. 16 & 18, 
Rule 23) 
 
Before whom depositions are taken 
 
A. Within the PH, depositions may be taken 
before any judge, notary public, or the 
person stipulated by the parties in writing.  
(Sec. 10, Rule 23) 
 
B. Outside the PH or in a foreign state, 
depositions may be taken: 
 
a. On notice before a secretary or 
embassy or legation, consul general, 
consul, vice consul, or consular agent 
of the Republic of the PH 
b. Before such person or officer as may 
be appointed by commission or letters 
rogatory 
c. The person stipulated by the parties in 
writing.  (Sec. 11, Rule 23)

1. Contradicting 
or

2. Any purpose if the deponent is a party

b. The witness resides at a distance

Objection to the admissibility of a

Subject to the provisions of effect of errors 
and irregularities of the depositions  (Sec. 9, 
Rule 23), objections may be made at the trial 
or hearing to receiving in evidence any

which would require the exclusion of the

1.  DEPOSITIONS PENDING ACTION 
(RULE 23)   
 
Upon ex parte motion of a party, the 
testimony of any person, whether a party or 
not, may be taken, at the instance of any 
party, by deposition upon oral examination or 
written interrogatories. (Sec. 1, Rule 23) 
 
GR: Rule 23 is not applicable in criminal 
cases 
 
XPN: Compelling reason 
 
The Supreme Court permitted the taking of 
the testimony of Mary Jane Veloso, who was 
imprisoned 
in 
Indonesia, 
by 
way 
of 
deposition 
by 
written 
interrogatories. 
Although the rule on deposition by written 
interrogatories is inscribed under Rule 23 of 
the Rules on Civil Procedure, the Supreme 
Court held that it may be applied 
suppletorily in criminal proceedings so 
long as there is compelling reason. 
(People vs. Sergio, G.R. No. 240053, 2019) 
 
 
2.  DEPOSITIONS BEFORE ACTION OR 
PENDING APPEAL (RULE 24)   
 
To perpetuate one’s own testimony or that of 
another person. (Sec. 1, Rule 24) 
 
A person who desires to perpetuate his or 
her own testimony or that of another person 
regarding any matter that may be cognizable 
in any court of the Philippines, may file a 
verified petition in the court of the place of 
the residence of any expected adverse party.  
(Sec. 1, Rule 24). 
 
 
3.  INTERROGATORIES TO PARTIES 
(RULE 25)   
 
To elicit material and relevant facts from any 
adverse parties. (Sec. 1, Rule 25) 
 
Upon ex parte motion, any party desiring to 
elicit material and relevant facts from any 
adverse parties shall file and serve upon the 
latter written interrogatories to be answered 
by the party served or, if the party served is 
a public or private corporation or a 
partnership or association, by any officer 
thereof competent to testify in its behalf. 
(Sec. 1, Rule 25) 
 
Note: The interrogatories shall be answered 
fully in writing and shall be signed and sworn 
by the person making them (Sec. 2, Rule 25) 
Consequences of willful refusal to answer 
written interrogatories 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 103 -->

 
 
91 
Consequences of willful refusal to answer 
written interrogatories 
 
If a party or an officer or managing agent of 
a party willfully fails to appear before the 
officer who is to take his or her deposition, 
after being served with a proper notice, or 
fails to serve answers to interrogatories, the 
court on motion and notice, may: 
 
1. Strike out all or any part of any 
pleading of that party or 
2. Dismiss the action or proceeding or 
any part thereof, or 
3. Enter a judgment by default against 
that party, and in its discretion, order 
him or her to pay reasonable 
expenses incurred by the other, 
including attorney's fees. (Sec. 5, Rule 
29). 
 
 
4.  ADMISSION BY ADVERSE PARTY 
(RULE 26)   
 
A request for admission is not intended 
merely to reproduce or reiterate the 
allegations of the requesting party’s pleading 
but should set forth relevant evidentiary 
matters of fact, or documents described in 
and exhibited with the request, whose 
purpose is to establish said party’s cause of 
action or defense. (Fortunata v. Duque, G.R. 
No. 125383, 2002). 
 
Duty of the party against whom a request 
for admission is served 
 
The party to whom the request is directed 
shall file and serve upon the party requesting 
the admission a sworn statement either 
denying specifically the matters of which an 
admission is requested or setting forth in 
detail the reasons why he or she cannot 
truthfully either admit or deny those matters.  
(Sec. 2, Rule 26). 
 
Refusal to admit or serve a sworn denial 
 
If the party requesting the admissions 
thereafter proves the genuineness of such 
document or the truth of any such matter of 
fact, the court may, upon application, issue 
an order requiring the other party to pay him 
or her the reasonable expenses incurred in 
making such proof, including attorney's fees.  
(Sec. 4, Rule 29). 
 
Effect of a party’s failure to properly 
respond to a request for admission 
 
Each of the matters of which an admission is 
requested shall be deemed admitted.  (Sec. 
2, Rule 26) 
 
Admissions made by a party pursuant to 
a request CANNOT be used against him 
outside the pending action 
 
Any admission made by a party pursuant to 
such request is for the purpose of the 
pending action ONLY and shall not constitute 
an admission by him or her for any other 
purpose nor may the same be used against 
him or her in any other proceeding.  (Sec. 5, 
Rule 26) 
 
 
5.  PRODUCTION OR INSPECTION OF 
DOCUMENTS OR THINGS (RULE 27)   
 
In order to enable not only the parties, but 
also the court to discover all relevant and 
material facts in connection with the case 
pending before it. (Eagleridge v. Cameron 
Granville, G.R. No. 204700, 2013, citing 
Republic v. Sandiganbayan, 1991).

Subject of a production or inspection 
order 
 
Upon motion of any party showing good 
cause, the court in which an action is 
pending may: 
 
(a) Order any party to produce and permit the 
inspection 
and 
copying 
or 
photographing, by or on behalf of the 
moving party, of any designated: 
 
documents, papers, books, accounts, 
letters, photographs, objects or tangible 
things, not privileged, which are in his or 
her possession, custody or control; OR 
 
(b) Order any party to permit entry upon 
designated land or other property in his or

inspecting,

or

the 
property 
or 
any 
designated relevant object or operation 
thereon.  
 
The order shall specify the time, place and 
manner of making the inspection and taking 
copies and photographs, and may prescribe 
such terms and conditions as are just.

AND

Rule 28 contemplates a situation where the

proper judgment can be rendered. 
 
Requisites for the issuance of an order for 
the physical and mental examination of a

filed 
for

and

2. To produce documents

examination 
 
The court may make the following orders: 
 
1. The facts sought to be established by the

obtaining the order;

3. The striking out of pleadings or parts 
thereof 
 
4. That further proceedings be stayed until

default against the disobedient party; or 
 
6. In lieu of any of the foregoing or in addition 
thereto, the arrest of any party or agent of a 
party for disobeying its orders, except an 
order to submit a physical or mental 
examination.  (Sec. 3, Rule 29) 
 
Consequences where the party examined 
refuses to deliver a report upon request  
 
The court, on motion and notice, may make 
an order requiring delivery on such terms as 
are just, and if a physician fails or refuses to 
make such a report, the court may 
EXCLUDE his or her testimony if offered at 
the trial. (Sec. 3, Rule 28) 
 


<!-- PAGE 105 -->

 
 
93 
7.  CONSEQUENCES OF REFUSAL TO 
COMPLY WITH MODES OF DISCOVERY 
(RULE 29)   
 
Contempt of court in the refusal to comply 
with Modes of Discovery 
 
If a party or other witness refuses to be sworn 
or refuses to answer any question after being 
directed to do so by the court of the place 
where the deposition is being taken, the 
refusal may be considered as a contempt of 
that court. (Sec. 2, Rule 29) 
 
 
O. TRIAL – RULE 30 
 
A trial is a judicial process of investigating 
and determining the legal controversies, 
starting with the production of evidence by 
the plaintiff and ending with his closing 
argument. (Acosta v. People, G.R. No. L-
17427 July 31, 1962)  
 
1.  CONTINUOUS TRIAL   
 
Applicability 
 
The Revised Guidelines for Continuous Trial 
of Criminal Cases (Revised Guidelines) shall 
apply to:  
 
(1) All newly-filed criminal cases files 
before the:  
 
(a) First level courts  
(b) Second level courts  
(c) Sandiganbayan  
(d) Court of tax appeals  
 
(2) Pending criminal cases with respect to 
the rest of the proceedings  
 
Note: Shall not apply to cases under Rules 
on Summary Procedures 
 
Objectives 
 
(1) To protect and advance the constitutional 
right of persons to a speedy disposition of 
their criminal cases; 
 
(2) To reinforce and give teeth to the existing 
rules on criminal procedure and other special 
rules prescribing periods for court action and 
those which promote speedy disposition of 
criminal cases; and  
 
(3) To introduce innovations and best 
practices for the benefit of the parties. 
 
2. AJOURNMENTS AND 
POSTPONEMENTS   
 
A court may adjourn a trial from day to day, 
and to any stated time, as the expeditious 
and convenient transaction of business may 
require (Sec. 2, Rule 30). 
 
Note: 
The 
party 
who 
caused 
the 
postponement is warned that presentation of 
its evidence must be terminated on the 
remaining dates previously agreed upon. 
 
Limitations on the authority to adjourn  
 
GR: The court has no power to adjourn a trial 
for a period longer than 1 month for each 
adjournment; nor more than 3 months in all.  
 
XPN: When authorized in writing by the 
Court Administrator, Supreme Court (Sec. 2, 
Rule 30).  
 
Motion for Postponement; When allowed 
 
A motion for postponement may be allowed 
if it is based on: (G-Force-PI) 
 
1. Acts of God 


<!-- PAGE 106 -->

 
 
94 
2. Force Majeure; or 
3. Physical inability of the witness to 
appear and testify (Sec. 12(f). Rule 15)  
 
Note: Trial may no longer be postponed on 
the ground of absence of evidence. 
 
Requisites of a motion for postponement 
on the ground of illness of party or 
counsel 
 
1. A motion for postponement stating the 
ground relied upon must be filed 
 
2. The motion must be supported by an 
affidavit or sworn certification showing 
that: 
 
a. The presence of such party or counsel 
is indispensable; and 
 
b. The character of the illness is such as 
to 
render 
his 
non-attendance 
as 
excusable. (Sec. 3, Rule 30) 
 
Violation 
of 
the 
right 
to 
speedy 
disposition of cases 
 
It is doctrinal that in determining whether a 
party is denied the right to speedy 
disposition of cases, the following factors 
are considered and weighed:  
 
(1) length of delay;  
(2) the reasons for the delay;  
(3) the assertion or failure to assert such 
right by the accused; and  
(4) the prejudice caused by the delay.  
(★Former Municipal Mayor Helen C. De 
Castro 
v. 
COA, 
G.R. 
No. 
228595, 
September 22, 2020, as penned by J. 
Gaerlan)  
Agreed Statement of Facts 
 
The parties to any action may agree, in 
writing, upon the facts involved in the 
litigation, and submit the case for judgment 
on the facts agreed upon, without the 
introduction of evidence.  
 
If the parties agree only on some of the facts 
in issue, trial shall be held as to the disputed 
facts in such order as the court shall 
prescribe. (Sec. 7, Rule 30) 
Just take note of the order of trial in ordinary 
civil actions (Sec. 5, Rule 30) 
 
Reverse Trial 
 
The court may order a modification of the 
order of the trial for special reasons. (Sec. 5, 
Rule 30) 
 
Example: Where special defenses were 
pleaded, the plaintiff has every right to insist 
that it is for the defendant to come forward 
with evidence in support of his special 
defenses. (Yu v. Mapayo, G.R. No. L-29742, 
1972) 
 
3.  ORDER OF TRIAL   
 
 
GR: The presentation of evidence of all 
parties shall be terminated within 10 months 
or 300 calendar days.  
 
XPN: If there are no third (fourth-etc.)- party 
claim, counterclaim, or cross-claim, the

95 
presentation of evidence shall be terminated 
within 6 months or 180 calendar days. 
 
 
P. CONSOLIDATION OR SEVERANCE – 
RULE 31 
 
Consolidation 
is 
a 
procedural 
device, 
granted to the court as an aid in deciding how 
cases in its docket are to be tried, so that the 
business of the court may be dispatched 
expeditiously while providing justice to the 
parties (Republic v. Heirs of Oribello, G.R. 
No. 199501, 2013). 
 
There should be a common question of 
law or fact for there to be consolidation 
 
 
When actions involving a common question 
of law or fact are pending before the court, 
it may  
 
1. Order a joint hearing or trial of any or all 
the matters in issue in the actions;  
 
2. Order all the actions consolidated;  
 
3. Make such orders concerning proceedings 
therein as may tend to avoid unnecessary 
costs or delay.  
 
Consolidation 
of 
cases 
pending 
in 
different courts 
 
The rules do not distinguish between cases 
filed before the same branch or judge and 
those that are pending in different branches, 
or before different judges of the same court, 
in order that consolidation may be proper, as 
long as the cases involve the resolution 
of common questions of law or fact. 
(Active Wood Products v. CA, et al, G.R. No. 
86603, 1990). 
 
 
Kinds of consolidation  
 
a. Quasi-consolidation 
 
Where all, except one, of several actions are 
stayed until one is tried, in which case, the 
judgment in the one trial is conclusive as to 
others; not actually consolidation but referred 
to as such  
 
b. Actual consolidation 
 
Where several actions are combined into 
one, lose their separate identity, and become 
one single action in which judgment is 
rendered. 
 
c. Consolidation for Trial 
 
Where several actions are ordered to be tried 
together, but each retains its separate 
character, and requires the entry of separate 
judgment 
 
Separate trial 
 
The court, in furtherance of convenience 
or to avoid prejudice, may order a separate 
trial of any claim, cross-claim, counterclaim, 
or third-party complaint, or of any separate 
issue or of any number of claims, cross-
claims, counterclaims, third-party complaints 
or issues.  
 
 
Q. DEMURRER TO EVIDENCE – RULE 33 
 
After the plaintiff has completed the 
presentation of his evidence, the defendant 
may move for dismissal on the ground that 
upon the facts and the law the plaintiff has 
shown no right to relief. (Sec. 1, Rule 33) 
 


<!-- PAGE 108 -->

 
 
96 
A demurrer to evidence is an allowable 
litigious motion under Rule 15 (Motions). 
There must be proof of service to the other 
party who shall have 5 calendar days to file 
an opposition. The court shall then resolve 
the motion within 15 calendar days from the 
receipt of such opposition, or upon expiration 
of the period to file opposition. 
 
 
1. DENIAL 
 
a. Consequences 
 
The defendant shall have the right to present 
his evidence. 
 
b. Remedy 
 
The remedy is to proceed to trial. If the 
defendant loses, appeal the judgment and 
include in the assigned errors the denial of 
the demurrer to evidence. 
 
The order denying the demurrer to evidence 
shall NOT be the subject of an appeal or 
petition 
for 
certiorari, 
prohibition, 
or 
mandamus before judgment. 
 
 
2. CONSEQUENCES OF GRANT 
 
The case shall be dismissed. The grant of 
a demurrer is considered an adjudication 
on the merits. 
 
If the motion is granted but on appeal the 
order of dismissal is reversed, he or she 
shall be deemed to have waived his right to 
present evidence. 
 
Remedy: Appeal 
  
 
 
3. REVERSAL OF DEMURRER ON 
APPEAL 
 
If the appellate court reverses the trial court’s 
order granting the appeal, the appellate court 
should NOT remand the case for further 
proceedings but should render judgment 
on the basis of the evidence submitted by 
the plaintiff. 
 
 
R. JUDGMENTS AND FINAL ORDERS 
 
 
 
A final judgment or order is one that finally 
disposes of a case, leaving nothing more 
for the court to do with respect to it. It is 
an adjudication on the merits which, 
considering the evidence presented at the 
trial, declares categorically what the rights 
and obligations of the parties are; or it may 
be an order or judgment that dismisses an 
action. (Neypes v. CA, G.R. No. 141524, 
2005) 
 
Requisites of a Valid Judgment 
 
1. Court or tribunal must be clothed with 
authority to hear and determine the matter 
before it. 
 
2. Court must have jurisdiction over the 
parties and the subject matter.  
 
3. Parties must have been given an 
opportunity to adduce evidence on their 
behalf. 
 
4. Evidence must have been considered by 
the tribunal in deciding the case.  
 
5. Judgment must be in writing, personally 
and directly prepared by the judge  
 


<!-- PAGE 109 -->

 
 
97 
6. Judgment must state clearly the facts and 
the law upon which the decision is based, 
signed by the judge and filed with the clerk of 
court.  
 
 
1. HOW RENDERED – RULE 36 
 
Pronouncement of the judgment in open 
court does not constitute rendition of 
judgment. It is the filing of the signed decision 
with the Clerk of Court that constitutes 
rendition. Even if the judgment has already 
been put in writing and signed, it is still 
subject to amendment if it has not yet been 
filed with the COC (Ago v. CA, G.R. No. L-
17898, 1962).  
 
Period for rendition  
 
a. All cases filed must be decided or resolved 
by the Supreme Court within 24 months from 
the date of their submission for decision.  
 
b. Unless reduced by the SC, within 12 
months for lower collegiate courts and within 
3 months for all other lower courts. (Sec. 15, 
Art. VIII, Constitution). 
 
For easy reference: 
 
Extension 
 
An extension of the period may be set by the 
SC upon request by the judge concerned on 
account of heavy caseload or by other 
reasonable excuse. Without an extension, a 
delay in the disposition of cases is 
tantamount to gross inefficiency on the part 
of the judge  
 
Note: A case is deemed submitted for 
resolution upon the filing of the last pleading, 
brief or memorandum required by the Rules 
of Court or by the court. 
 
Entry of judgment 
 
 
The entry of judgment refers to the physical 
act performed by the clerk of court in entering 
the dispositive portion of the judgment in the 
book of entries of judgment after the same 
has become final and executory 
 
If no appeal, or motion for new trial or 
reconsideration is filed within the time 
provided in the Rules, the judgment or final 
order shall forthwith be entered by the clerk 
in the book of entries of judgments. (Sec. 2, 
Rule 36).  
 
Date of Finality is the date of Entry 
 
The date of finality of the judgment or final 
order shall be deemed to be the date of its 
entry [Sec. 2, Rule 36]. This is regardless of 
the date when the physical act of entry was 
done   
 
Finality 
of 
Judgment; 
Doctrine 
of 
Immutability of Judgment 
 
GR: A judgment that has acquired finality 
becomes immutable and unalterable, and 
may no longer be modified in any respect, 
even if the modification is meant to correct 
erroneous conclusions of fact and law, and 
whether it be made by the court that 
rendered it or by the Highest Court of the 
land (PNB v. Spouses Maranon, G.R. No. 
189316, 2013).  
 
XPNs:  
 
a. Correction of clerical errors  
b. Nunc pro tunc entries  
c. Whenever circumstances transpire after 
finality of the decision, rendering its 
execution unjust and inequitable. 


<!-- PAGE 110 -->

 
 
98 
d. In cases of special and exceptional 
nature, when it is necessary in the interest 
of justice to direct modification in order to 
harmonize 
the 
disposition 
with 
the 
prevailing circumstances.  
e. In case of void judgments 
f. Where there is a strong showing that a 
grave injustice would result from an 
application of the Rules. 
g. When there are grounds for annulment of 
judgment or petition for relief. 
 
Rationale of the Doctrine of Immutability 
of Judgment 
 
a. To avoid delay in the administration of 
justice, and procedurally to make orderly 
the discharge of judicial business, and  
b. To put an end to judicial controversies at 
the risk of occasional errors. 
 
 
2. JUDGMENT ON THE 
PLEADINGS – RULE 34 
 
Who can avail: PLAINTIFF or CLAIMANT 
ONLY 
 
When filed: Only after the answer is served 
 
Basis: Pleadings alone 
 
Grounds 
 
The court may, motu proprio or on motion 
by a party, direct judgment on such pleading 
when the ANSWER: 
 
 
a. Fails to tender an issue 
b. Admits the material allegations of 
the adverse party’s pleading (Sec. 1 
and 2, Rule 34). 
 
Meaning of “Fails to tender an issue” or 
“Admits the material allegations of the 
adverse party’s pleading” 
 
1. If it does not comply with the requirements 
for specific denial set out in Rule 8; 
 
To illustrate under Rule 8: 
 
You learned that a specific denial under 
oath is required to deny the genuineness 
and due execution of an actionable 
document. 
 
Now, if the defendant fails to specifically 
deny UNDER OATH, there is already a 
failure on his part to observe the 
requirements for specific denial. Because 
of this failure, the genuineness and due 
execution of an actionable shall be 
deemed ADMITTED. As a consequence, 
thereof, the plaintiff may now move for 
Judgment on the Pleadings. 
 
2. Admission of the material allegations of 
the adverse party’s pleadings not only where 
it expressly confesses the truthfulness 
thereof but also if it OMITS TO DEAL WITH 
THEM AT ALL. (Asian Construction Dev’t 
Corp. v. Sannaedle Co., Ltd, G.R. No. 
181676, 2014)

99 
Note: In order for the plaintiff to avail of Rule 
34, there should be an ANSWER. No 
answer, no judgment on the pleadings. 
Instead, the proper remedy is to move that 
the defendant be declared in DEFAULT. 
(Sec. 3, Rule 9) 
 
 
Judgment on the pleadings is NOT proper 
in the ff. cases:  
 
a. Declaration of Nullity of Marriage;  
b. Annulment of marriage; and  
c. Legal Separation. 
 
Note: In these cases, the material facts 
alleged in the complaint shall always be 
proved.  (Sec. 1, Rule 34) 
 
Action on Judgment on the Pleadings 
 
Any action of the court on a motion for 
judgment on the pleadings shall NOT be 
subject of an appeal or petition for certiorari, 
prohibition, or mandamus. 
 
In a proper case for judgment on the 
pleadings, there is no ostensible issue at 
all because of the failure of the defending 
party's answer to raise an issue. 
 
Here, Solar's opposition which is the 
functional equivalent of an answer did tender 
an issue in refutation of Central's factual 
allegations 
for 
cancellation 
of 
Solar's 
annotation of adverse claim. As issues arise 
from these affirmative defenses, this Court 
rules that a judgment on the pleadings is 
improper and unwarranted in this case. 
(Central Realty V. Solar Resources, GR No. 
229408)

2. Accident 
 
An unforeseen and unintended injurious

3. Mistake

Jurisprudential Example on MNT 
 
It is settled that a defendant, who discovered 
the default order after judgment has been 
rendered but before the same has become 
final and executory, may file a motion for new 
trial under Section 1(a) of Rule 37 of the 
Rules of Court, which was what Marivic 
precisely did in the instant case. It is through 
her Motion for New Trial that she averred the 
improper service of summons upon her due 
to the extrinsic fraud perpetrated by 
Salvador. Despite her meritorious grounds, 
however, the RTC denied Marivic’s Motion 
for New Trial and sustained the order of 
default against her. 
 
On this score, it has been held that fraud as 
a ground for new trial refers to a fraud 
committed to the unsuccessful party by the 
opponent preventing the former from fully 
exhibiting his/her case by keeping him/her 
away from court, a false promise of a 
compromise; or where the defendant never 
had knowledge of the suit, being kept in 
ignorance by the acts of the plaintiff; or when 
an attorney fraudulently or without authority 
connives at his defeat. 
 
Evidently, Marivic did not know of the case 
against her because Salvador indicated an 
incorrect address in the complaint, which 
address he also utilized in the defective 
extraterritorial service of summons. In this 
light, it cannot be gainsaid that while Marivic 
had been notified of the case before the RTC 
(as a result of her voluntary appearance), 
she was nonetheless deprived of the 
opportunity to be heard due to the RTC’s 
insistence on the validity of the default order, 
which paved the way for Salvador’s 
presentation of evidence ex-parte. 
 
To the mind of the Court, the more prudent 
course of action is to remand the case to the 
RTC for trial anew and allow Marivic to 
present her evidence, in the interest of 
substantial justice, and considering Marivic’s 
voluntary submission to the trial court’s 
jurisdiction and her plea to participate in the 
proceedings before the RTC despite the 
violation of her right to due process. After all, 
court litigations are primarily for the search of 
truth, and a liberal interpretation of the rules 
by which both parties are given the fullest 
opportunity to adduce proof is the best way 
to ferret out such truth. By remanding the 
case to the RTC for a full-blown trial, both 
parties will be able to present their evidence, 
this affording them the opportunity to enforce 
and protect their respective rights. (★Solis v. 
Laynes, G.R. No. 235099, March 29, 2023, 
as penned by J. Gaerlan) 
 
 
B. NDE - Newly Discovered Evidence 
 
PARM 
(a) It was discovered After the trial, or  
 
(b) It could not have been discovered and 
produced at the trial even with the exercise 
of Reasonable diligence; and  
 
(c) The evidence is of such weight that if 
admitted, would Probably alter the result of 
the action; and  
 
(d) It must be Material and not merely 
collateral, cumulative, or corroborative   
 
Content of a Motion a Motion for New Trial 
 
A MNT shall include all grounds then 
available and those not so included shall be 
deemed waived. 
 
Note: A second MNT may be allowed if it is 
based on a ground NOT existing or available 
when the first MNT was made.
