Effect 
when 
motion 
for 
MNT 
is 
granted/Court Action 
 
The trial court may set aside the judgment or 
final order and grant a new trial, upon such 
terms as may be just.  
 
The original judgment or final order shall be 
vacated, and the action shall stand for trial 
de novo. However, the recorded evidence 
shall be used in the new trial without retaking 
the same. 
 
When to file MNT: After promulgation of 
judgment 
 
 
2. RECONSIDERATION – RULE 37 
 
Grounds (Sec. 1, Rule 37) 
 
1. Damages awarded are excessive  
 
2. That the evidence is insufficient to justify 
the decision or final order  
 
3. That the decision or final order is contrary 
to law. 
 
Content of a Motion for Reconsideration 
 
A Motion for Reconsideration shall point out 
specifically the findings or conclusions of the 
judgment or final order which are not 
supported by the evidence or which are 
contrary to law, making express reference to 
the testimonial or documentary evidence or 
to the provisions of law alleged to be contrary 
to such findings or conclusions. 
 
Note: A second MR is NOT allowed. 
However, this prohibition does not apply to 
interlocutory orders. 
 
Effect when MR is granted/Court Action 
 
The court may amend such judgment or final 
order accordingly if the court finds that: 
Ex Co 
 
a. Excessive damages have been awarded 
or that, or  
 
b. Judgment or final order is contrary to the 
evidence or law  
 
Note: A Motion for Reconsideration is 
directed against a judgment or final order. 
It does NOT refer to interlocutory orders, 
which often precedes a petition for certiorari 
under Rule 65. 
 
When to file MR: Within the period for taking 
an appeal (See discussions on Period of  
Appeal) 
 
Pro forma MNT/MR 
 
A pro forma MNT/MR shall not toll the 
reglementary period of appeal (Sec. 2, Rule 
37). 
 
A Motion for New Trial is considered pro 
forma when: 
 
1. Based on the same ground raised in 
preceding MNT/MR already denied;  
 
2. Contains the same arguments and manner 
of discussion in the prior opposition to a 
motion to dismiss which was granted;  
 
3. The new ground alleged in the 2nd MNT 
was available and could have been alleged 
in the first MNT which was denied;  
 


<!-- PAGE 116 -->

 
 
104 
4. Based on the ground of insufficiency of 
evidence/that the judgment is contrary to law, 
but does not specify the supposed defects in 
judgment; or  
 
5. Based on FAME but does not specify the 
facts constituting these grounds and/or is not 
accompanied by an affidavit of merits.  
 
Court resolution of MNT/MR 
 
The motion shall be resolved within 30 days 
from the time it is submitted for resolution. 
The 30-day period to resolve the motion is 
mandatory.  
 
 
a. Remedy against Denial 
 
The trial court may deny the Motion for New 
Trial or Motion for Reconsideration (Sec. 3, 
Rule 37) 
 
An order denying a MNT or MR is not 
appealable. The remedy is an appeal from 
the judgment or final order (Sec. 9, Rule 37). 
However, the order denying the motion may 
itself be assailed by a petition for certiorari 
under Rule 65. 
 
In simpler terms, what is appealable is not 
the denial of the MNT/MR but the judgment 
or final order rendered by the court. Always 
remember that the remedy of appeal may 
only be availed of when there is already a 
judgment or final order. The denial of 
MNT/MR is not a final order. Nevertheless, a 
petition for certiorari under Rule 65 may be 
availed of by a party if his or her MNT/MR is 
denied. 
 
Partial 
grant 
of 
new 
trial 
or 
reconsideration  
 
If the grounds for a motion under this Rule 
appear to the court to affect:  
 
1. The issues as to only a part, or  
 
2. Less than all of the matter in controversy, 
or 
3. Only one, or less than all, of the parties to 
it, the court may order a new trial or grant 
reconsideration 
as 
to 
such 
issues 
if 
severable 
without 
interfering 
with 
the 
judgment or final order upon the rest (Sec. 7, 
Rule 37).  
 
Partial new trial; effect  
 
When less than all of the issues are ordered 
retried, the court may either: 
 
1. Enter a judgment or final order as to the 
rest, or  
 
2. Stay the enforcement of such judgment or 
final order until after the new trial. 
 
 
b. Fresh Period Rule 
 
The adverse party has a fresh period of 
fifteen (15) days within which to file the 
notice of appeal, counted from receipt of the 
order dismissing a motion for a new trial or 
motion for reconsideration. (Neypes vs. CA, 
G.R. No. 141524 September 14, 2005) 
 
The fresh period of 15 days becomes 
significant only when a party opts to file a 
motion for new trial or motion for 
reconsideration.  
 
“The appeal shall be taken within fifteen 
(15) days from notice of the judgment OR 
final order appealed from” 
(Sec. 2, Rule 40) 
 
It means that the notice of appeal may be 
filed within 15 days from the notice of 
judgment or within 15 days from notice of the 
"final order," which can be an order denying 
the 
motion 
for 
a 
new 
trial 
or 
reconsideration.

3. RELIEF FROM JUDGMENT – 
RULE 38 
 
 
It is a legal remedy whereby a party seeks to 
set aside a judgment rendered against him 
by a court whenever he was unjustly 
deprived of a hearing or was prevented 
from taking an appeal because of fraud, 
accident, 
mistake, 
or 
excusable 
negligence (FAME). 
A petition for relief from judgment is an 
equitable 
remedy 
allowed 
only 
in 
exceptional cases when there is no other 
available or adequate remedy. 
 
Note: In Petition for Relief from Judgment, 
there is no NDE (Newly Discovered 
Evidence), only FAME. Fraud refers only to 
“Extrinsic Fraud”. 
 
When proper; grounds 
 
1. When a judgment or final order is entered, 
or any other proceeding is thereafter taken 
against a party in any court through FAME 
(Sec. 1, Rule 38). 
 
Petition is filed in the same court, in the 
same case with prayer for the judgment, 
order, proceeding to be set aside. 
 
2. When petitioner has been prevented from 
taking an appeal by FAME  
 
Petition is filed in the same court, in the 
same case with prayer for the appeal to 
be given due course. 
 
When PRJ is also applicable 
 
A petition for relief is also applicable to a 
proceeding take nafter entry of judgment or 
final order such as an: 
 
a. Order of execution (Cayetano v. 
Ceguerra, G.R. No. L-18831, 1965) 
b. Order dismissing an appeal (Medran 
v. CA, G.R. No. L-1350,1949) 
 
When PRJ is NOT applicable  
 
a. A party who has filed a timely MNT or 
MR can NO longer file a petition for 
relief from judgment after his motion 
has been denied. 
b. A petition for relief is NOT an available 
remedy in the SC or the CA (Purcon vs 
MRM Philippines Inc., G.R. No. 182718 
(2008).   
 
Negligence or mistake of a party or his 
counsel 
 
When the loss of the remedy of law was due 
to a party’s own inexcusable negligence, or a 
mistaken mode of procedure, by him or his 
counsel, Rule 38 shall be denied. 
 
Negligence of counsel 
 
GR: The negligence of counsel is binding on 
the client. 
 
XPN: If it was so great as to prejudice the 
client and prevent fair presentation of the 
case.  
 
Contents of Petition 
 
The petition must be: 
 
1. Verified;  
 
2. Accompanied by an affidavit showing 
the FAME relied upon;  
 
GR: Jurisprudence provides that the 
absence of an affidavit of merits is a 
FATAL defect and warrants denial of the 
petition.  
 
XPN: NOT a fatal defect so long as the 
facts required to be set out also appear in 
the verified petition.  
 


<!-- PAGE 118 -->

 
 
106 
When affidavit of merit is NOT 
necessary:  
 
1. When there is lack of jurisdiction over 
the defendant;  
 
2. When there is lack of jurisdiction over 
the subject matter;  
 
3. When judgment was taken by default;  
 
4. When judgment was entered by 
mistake or was obtained by fraud; or  
 
5. Other similar cases. 
 
3. The facts constituting the petitioner’s 
good and substantial cause of action or 
defense, as the case may be. (Sec. 3, Rule 
38)  
 
Time to File PRJ (60:6 Requirement) 
 
1. Within 60 days after the petitioner learns 
of the judgment, final order, or other 
proceeding to be set aside, and  
 
2. Not more than 6 months after such 
judgment or final order was entered, or such 
proceeding was taken. (Sec. 3, Rule 38) 
 
To Illustrate: 
 
 
Note: These two periods must concur, are 
not extendible and are never interrupted. 
PRJ is the “last chance” given by law to 
litigants to question a final judgment or order.  
 
As such, Failure to avail of such chance, 
within the grace period fixed by the Rules, is 
FATAL. 
 
 
 
Order to file answer  
 
If the petition is sufficient in form and 
substance to justify relief, the court in which 
it is filed, shall issue an order requiring the 
adverse parties to answer the same within 15 
days from the receipt thereof. (Sec. 4, Rule 
38) 
 
Note: Failure to answer the petition for relief 
does NOT constitute default. Even without it, 
the court will still have to hear the petition on 
the merits.  
 
Court Action; Proceedings after answer is 
filed 
 
Allegations are 
not true 
Allegations are 
true 
Petition shall be 
DISMISSED. 
The court shall set 
aside the judgment 
or final order or other 
proceeding 
complained of upon 
such terms as may 
be just and the case 
shall stand as if such 
judgment, final order 
or other proceeding 
had 
never 
been 
rendered, issued or 
taken.  
 
The court shall then 
proceed to hear and 
determine the case 
as if a timely motion 
for a new trial or 
reconsideration had 
been granted by it. 
 
Note: A petition for relief from judgment may 
only be availed of by a party to the 
proceeding (Alaban vs CA, 470 SCRA 697, 
705).

Remedy for denial of PRJ 
 
An order granting a petition for relief is 
interlocutory 
and 
non-appealable. 
The 
remedy against a denial of a petition for relief 
is certiorari under Rule 65, when proper. 
 
 
4. ANNULMENT OF JUDGMENT – 
RULE 47 
 
A petition for annulment of judgment under 
Rule 47 of the Rules of Court is a remedy 
available to assail judgments or final 
orders and resolutions in civil actions of 
RTCs for which the ordinary remedies of 
new trial, appeal, petition for relief or 
other appropriate remedies are no longer 
available 
through 
no 
fault 
of 
the 
petitioner. 
 
 
This remedy is allowed only in exceptional 
cases where there is no other available or 
adequate remedy for a party. It also 
disregards 
the 
time-honored 
rule 
of 
immutability 
and 
unalterability 
of 
final 
judgments and thus may be granted only 
after strict compliance with its stringent 
requirements. (★Isabel Cojuangco-Suntay 
v. Emilio A.M. Suntay III, G.R. No. 251350, 
August 2, 2023, as penned by J. Gaerlan) 
 
It is a remedy in equity independent of the 
case where the judgment sought to be 
annulled is rendered. Unlike PRJ, AJ is not 
the continuation of the same case, like in the 
reliefs of MR, appeal, or petition for relief 
(CIR vs Kepco Ilijan Corp., G.R. No. 199422, 
2016). 
 
 
 
 
Purpose: 
 
The purpose of such action is to have the 
final and executory judgment set aside so 
that there will be a renewal of litigation. (Sps. 
Teaño vs. The Municipality of Navotas, G.R. 
No. 205814, February 15, 2016).  
 
Grounds (Rule 47, Sec. 2) 
 
(a) Extrinsic fraud  
 
Extrinsic fraud shall NOT be a valid ground if 
it was availed of, or could have been availed 
of, in a motion for new trial or petition for 
relief. 
 
When to file: Within four (4) years from its 
discovery of fraud (Rule 47, Sec. 3). 
 
(b) Lack of jurisdiction.  
 
Lack of jurisdiction refers to either lack of 
jurisdiction over the person of the defending 
party or over the subject matter of the claim. 
 
When to file: Before it is barred by laches or 
estoppel (Rule 47, Sec. 3) 
 
(c) Denial of due process (Benatiro vs. 
Heirs of Cuyos, G.R. NO. 161220, 2008) 
 
Due process requires that those with interest 
to the subject matter in litigation be notified 
and be afforded an opportunity to defend 
their interests.  A decision rendered in 
disregard of that right is void for lack of 
jurisdiction. (Thomas vs. Trono, G.R. No. 
241032, 2021) 
 
A petition for annulment of judgment is a 
remedy in equity which courts view with an 
attitude of reluctance as it is an exception to 
the time-honored doctrine of immutability of 
final judgments. Thus, to prevent parties 


<!-- PAGE 120 -->

 
 
108 
aggrieved by final judgments, orders, or 
resolutions from abusing this exceptional 
remedy, the Court installed safeguards 
limiting its application under Rule 47 of the 
Rules of Court. Under the rules, the grounds 
for annulment are limited to extrinsic fraud 
and lack of jurisdiction. In Arcelona v. Court 
of Appeals, however, recognized a third 
ground -- denial of due process. (Sps. 
Marcelo G. Flores And Medelyn Flores V. 
Sps. Leopoldo A. Estrellado And Enriqueta 
Estrellado)

6. APPEAL AND REVIEW  
 
a. Coverage  
 
i. Subjects of Appeal and Review  
 
An appeal may be taken only from judgments or 
final orders that completely dispose of the 
case, or of a particular matter therein when 
declared by the Rules of Court to be appealable. 
(Sec. 1, Rule 41, ROC, as amended)  
 
Judgment 
 
The conclusion of the law 
upon the matters contained 
in 
the 
record, 
or 
the 
application of the law to the 
pleadings and to the facts, as 
found 
by 
the 
court 
or 
admitted by the parties or 
deemed to exist upon default 
in 
a 
course 
of 
judicial 
proceedings. (Gotamco v. 
Chan Seng, G.R. No. 22737, 
28 Nov. 1924)  
 
Final Order  
 
One that puts an end to the 
particular matter resolved, 
leaving 
thereafter 
no 
substantial proceedings to 
be 
had 
in 
connection 
therewith, 
except 
its 
execution. (Bairan v. Tan Siu 
Lay, G.R. No. L-19460, 28 
Dec. 1966)  
 
Interlocutory 
Order  
 
It is an order which does not 
dispose the case but leave 
something to be done by the 
trial court on the merits of the 
case. 
 
ii. Matters not Appealable  
 
No appeal may be taken from: 
 
(a) An order denying a motion for new trial or 
reconsideration; 
(b) An order denying a petition for relief or any 
similar motion seeking relief from judgment; 
(c) An interlocutory order; 
(d) An order disallowing or dismissing an appeal; 
(e) An order denying a motion to set aside a 
judgment 
by 
consent, 
confession 
or 
compromise on the ground of fraud, mistake 
or duress, or any other ground vitiating 
consent; 
(f) An order of execution; 
(g) A judgment or final order for or against one or 
more of several parties or in separate claims, 
counterclaims, cross-claims and third-party 
complaints, while the main case is pending, 
unless the court allows an appeal therefrom; 
and 
(h) An order dismissing an action without 
prejudice. 
 
In all the above instances where the judgment or 
final order is not appealable, the aggrieved party 
may file an appropriate special civil action under 
Rule 65. 
 
Appeals from Decisions of RTC exercising 
original jurisdiction, when appeal involves 
PURE QUESTIONS OF LAW 
 
Appeals to the CA from RTC decisions in the 
exercise of original jurisdiction must be taken 
by notice of appeal only when factual issues 
are involved; where the appeal raises purely 
questions of law, the proper recourse is a 
petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 
DIRECTLY to the Supreme Court.

Fresh period rule. 
 
The adverse party has a fresh period of fifteen (15) days within which to file the notice of appeal, counted from receipt 
of the order dismissing a motion for a new trial or motion for reconsideration. (Neypes vs. CA, G.R. No. 141524 
September 14, 2005) 
 
The fresh period of 15 days becomes significant only when a party opts to file a motion for new trial or motion for 
reconsideration.  
 
Relaxation of Rules on Period to Appeal 
 
While appeal periods are generally mandatory, the Court may relax procedural 
rules to serve substantial justice, prevent grave miscarriage, and address 
compelling public interest. (★Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority v. Subic Bay 
Marine Exploratorium, G.R. No. 237591, November 10, 2021, as penned by J. 
Gaerlan)

vi. Review of Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions of the Commission on Audit and 
Commission on Elections – Rule 64  
Rule 64 
Scope 
Governs the review of judgments and final orders or resolutions of the 
Commission on Elections (COMELEC) and the Commission on Audit (COA). 
(Sec. 1) 
Mode of Review 
Review is brought to the Supreme Court on certiorari under Rule 65, except as 
otherwise provided. (Sec. 2) 
Nature of Remedy 
Special civil action for certiorari, not an appeal. 
Period to File Petition 
Petition must be filed within 30 days from notice of the judgment, final order, or 
resolution sought to be reviewed. (Sec. 3) 
Effect of Motion for New 
Trial or Reconsideration 
The filing of a motion for new trial or reconsideration, if allowed under the rules 
of the Commission concerned, interrupts the 30-day period. (Sec. 3) 
Period After Denial of 
MNT/MR 
If the motion is denied, the petition may be filed within the remaining period, but 
not less than five (5) days, reckoned from notice of denial. (Sec. 3) 
Fresh Period Rule 
Does not apply. The Rule expressly adopts the remaining period rule, subject to 
the minimum of five (5) days. 
Docket and Other Lawful 
Fees 
Upon filing, petitioner shall pay the docket and other lawful fees and deposit 
₱500.00 for costs. (Sec. 4) 
Form of Petition 
Petition must be verified and filed in eighteen (18) legible copies. (Sec. 5) 
Parties 
Aggrieved party is the petitioner; respondents include the Commission 
concerned and the person or persons interested in sustaining the judgment, 
final order, or resolution a quo. (Sec. 5) 
Contents of Petition 
Must state facts with certainty, clearly present the issues, set forth the grounds and 
brief arguments, and pray for judgment annulling or modifying the assailed 
decision. (Sec. 5) 
Review of Findings of Fact 
Findings of fact of the Commission supported by substantial evidence are final 
and non-reviewable. (Sec. 5) 
Required Attachments 
Certified true copy of the assailed judgment, final order, or resolution, and certified 
true copies of material portions of the record and relevant documents. (Sec. 5) 
Material Dates and 
Certification 
Petition must state specific material dates showing timeliness and contain a 
sworn certification against forum shopping. (Sec. 5) 
Proof of Service 
Must be accompanied by proof of service on the Commission concerned and the 
adverse party, and proof of timely payment of docket and other lawful fees. (Sec. 
5) 
Grounds for Dismissal 
Failure to comply with any of the foregoing requirements is sufficient ground for 
dismissal. (Sec. 5) 
Order to Comment 
If sufficient in form and substance, the Supreme Court shall order respondents to 
file comments within 10 days; otherwise, the petition may be dismissed outright. 
(Sec. 6) 
Dismissal for Delay or 
Unsubstantial Issues 
The Court may dismiss the petition if filed manifestly for delay or if the issues raised 
are too unsubstantial. (Sec. 6) 
Comments of Respondents 
Comments must be filed in eighteen (18) legible copies, with certified true copies 
of material portions of the record and supporting papers, and served on the 
petitioner. (Sec. 7) 
Further Pleadings 
No other pleading may be filed unless required or allowed by the Court. (Sec. 7) 
Effect of Filing 
Filing of the petition does not stay execution of the assailed judgment, final order, 
or resolution, unless the Supreme Court directs otherwise. (Sec. 8) 
Submission for Decision 
Case is deemed submitted for decision upon filing of the comments, required 
pleadings, or expiration of the period to do so, unless oral argument or memoranda 
are required. (Sec. 9)

T. EXECUTION, SATISFACTION, AND 
EFFECT OF JUDGMENTS – RULE 39 
 
Execution is a remedy afforded by law for the 
enforcement of a judgment. It is a judicial 
writ issued to an officer authorizing and 
requiring him to execute the judgment of the 
court. 
 
Finality of judgment for purposes of 
appeal vs. for purposes of execution 
 
For Purposes 
of Appeal 
For Purposes 
of Execution 
A "final" judgment or 
order 
is 
one 
that 
finally disposes of a 
case, leaving nothing 
more to be done by 
the Court in respect 
thereto. 
 
 
A judgment is “final 
and 
executory” 
when the law/rules do 
not provide for an 
appeal or the period 
to appeal has lapsed 
without 
an 
appeal 
being 
taken, 
upon 
which execution shall 
matter issue as a of 
right 
according 
to 
Sec. 
1, 
Rule 
39 
(Calilung 
vs. 
Paramount Insurance 
Corporation, G.R. No. 
195641, February 3, 
2016). 
 
 
1. IMMUTABILITY OF FINAL 
JUDGMENTS 
 
A judgment that has acquired finality 
becomes immutable and unalterable, and 
may no longer be modified in any respect, 
even if the modification is meant to correct 
erroneous conclusions of fact and law, and 
whether it be made by the court that 
rendered it or by the Highest Court of the 
land (PNB v. Spouses Maranon, G.R. No. 
189316, 2013). 
 
The Court reiterated that execution is the 
final stage of litigation, and once a judgment 
is fully satisfied, no further modifications are 
allowed. Permitting a recomputation of the 
monetary award would violate the principle 
of immutability of final judgments and 
lead to unjust enrichment. Therefore, the 
Supreme Court partially granted the petition, 
reinstating the ELA’s order dated February 
19, 2009, and denying the recomputation of 
the monetary award. (Validity of Bir 
Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 65-
2012 On Taxability of Association Dues, 
GR No. 215801) 
 
 
2. EXECUTION AS A MATTER OF 
RIGHT AND OF DISCRETION 
 
As a Matter of Right (Sec. 1, Rule 39) 
 
a. Upon the expiration of the period to appeal 
therefrom if no appeal has been duly 
perfected. 
 
b. Appeal has been duly perfected and finally 
resolved. [Sec. 1, Rule 39 
 
As a Matter of Discretion (Sec. 2, Rule 39) 
 
The issuance of a writ of execution is 
discretionary on the part of the court when it 
is for the 
 
a. Execution of a judgment or final order 
pending appeal, or 
 
b. Execution of several, separate, or partial 
judgments. [Sec. 2, Rule 39] 
 


<!-- PAGE 129 -->

 
 
117 
3. WHEN EXECUTION SHALL 
ISSUE 
 
GR: Execution of a judgment or final order 
shall issue as a matter of right, upon motion 
of the prevailing party in the court of origin, 
when no appeal is taken therefrom or upon 
the lapse of the period to do so. (Salazar, 
The Fundamentals of Civil Procedure, p. 
295, 2021) 
 
XPNs: 
 
The following are immediately executory 
without the expiration of the period to appeal: 
 
(a) Judgments in actions for injunction, 
receivership, accounting, and support, 
and such other judgments, unless otherwise 
ordered by the court (Sec. 1, Rule 39). 
 
(b) Judgments in an action for forcible entry 
or unlawful detainer rendered against the 
defendant (Sec. 19, Rule 39). 
 
(c) Decisions of the Regional Trial Court in 
civil cases governed by the Rules on 
Summary Procedure (Sec. 21, Rules on 
Summary Procedure). 
 
(d) The decision of the Labor Arbiter 
reinstating a dismissed or separated 
employee (Labor Code, Art. 229). 
 
(e) Awards, judgment, final order or 
resolution 
of 
quasi-judicial 
bodies 
appealable to the Court of Appeals (Feria 
and Noche, Civil Procedure Annotated, 2013 
ed., Vol. 2, p. 127). 
 
(f) Discretionary execution (Rule 39, Sec. 
2). 
 
Requisites for discretionary execution 
 
a) A motion filed by the prevailing party 
with notice to the adverse party;  
 
b) Hearing of the motion for discretionary 
execution;  
c) The motion must be filed in the trial 
court while it has jurisdiction over the 
case and is in possession of either the 
original record or the record on 
appeal;  
d) There must be good reasons to justify 
the discretionary execution; and  
e) The good reasons must be stated in a 
special order 
 
Stay of discretionary execution 
 
GR: An appeal perfected in due time stays 
the execution of a judgment (Riano, Civil 
Procedure : The Bar Lecture Series, Vol. I, 
2022 Edition, p. 709-710). 
 
XPNs: There are, however, judgments, the 
execution of which is not stayed by a pending 
appeal. These judgments may be classified 
into two general categories, namely:  
 
(a) Those judgments which by express 
provision of the rules are immediately 
executory and are not stayed by an appeal 
(Rule 39, Sec. 4).  
 
(b) Those judgments that have become 
the object of discretionary execution (Rule 
39, Sec. 2). 
 
 
4. HOW A JUDGMENT IS 
EXECUTED 
 
a. By Motion or Independent Action 
 
A final and executory judgment or order may 
be executed on motion or by independent 
action within five (5) years from the date of 
its entry. 
 
A judgment may be enforced by action: 
 
1. After the lapse of (5) years from the 
date of its entry and  
 
2. Before it is barred by the statute of 
limitations 
 


<!-- PAGE 130 -->

 
 
118 
Revived judgment 
 
The revived judgment may also be enforced 
by motion within five (5) years from the date 
of its entry and thereafter by action before it 
is barred by the statute of limitations.  
 
b. Execution of Judgments for Money 
 
Three successive modes: 
 
(a) Immediate payment on demand 
(b) Satisfaction by levy 
(c) Garnishment of debts and credits 
 
a. Immediate payment on demand 
 
The SC held that in the execution of a money 
judgment, the sheriff is required to first make 
a demand on the obligor for the immediate 
payment of the full amount stated in the writ 
of execution (Sibulo vs. San Jose, 474 SCRA 
464). 
 
b. Satisfaction by levy 
 
If the judgment obligor cannot pay all or part 
of the obligation in cash, certified check or 
other mode of payment, the officer shall levy 
upon the properties of the judgment obligor. 
The judgment obligor shall have the option to 
choose which property or part thereof may be 
levied upon.  
 
Personal properties shall be levied first; Real 
properties 
if 
personal 
properties 
are 
insufficient 
 
If the judgment obligor does not exercise the 
option, the officer shall first levy on the 
personal properties, if any, and then on the 
real properties if the personal properties are 
insufficient to answer for the personal 
judgment but the sheriff shall sell only so 
much of the property that is sufficient to 
satisfy the judgment and lawful fees. 
 
Bidder is not required to pay bid in cash 
 
Section 21, Rule 39 does not require 
payment of the bid in cash. What the Rule 
emphasizes is that in the absence of a third 
party claim, the purchaser in an execution 
sale need not pay his bid if it does not exceed 
the amount of the judgment, otherwise, he 
shall only pay the excess. By implication, if 
there is a third party claim, the purchaser 
should pay the amount of his bid without, 
however, requiring that it be made in cash. 
 
Further, the rationale for the requirement of 
annotation of third-party claim in the 
Certificate of Sale under Section 26, Rule 39 
is to protect the interest of a third-party 
claimant. Thus, where the third-party claim 
has been dismissed or when such claim is 
adequately protected, the failure of the 
Certificate of Sale to expressly state the 
existence of a third-party claim shall not 
affect the validity of the sale. Here, the 
winning bidders (Petitioners Hao) filed an 
indemnity bond to answer for the damages 
which respondents third-party claimants may 
suffer. Hence, the respondents’ interest are 
adequately protected. Hence, the validity of 
the Certificate of Sale must be upheld. 
(★Jesus G. Crisologo v. Alicia Hao, G.R. 
No. 216151, December 2, 2020, as penned 
by J. Gaerlan) 
 
(c) Garnishment of debts and credits 
 
The officer may levy on debts due the 
judgment obligor and other credits, including 
bank deposits, financial interests, royalties, 
commissions and other personal property not 
capable of manual delivery in the possession 
or control of third parties. The garnishment 
shall cover only such amount as will satisfy 
the judgment and all lawful fees. 
 
c. Execution of Judgments for Specific 
Acts 
 
(a) Conveyance, delivery of deeds, or 
other specific acts; vesting title. 
 
If a judgment directs a party to execute a: 
 
1. Conveyance of land or personal 
property, or 


<!-- PAGE 131 -->

 
 
119 
2. Deliver deeds or other documents, or 
to  
3. Perform any other specific act in 
connection therewith 
 
And the party fails to comply within the 
time specified, the court may direct the 
act to be done at the cost of the 
disobedient party by some other person 
appointed by the court. 
 
Effect: The act when so done shall have 
like effect as if done by the party. 
 
(b) Sale of real or personal property 
 
(c) Delivery or restitution of real property 
 
(d) Removal of improvements on property 
subject of execution 
 
(e) Delivery of personal property 
 
 
d. Execution of Special Judgments 
 
Special Judgment is one which can only be 
complied with by the judgment obligor 
because 
of 
his/her 
personal 
or 
circumstances (Sia vs. Arcenas, G.R No. 
209672 74, January 14, 2015). 
 
When judgment requires the performance of 
any act, other than for money and delivery of 
property, the writ of execution shall be served 
upon the party required to obey the same 
and such party may be punished for 
contempt by imprisonment, if he disobeys. 
(Rule 39, Sec. 11). 
 
Requisites: 
 
(1) The judgment requires performance of 
any act other than payment of money, or the 
sale or delivery of real or personal property.  
 
(2) A certified copy of the judgment shall be:  
 
(a) Attached to the writ of execution; and  
(b) Served by the office upon the party

or by law, to obey the same (Rule 39, Sec. 
11). 
 
 
e. Requisites before Demolition Order is 
Issued 
 
A special order of demolition is an order from 
the court authorizing the sheriff to destroy, 
demolish or remove improvements on 
property subject of execution.  
 
It 
is 
issued 
UPON 
HEARING 
AND 
REASONABLE NOTICE. Without one, the 
sheriff cannot destroy, demolish, or remove

v. Ragsac, A.M. No. P-08-2571 (2009); see

f. Effect of Levy on Third Persons 
 
Terceria/Third-party claim 
 
The right of a third-party claimant to file a 
terceria is founded on his title or right of 
possession. Corollary thereto, before the 
court can exercise its supervisory power to 
direct the release of the property mistakenly 
levied and the restoration thereof to its 
rightful owner, the claimant must first 
unmistakably establish his ownership or right 
of possession thereon (Villasi v. Garcia, G.R. 
No. 190106, 2014).  
 
For a third-party claim to be sufficient: 
 
a. Must be filed by a person other than the 
defendant or his agent, at any time before 
sale 
 
b. Must be under oath or supported by 
affidavit stating the claimant’s title to, or right

120 
of possession of, the property, and grounds 
therefor 
 
c. Must be served upon the officer making 
levy and a copy thereof upon the judgment 
creditor (Sec. 16, Rule 39).   
 
When to file: Any time, as long as:  
 
a. Sheriff has the possession of the property 
levied upon, or  
 
b. Before the property shall have been sold 
under execution.   
 
Bond 
 
To enforce a claim for damages against the 
bond, the action must be filed within 120 
days from the filing of the bond.  
 
The officer shall not be liable for damages for 
the taking or keeping of the property, to any 
third-party claimant if such bond is filed.  
 
When bond not required 
 
When the writ of execution is issued in favor 
of the Republic of the Philippines, or any 
officer duly representing it, the filing of such 
bond shall not be required.

7. EFFECT OF JUDGMENT OR 
FINAL ORDERS 
 
Effect of Judgments or Final Orders 
 
The effect of a judgment or final order may 
be as follows: 
 
(a) In case of a judgment or final order 
against: 
 
1. A specific thing, or  
 
2. Probate of a will, or  
 
3. Administration of the estate of a 
deceased person, or  
 
4. Personal, political, or legal condition or 
status of a particular person or his 
relationship to another  
 
The 
judgment 
or 
final 
order 
is 
CONCLUSIVE 
upon 
the 
four 
enumerations. However, the probate of a 
will or granting of letters of administration 
shall only be prima facie evidence of the 
death of the testator or intestate. 
 
(b) In other cases such as: 
 
1. Matter directly adjudged or  
 
2. As to any other matter that could have 
been raised in relation thereto 
 
The judgment or final order is conclusive 
between the parties and their successors 
in interest by title subsequent to the 
commencement of the action or special 
proceeding, litigating for the same thing 
and under the same title and in the same 
capacity. 
 
(c) In any other litigation between the same 
parties, that only is deemed to have been 
adjudged in a former judgment or final order 
which appears upon its face to have been so 
adjudged, or which was actually and 
necessarily included therein or necessary 
thereto. 
 
In simpler terms, in a case involving the 
same parties or their successors in interest, 
only what is clearly stated or was directly part 
of a previous judgment is considered as 
having been decided in that earlier judgment 
or final order. 
 
 
8. RES JUDICATA 
 
Elements of Res Judicata: FJM(Pa SM Ca) 
 
1. The judgment or order rendered must be 
final 
 
2. The court rendering the same must have 
jurisdiction over the subject matter and over 
the parties 
 
3. The judgment must be on the merits

(Pa-SM-Ca) 
 
a. Identity of parties 
b. Identity of subject matter 
c. Identity of causes of action (San Diego 
v. Cardona, G.R. NO. 46655, 1940) 
 
GR: For res judicata to apply, trial must be 
made on the merits of the case.  
 
XPN: Dismissal upon fault of plaintiff (Sec. 3, 
Rule 17) 
 
If for no justifiable cause, the plaintiff:  
 
1. Fails to appear on the date of the

the complaint 
 
2. Fails to prosecute his action for an 
unreasonable length of time, also called 
as non-prosequitur. 
 
3. Fails to comply with the ROC or any 
court order (Sec. 3, Rule 17). 
 
a. 
Bar 
by 
Prior 
Judgment; 
b. 
Conclusiveness of Judgment 
 
Res Judicata 
 
Under Section 47, Rule 39 of the Rules of 
Court, res judicata is applicable either under 
the concept of "bar by prior judgment" under 
Sec. 47 (b), Rule 39; or "conclusiveness of 
judgment" under Sec. 47 (c), Rule 39. 
 
Therefore, if there is identity of parties, 
subject matter, and causes of action in the 
two cases, then res judicata, in its aspect as 
a "BAR BY PRIOR JUDGMENT" would 
apply. 
 
If, as between the two cases, only identity of 
parties can be shown, but not identical 
causes of action, then res judicata as 
"CONCLUSIVENESS 
OF 
JUDGMENT" 
applies. (City Government of Tacloban v. 
CAs, et al. (G.R. No. 221554 February 3, 
2021)

9. ENFORCEMENT AND EFFECT 
OF FOREIGN JUDGMENTS OR 
FINAL ORDERS 
 
A valid judgment rendered by a foreign 
tribunal may be recognized insofar as the 
immediate parties the underlying cause of 
action are concerned so long as it is 
convincingly shown that:  
 
a. There has been an opportunity for a fair 
hearing before a court of competent 
jurisdiction,  
 
b. Trial upon registered proceedings has 
been conducted, and  
 
c. There is nothing to indicate either a 
prejudice in court and in the system of laws 
under which it is sitting or fraud in procuring 
the judgment. (Philippine Aluminum v. 
Fasgi Enterprises, G.R. No. 137378, 2000) 
 
 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 135 -->

 
 
123 
Presumption of Validity 
 
A foreign judgment is presumed to be valid 
and binding in the country from which it 
comes, until a contrary showing, on the basis 
of a presumption of regularity of proceedings 
and the giving of due notice in the foreign 
forum. (Asiavest Merchant Bankers v CA, 
G.R. No 110263 (2001) 
 
Purpose 
 
a. To avoid repetitive litigation on claims and 
issues 
 
b. Prevent harassment of the parties, and  
 
c. Avoid undue imposition on the courts.

IV. PROVISIONAL REMEDIES 
 
 
A. NATURE AND PURPOSE 
 
Nature 
 
They are interlocutory and cannot be the 
subject of an appeal. Provisional remedies 
are temporary, auxiliary, and ancillary 
remedies available to a litigant for the 
protection and preservation of his rights while 
the main action is pending. They depend on 
the existence of a principal action. 
 
Purpose 
 
a. To preserve or protect litigants’ rights or 
interests during the pendency of the 
principal action; 
 
b. To secure the judgment; 
 
c. To preserve the status quo of the the 
things 
subject to the action or the relation 
between the parties; and 
 
d. To preserve the subject matter of the 
action 
 
Kinds of provisional remedies (AIRRS) 
 
a. Preliminary Attachment (Rule 57) 
b. Preliminary Injunction (Rule 58) 
c. Receivership (Rule 59) 
d. Replevin (Rule 60) 
e. Support pendente lite (Rule 61) 
 
B. PRELIMINARY ATTACHMENT – RULE 
57 
 
Attachment is defined as a provisional 
remedy by which the property of an adverse 
party is taken into legal custody, either at the 
commencement of an action or at any time 
thereafter, as a security for the satisfaction of 
any judgment that may be recovered by the 
plaintiff or any proper party. (Northern 
Islands, Co., Inc. v. Spouses Garcia, G.R. 
No. 203240, March 18, 2015) 
 
Ancillary to the principal 
 
Being a mere ancillary to a principal 
proceeding, the attachment must fail if the 
principal suit itself cannot be maintained. 
 
Discretionary  
 
GR: In order for the court to issue an order of 
preliminary attachment, the applicant must 
file a motion with notice and hearing by the 
court in which the action is pending.  
 
XPN: The court may nonetheless issue an 
order of attachment ex parte. 
 
When Obtained; Who can obtain 
 
The plaintiff or any proper party may, at the 
commencement of action or at any time but 
before entry of final judgment, apply for 
the issuance of a writ of attachment.  
 
Who can obtain 
 
Plaintiff or “Proper party” which includes a 
defendant who filed a counterclaim, 
cross-claim, or a third party complaint.  
 


<!-- PAGE 137 -->

 
 
125 
1. GROUNDS FOR ISSUANCE 
 
a. For the recovery of a specified amount of 
money or damages, other than moral and 
exemplary, on a cause of action arising from 
law, contract, quasi-contract, delict or quasi-
delict against a party who is about to depart 
from the Philippines with intent to defraud his 
creditors. 
 
b. For money or property embezzled or 
fraudulently misapplied or converted to his 
own use by a public officer, or an officer of a 
corporation, or an attorney, factor, broker, 
agent, or clerk, in the course of his 
employment as such, or by any other person 
in a fiduciary capacity, or for a willful violation 
of duty. 
 
c. To recover the possession of property 
unjustly or fraudulently taken, detained, or 
converted, when the property, or any part 
thereof, has been concealed, removed, or 
disposed of to prevent its being found or 
taken by the applicant or an authorized 
person. 
 
d. Against a party who has been guilty of 
fraud in contracting the debt or incurring the 
obligation upon which the action is brought, 
or in the performance thereof.  
 
e. Against a party who has removed or 
disposed of his property, or is about to do so, 
with intent to defraud his creditors.  
f. Against a party who does not reside and is 
not found in the Philippines, or on whom 
summons may be served by publication 
 
 
2. GROUNDS FOR DISSOLUTION 
 
After a writ of attachment has been enforced, 
the party whose property has been attached, 
or the person appearing on his behalf, may 
move for the discharge of the attachment 
wholly or in part on the security given (Sec. 
12, Rule 57). 
 
 
GROUNDS 
 
a. Debtor has posted a COUNTER-BOND 
or has made the requisite cash deposit.  
 
Note: The mere posting of a counter-
bond does not automatically discharge 
the writ of attachment. It is only after due 
notice and hearing and after the judge 
orders the discharge of the attachment 
that the same is properly discharged. 
 
b. Attachment was IMPROPERLY OR 
IRREGULARLY ISSUED 
 
1. As where there was no ground for 
attachment, or 
2. The affidavit and/or bond filed are 
defective or insufficient.  
 
c. Judgment is rendered against attaching 
creditor 
 
d. Attachment is excessive; but the 
discharge shall be limited to the excess 
 
e. Property attached is exempt from 
execution.  
 
f. Belated service of summons 
 
Rule on Prior or Contemporaneous 
Service of Summons (in relation to 
“Belated Service of Summons) 
 
Note: This topic is crucial because it has 
been asked many times in previous bar 
exams.  
 
GR: The sheriff is not allowed to make a levy 
on attachment if such levy is not made with 
prior or contemporaneous service of the 
following:  
 
a. Service of summons  
b. Copy of the complaint  
c. Application for attachment  
d. Applicant’s affidavit and bond, and 
e. Order for writ of attachment (Sec. 5, 
Rule 57).  
 


<!-- PAGE 138 -->

 
 
126 
In simpler terms, the levy on attachment 
may only be enforced if it is served 
together with summons OR if summons is 
served prior to the levy on attachment.  
 
Effect of a “late” or subsequently 
served summons 
 
It will not cure the levy on attachment. As 
a consequence, the attachment will be 
considered as improperly or irregularly 
enforced. The proper remedy for the 
Sheriff is to serve the summons anew. 
 
XPNs: 
 
Levy on attachment would be justified even 
without prior or contemporaneous summons 
under the following circumstances:  
 
a. Summons could not be served personally 
or by substituted service despite diligent 
efforts, or 
b. Defendant is a resident of the Philippines 
temporarily absent therefrom, or  
c. Defendant is a non-resident of the 
Philippines, or  
d. The action is in rem or quasi in rem 
 
Effects of Discharge of the Attachment 
 
Upon the discharge of an attachment in 
accordance with the provisions of this section 
it has the following effects: 
 
(1) the property attached, or the proceeds of 
any sale thereof, shall be delivered to the 
party making the deposit or giving the 
counter-bond, or to the person appearing on 
his behalf; 
 
(2) the deposit or counter-bond aforesaid 
standing in place of the property so released. 
Should such counter-bond for any reason be 
found to be or become insufficient, and the 
party furnishing the same fail to file an 
additional counter-bond, the attaching party 
may apply for a new order of attachment. 
(Rule 57, Sec. 12) 
 
 
3. POSTING OF A 
COUNTERBOND 
 
Requirements for the Discharge (or 
Dissolution of the Attachment 
 
The court shall, after due notice and hearing, 
order the discharge of the attachment subject 
to the condition that: 
 
(a) The movant makes a cash deposit, or 
files a counter-bond executed to the 
attaching party with the clerk of the court 
where the application is made, in an amount 
equal to that fixed by the court in the order of 
attachment, exclusive of costs. 
 
(b) But if the attachment is sought to be 
discharged with respect to a particular 
property, the counter-bond shall be equal to 
the value of that property as determined by 
the court. 
 
(c) In either case, the cash deposit or the 
counter-bond shall secure the payment of 
any judgment that the attaching party may 
recover in the action. A notice of the deposit 
shall forthwith be served on the attaching 
party. (Rule 57, Sec. 12)

Requisites for the Issuance of Order of 
Preliminary Attachment 
 
In order for the court to issue an order of 
preliminary attachment, the applicant must 
file a motion with notice and hearing by the 
court in which the action is pending. 
 
However, the court may nonetheless issue 
an order of attachment ex parte. [Sec. 2, 
Rule 57] 
 
Regardless of whether the order was granted 
through motion or ex parte, the following are 
the requisites for the issuance of an order of 
preliminary attachment, to wit: 
 
1. The applicant, or some other who 
personally knows the facts, must file an 
affidavit; 
 
2. Applicant must post a bond executed to 
the adverse party in the amount fixed by the 
court in its order granting the issuance of the 
writ. [Secs. 3-4, Rule 57] 
 
Contests of the order of attachment 
 
It must: 
 
1. Require the sheriff of the court to attach 
so much of the property in the Philippines of 
the party against whom it is issued, not 
exempt from execution, as may be sufficient 
to satisfy the applicant’s demand 
 
2. Fix the amount of deposit or bond, 
which may be the 
 
a. Amount sufficient to satisfy the 
applicant’s demand or 
b. Value of the property to be attached 
as stated by the applicant, exclusive 
of costs. [Sec. 2, Rule 57] 
 
Affidavit (First Requisite) 
 
An order of attachment shall be granted only 
when the affidavit of the applicant, or of some 
other person who personally knows the facts, 
alleges that: 
 
1. A sufficient cause of action exists, 
2. The case is one of those mentioned in 
Rule 57, Sec. 1 
3. There is no other sufficient security for the 
claim sought to be enforced by the action, 
and 
 
Therefore, if a mortgage exists to 
secure the obligation, a writ of 
preliminary 
attachment 
cannot 
be 
granted. [2 Riano 30, 2016 Bantam Ed.] 
 
4. the amount due to the applicant, or the 
value of the property the possession of 
which he is entitled to recover, is as much 
as the sum for which the order is granted 
above all legal counterclaims. [Sec. 3, 
Rule 57] 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 140 -->

 
 
128 
Bond (Second Requisite) 
 
The party applying for the order of 
attachment must likewise give a bond 
executed to the adverse party. The amount 
of such bond is the amount fixed by the court 
in the order of attachment. [Sec. 4, Rule 57] 
 
The party applying for the order will pay all 
the costs which may be adjudged to the 
adverse party and all damages which he may 
sustain by reason of the attachment, if the 
court shall finally adjudge that the applicant 
was not entitled thereto. [Sec. 4, Rule 57] 
 
 
C. PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION – RULE 58 
 
 
1. DEFINITIONS AND 
DIFFERENCES: PRELIMINARY 
INJUNCTION, TEMPORARY 
RESTRAINING ORDER, AND 
STATUS QUO ANTE ORDER 
 
A writ of preliminary injunction is issued by 
the court to prevent threatened or continuous 
irreparable injury to parties before their 
claims can be thoroughly studied and 
adjudicated and during the pendency of an 
action. 
 
It is an equitable remedy, and one who 
comes to claim for equity must do so with 
clean hands. It is to be resorted to by a 
litigant to prevent or preserve a right where 
there is a pressing necessity to avoid 
injurious consequences which cannot be 
remedied 
under 
any 
standard 
of 
compensation (Sps. Nisce v. Equitable PCI, 
G.R. No. 170038, 2012).  
 
When Obtained 
 
A Writ of Preliminary Injunction may be 
granted at any stage of an action or 
proceeding prior to the judgment or final 
order.

1. Under RA 8975 (An Act to Ensure the

TRO or a preliminary injunction against

enforce environmental laws 
 
3. No TRO or injunction in any case involving 
or growing out of a labor dispute shall be

provided in Arts. 218 and 264 of the Labor 
Code. It is the NLRC which may grant

4. No court shall have the authority to grant

5. An injunction cannot be issued against

2. REQUISITES 
 
Jurisprudence has laid down four essential 
requisites for the issuance of an injunctive 
writ: 
 
(1) That the petitioner applicant must 
have a clear and unmistakable right; 
(2) That there is a material and 
substantial invasion of such right; 
(3) That there is an urgent and 
permanent necessity for the writ to 
prevent serious damage; and 
(4) No other ordinary, speedy, and 
adequate (OSA) remedy exists to 
prevent the infliction of irreparable 
injury. (★Reynaldo Dela Cruz v. 
Leopoldo V. Parumog, G.R. No. 
192692, June 17, 2020, penned by J. 
Gaerlan) 
 
3. KINDS 
 
There 
are 
2 
kinds 
of 
Preliminary 
Injunction: 
 
1. Preliminary Prohibitory Injunction- To 
refrain someone from performing a particular 
act or acts) 
 
2. Preliminary Mandatory Injunction - To 
command the performance of some positive 
act to correct a wrong made in the past) 
 
Kinds of Temporary Restraining Orders 
 
1. 20-day TRO (to be issued ex parte) 
 
If it appears from the facts that great or 
irreparable injury would result to the 
applicant before the matter can be heard 
on notice.  
 
2. 72-hour TRO (to be issued ex parte) 
 
If the matter is of extreme urgency and the 
applicant will suffer grave injustice and 
irreparable injury. 
 
Note: Only the executive judge of a multi-sala 
court or the presiding judge of a single-sala 
can issue a TRO. 
 
 
Summary Hearing for 20-day/75-hr TRO 
 
Within this period, a summary hearing to 
determine whether to extend the TRO to 20 
days must be conducted. The 72-hour period 
shall be included in the maximum 20-day 
period set by the Rules. 
 
 
4. GROUNDS FOR ISSUANCE 
 
The applicant must establish: 
 
a. 
The 
existence 
of 
a 
clear 
and 
unmistakable right that must be protected; 
that is, right in esse  
 
Right in esse 
 
The applicant's right must be CLEAR 
OR UNMISTAKABLE, that is, that the

130 
right is actual, clear and positive 
especially calling for judicial protection.  
 
b. This right in esse is directly threatened 
by an act sought to be enjoined  
 
c. A material and substantial invasion of 
such right; and 
 
d. An urgent and paramount necessity for 
the writ to prevent serious damage or 
irreparable injury. (Dulnuan v. Metrobank, 
G.R. No. 196864,2015). 
 
 
D. Receivership – Rule 59 
 
“Receiver” refers to a person appointed by 
the court on behalf of all the parties to the 
action for the purpose of preserving and 
conserving the property in litigation and 
preventing 
its 
possible 
destruction 
or 
dissipation if it were left in the possession of 
any of the parties. 
 
A receiver is not an agent of any party to the 
action. He is an officer of the court exercising 
his functions in the interest of neither plaintiff 
nor defendant but for the common benefit of 
all the parties in interest. 
 
Receivership, like injunction, may be the 
principal action itself or just an ancillary 
remedy. 
 
Purpose 
 
The purpose of a receivership as a 
provisional remedy is to protect and preserve 
the rights of the parties during the pendency 
of the main action, during the pendency of an 
appeal, or as an aid in the execution of a 
judgment when the writ of execution has 
been returned unsatisfied 
 
Unlike the other provisional remedies which 
can be availed of only before final judgment, 
receivership may be resorted to even after 
the 
judgment 
has 
become 
final 
and 
executory, under Sec. 1(c), Rule 59 in 
relation to Sec. 41, Rule 39. 
 
Cases when a receiver may be appointed 
 
a. When it appears from the verified 
application, and such other proof as the court 
may require, that the party applying for the 
appointment of a receiver has an interest in 
the property or fund which is the subject of 
the action or proceeding, and that such 
property or fund is in danger of being lost, 
removed, or materially injured unless a 
receiver be appointed to administer and 
preserve it; 
 
b. When it appears in an action by the 
mortgagee for the foreclosure of a mortgage 
that the property is in danger of being wasted 
or dissipated or materially injured, and that its 
value is probably insufficient to discharge the 
mortgage debt, or that the parties have so 
stipulated in the contract of mortgage; 
 
c. After judgment, to preserve the property 
during the pendency of an appeal, or to 
dispose of it according to the judgment, or to 
aid execution when the execution has been 
returned unsatisfied or the judgment obligor 
refuses to apply his property in satisfaction of 
the judgment, or otherwise to carry the 
judgment into effect; 
 
d. Whenever in other cases it appears that 
the appointment of a receiver is the most 
convenient 
and 
feasible 
means 
of 
preserving, administering, or disposing of the 
property in litigation. [Sec. 1, Rule 59] 
 
Specific cases: 
 
a. If a spouse without just cause abandons 
the other or fails to comply with his/her 
obligations to the family, the aggrieved 


<!-- PAGE 143 -->

 
 
131 
spouse 
may 
petition 
the 
court 
for 
receivership [Art. 101, FC] 
 
b. The court may appoint a receiver of the 
property of the judgment obligor; and it may 
also forbid a transfer or other disposition of, 
or any interference with, the property of the 
judgment obligor not exempt from execution 
[Sec. 41, Rule 39] 
 
c. After the trial court loses jurisdiction over 
the case (in appeals by notice of appeal) or 
only over the subject matter (in appeals by 
record on appeal), and prior to the transmittal 
of the original record or the record on appeal, 
the court may issue orders for the protection 
and preservation of the rights of the parties 
[Sec. 9, Rule 41], including necessarily the 
authority to appoint a receiver who has the 
power to take and keep possession of the 
property in controversy [Acuña v. Calauag, 
G.R. No. L-10736 (1957)] 
 
d. After final judgment, a receiver may be 
appointed as an aid to the execution of 
judgment [Philippine Trust Company v. 
Santamaria, G.R. 31951 (1929)] 
 
e. Appointment of a receiver over the 
property in custodia legis may be allowed 
when it is justified by special circumstances, 
as when it is reasonably necessary to secure 
and protect the rights of the real owner [Dolar 
v. Sundiam, G.R. No. 27361 (1971)] 
 
Who may appoint a receiver 
 
a. Court where the action is pending 
b. CA 
c. SC 
d. During the pendency of an appeal, the 
appellate court may allow an application for 
the appointment of a receiver to be filed in 
and decided by the court of origin [Sec. 1, 
Rule 59] 
 
 
Requisites of appointment of a receiver 
 
a. Verified application filed by the party 
requesting for the appointment of the 
receiver [Sec. 1, Rule 59] 
 
b. The grounds stated in Sec. 1, Rule 59 
enumerated in Part D.1 of this (Provisional 
Remedies) reviewer. 
 
c. Application must be with notice and must 
be set for hearing; 
 
d. Before appointing a receiver, the court 
shall require the applicant to post a bond 
executed to the party against whom the 
application is presented, in an amount to be 
fixed by the court. [Sec. 2, Rule 59] 
 
e. Before entering upon his duties, the 
receiver must be sworn to perform his duties 
faithfully and shall file a bond, executed to 
such person and in such sum as the court 
may direct [Sec. 4, Rule 59] 
 
Oath and bond requirement 
 
Before entering his duties, the receiver shall 
be sworn to perform them faithfully, and shall 
file a bond, executed to such person and in 
such sum as the court may direct, to the 
effect that he will faithfully discharge his 
duties. 
 
Powers of a receiver 
 
Subject to the control of the court in which the 
action or proceeding is pending, a receiver 
shall have the power to 
 
a. Bring and defend, in such capacity, actions 
in his own name 
 
b. Take and keep possession of the property 
in controversy 
 
c. Receive rents 


<!-- PAGE 144 -->

 
 
132 
 
d. Collect debts due to himself as receiver or 
to the fund, property, estate, person, or 
corporation of which he is the receiver 
 
e. Compound for and compromise the same 
 
f. Make transfers 
 
g. Pay outstanding debts 
 
h. Divide the money and other property that 
shall remain among the persons legally 
entitled to receive the same 
 
i. Generally to do such acts respecting the 
property as the court may authorize 
 
j. Invest funds in his hands, only by order of 
the court upon the written consent of all the 
parties [Sec. 6, Rule 59] 
 
Ground for termination of receivership 
 
The necessity for a receiver no longer exists. 
[Sec. 8, Rule 59 
 
Procedure for termination of receivership 
 
a. The court shall determine that the 
necessity for a receiver no longer exists 
 
i. Motu proprio or 
ii. On motion of either party 
 
b. Due notice should be given to all 
interested parties 
 
c. Hearing shall be conducted 
 
d. After due notice and hearing, the court 
shall 
 
i. Settle the accounts of the receiver 
ii. Direct the delivery of the funds and 
other property in his possession to the 
person adjudged to be entitled to 
receive them, and 
iii. Order the discharge of the receiver 
from further duty as such 
iv. Allow the receiver such reasonable 
compensation as the circumstances of 
the case warrant, to be taxed as costs 
against 
the 
defeated 
party, 
or 
apportioned, as justice requires. [Sec. 
8, Rule 59] 
 
 
E. REPLEVIN – RULE 60 
 
Replevin is an action for the recovery of 
personal property. It is both a principal 
remedy and a provisional relief. When 
utilized as a principal remedy, the objective 
is to recover possession of personal property 
that may have been wrongfully detained by 
another. In this sense, it no longer depends 
on the existence of a principal action. (This is 
an exception to the general rule the 
provisional remedies are ancillary remedies).  
 
When sought as a provisional relief, it allows 
a plaintiff to retain the contested property 
during the pendency of the action. 
 
When obtained; Who can obtain 
 
A party praying for the recovery of 
possession of personal property may, at the 
commencement of the action or at any time 
before answer, apply for an order for the 
delivery of such property to him. 
 
Scope of Applicant’s Title 
 
GR: Primarily, the action of replevin 
determines NOTHING MORE than the right 
of possession. 
 
XPN: When the title to the property is 
distinctly put in issue by the defendant's plea, 
the question of ownership may be resolved 
in the same proceeding (Chiao Liong v. CA, 
G.R. No. 106251 (1993) 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 145 -->

 
 
133 
Requisites for issuance: 
 
The applicant must show by his own affidavit 
or that of some other person who personally 
knows the facts: 
 
(a) That the applicant is the owner of the 
property claimed, particularly describing it, or 
is entitled to the possession thereof; 
 
(b) That the property is wrongfully detained 
by the adverse party, alleging the cause of 
detention thereof according to the best of his 
knowledge, information, and belief; 
 
(c) That the property has not been distrained 
or taken for a tax assessment or a fine 
pursuant to law, or seized under a writ of 
execution or preliminary attachment, or 
otherwise placed under custodia legis, or if 
so seized, that it is exempt from such seizure 
or custody; and 
 
(d) The actual market value of the property. 
 
Applicant’s Bond (Replevin Bond) 
 
The applicant must also give a bond, 
executed to the adverse party in double the 
value of the property as stated in the affidavit 
aforementioned. 
 
Return of property 
 
If the adverse party objects to the sufficiency 
of the  
 
a. Applicant’s bond, or  
 
b. Surety or sureties thereon 
 
He cannot immediately require the return of 
the property, but he may, at any time before 
the delivery of the property to the applicant, 
require the return thereof. As such, he must 
file redelivery bond with the court where the 
action is pending. 
 
 
 
Recovering damages on an applicant’s 
bond  
 
Requirements: 
 
a. The defendant- claimant has secured a 
favorable judgment the main action, meaning 
that the plaintiff has no cause of action and 
was not entitled to the replevin;  
 
b. The application for damages, showing 
claimant’s right thereto and the amount 
thereof, be filed in the same action before 
trial or before appeal is perfected or before 
the judgment becomes executory;  
 
c. Due notice be given to the other party and 
his surety or sureties, notice to the principal 
not being sufficient;  
 
d. A proper hearing and the award for 
damages should be included in the final 
judgment 
 
Judgment 
 
After trial of the issues, the court shall 
determine who has the right of possession to 
and the value of the property and shall render 
judgment in the alternative for the delivery 
thereof to the party entitled to the same, or 
for its value in case delivery cannot be made, 
and also for such damages as either party 
may prove, with costs. 
 
 
F. SUPPORT PENDENTE LITE – RULE 61 
 
Support 
pendente 
lite 
is 
an 
amount 
adjudicated by the trial court during the 
pendency of an action for support upon 
application by plaintiff at the commencement 
of the proper action or at any time afterwards.  


<!-- PAGE 146 -->

 
 
134 
As support pendente lite is a provisional 
remedy, it is not necessary that the court 
should inquire fully into the merits of the 
case, it being sufficient that the court 
ascertain the kind of evidence and the 
amount thereof that is deemed sufficient to 
enable it to justly resolve the application one 
way or the other. Mere affidavits may satisfy 
the court to pass upon the application for 
support pendente lite. 
 
When filed 
 
The application for support pendente lite may 
be filed by any party at the commencement 
of the proper action or proceeding, or at any 
time prior to the judgment or final order. (Rule 
61, Sec. 1) 
 
Is the order fixing the amount of support 
pendente lite final? 
 
No. The trial court's order fixing the amount 
of support pendente lite is not final in 
character because it can be the subject of 
modification, depending on the changing 
conditions affecting the liability of the obligor 
to pay the amount fixed for support. (San 
Juan v. Valenzuela, et al., G.R. No. L-59906, 
Oct. 23, 1982) 
 
It is to be understood that the order, whether 
denying or granting the support pendente 
lite, is interlocutory and consequently not 
appealable. However, if the application is 
granted, the order is immediately executory. 
Consequently, if an appeal is nevertheless 
taken thereon, and no objection is interposed 
hereto, the appeal shall be entertained as the 
objection is deemed waived. 
 
 
G. PROVISIONAL DEPOSIT – RULE 135, 
SECS. 5(G) AND 6, IN RELATION TO 
LORENZO SHIPPING CORP. V. VILLARIN, 
G.R. NOS. 175727 & 178713, MARCH 6, 
2019 AND GUERRERO ESTATE DEV’T. 
CORP. V. LEVISTE & GUERRERO REALTY 
CORP., G.R. NO. 253428, FEBRUARY 16, 
2022 
 
Nature 
and 
purpose 
of 
provisional 
deposit 
 
Based on jurisprudence, a deposit order is an 
extraordinary provisional remedy whereby 
money or other property is placed in custodia 
legis to ensure restitution to whichever party 
is declared entitled thereto after court 
proceedings. It is extraordinary because its 
basis is not found in Rules 57 to 61 of the 
Rules of Court on Provisional Remedies but 
rather, under Sections 5(g) and 6 of Rule 135 
of the same Rules[53] pertaining to the 
inherent power of every court "[t]o amend 
and control its process and orders so as to 
make them conformable to law and justice;" 
as well as to issue "all auxiliary writs, 
processes and other means necessary" to 
carry its jurisdiction into effect. (Lorenzo 
Shipping Corporation v. Villarin, et al., G.R. 
No. 174727, March 6, 2019) 
 
Legal 
basis 
for 
this 
extraordinary 
provisional remedy 
 
While deposit may not be included in the 
provisional remedies stated in Rules 57 to 61 
of the Rules of Court, this does not mean, 
however, that its concept as a provisional 
remedy is nonexistent. As correctly pointed 
out by the appellate court, Rule 135 gives 
courts wide latitude in employing means to 
carry their jurisdiction into effect. (Lorenzo 
Shipping Corporation v. Villarin, et al., G.R. 
No. 174727, March 6, 2019) 
 
In justifying the availability of deposit as a 
provisional remedy, the Court explained that 


<!-- PAGE 147 -->

 
 
135 
Rule 135 of the Rules of Court gives the 
courts wide latitude in employing means to 
carry 
their 
jurisdiction 
into 
effect. 
 
Specifically, Sections 5(g) and 6, Rule 135 of 
the Rules of Court, the provisions relied upon 
by the RTC in granting GEDCOR's Motion to 
Deposit, provide: 
 
Section 5. Inherent power of courts. - Every 
court shall have the power: xxx (g) To amend 
and control its process and orders so as to 
make them conformable to law and justice; 
 
Section 6. Means to carry jurisdiction into 
effect. - When by law jurisdiction is conferred 
on a court or judicial officer, all auxiliary writs, 
processes and other means necessary to 
carry it into effect may be employed by such 
court or officer; and if the procedure to be 
followed in the exercise of such jurisdiction is 
not specifically pointed out by law or by these 
rules, any suitable process or mode of 
proceeding may be adopted which appears 
conformable to the spirit of said law or rules. 
 
Two categories of provisional deposit 
 
 In the first category, the demandability 
of the money or other property to be 
deposited is not, or cannot—because of 
the nature of the relief sought—be 
contested by the party-depositor. 
 
Example: In interpleader cases, the 
plaintiff seeks to compel the litigation of 
two conflicting claims to the property in 
question. The plaintiff may then avail of 
the provisional remedy of provisional 
deposit, and the property in question 
shall be made under custodia legis, so 
that the amount/property deposited may 
easily be turned over to whoever would 
be adjudged properly entitled thereto. 
 
 In the second category, the party-
depositor regularly receives money or 
other property from a non-party during 
the pendency of the case, and the court 
deems it proper to place such money or 
other property in custodia legis pending 
final determination of the party truly 
entitled to the same. 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 148 -->

 
 
136 
 
V. SPECIAL CIVIL ACTIONS 
 
 
A. Concept 
Ordinary civil actions, governed by Rule 2, 
Section 1, involve disputes over private rights 
or wrongs wherein the plaintiff seeks the 
enforcement or protection of a right, or the 
prevention or redress of a wrong. They 
proceeded in accordance with general rules 
on civil procedure.  
In contrast, special civil actions, defined 
under Rule 1, Section 3, have unique 
procedural rules due to their subject matter 
or purpose, combining features of both civil 
and extraordinary remedies. These actions, 
enumerated in Rules 62 to 71, include 
interpleader, declaratory relief, certiorari, 
prohibition, and quo warranto, among others. 
B. Interpleader – Rule 62 
 
An interpleader is a special civil action filed 
by a person against whom two conflicting 
claims are made upon the same subject 
matter and over which he claims no interest 
whatsoever, or if he has an interest, it is one 
which, in whole or in part, is not disputed by 
the claimants [Sec. 1, Rule 62]. 
Purpose of the Remedy 
a. To compel the conflicting claimants to 
interplead and litigate their several claims 
among themselves [Sec. 1, Rule 62]. 
 
b. Not to protect a person against double 
liability but to protect him from double 
vexation in respect of one liability [Beltran 
v.PHHC, G.R. No. L-25138 (1969)]. 
Requisites for Interpleader 
a. There must be 2 or more claimants with 
adverse or conflicting interest; 
 
 b. The conflicting claims involves the same 
subject matter; 
 
c. The conflicting claims are made against 
the same person; and 
 
 d. The plaintiff has no claim upon the subject 
matter of the adverse claims or if he has an 
interest at all, such interest is not disputed by 
the claimants. 
When to File  
 
GR: Reasonable time after a dispute has 
arisen without waiting to be sued by either of 
the contending parties. Otherwise, it may be 
barred by laches.  


<!-- PAGE 149 -->

 
 
137 
XPN: Where the stakeholder acts with 
reasonable 
diligence 
in 
view 
of 
environmental circumstances, the remedy is 
not barred. 
Person to file 
 
The person against whom the conflicting 
claims are made and claims no interest in the 
subject matter. 
Effect of Failure to Answer 
If any claimant fails to plead within the time 
therein fixed, the court may, on motion, 
1. Declare him in default; and 
2. Render judgment barring him from any 
claim in respect to the subject matter. 
Dismissal 
Proper 
Grounds 
to 
Dismiss 
an 
Interpleader 
a. Impropriety of Interpleader 
b. Allowable grounds for a motion to dismiss, 
namely: 
 
1. Lack of jurisdiction over the subject 
matter 
2. Litis pendentia 
3. Res judicata 
4. Prescription (Sec. 12 (a), Rule 15) 
 
 
C. Declaratory Relief and Similar 
Remedies – Rule 63 
Types of Actions Under Rule 63 
1. Petition for declaratory relief; and 
 
2. Similar remedies 
 
a. Action for reformation of an instrument; 
b. Action to quiet title or remove clouds 
therefrom; and 
c. Action to consolidate ownership under  Art. 
1607, CC  
 
Petition for Declaratory Relief 
 
Under 
Rule 
63 
and 
jurisprudence, 
declaratory relief requires an actual 
justiciable controversy or at least the 
“ripening seeds” of one.  
 
 
Here, Proclamation No. 1027 specified areas 
to be retained by MIAA, effectively reducing 
the land earlier segregated for disposition 
under Proclamation No. 144 as amended by 
Proclamation No. 391. Since petitioners were 
actual occupants of the retained areas, they 
faced a real and imminent loss of their 
opportunity to benefit from the housing 
program. They need not wait for eviction 
before bringing suit, as the proclamation 
itself created the direct adverse effect. 
(★Toston v. People, G.R. No. 232049, 
March 3, 2021, as penned by J. Gaerlan) 
 
Proceedings 
Considered 
as 
Similar 
Remedies 
 
These remedies are considered similar to 
declaratory relief because they also result in 
the adjudication of legal rights of the litigants, 
often without the need of execution to carry 
the judgment into effect: 
 
1. An action for the reformation of an 
instrument, recognized under Articles 
1359 to 1369 of the Civil Code; 
 


<!-- PAGE 150 -->

 
 
138 
2. An action to quiet title, authorized by 
Articles 476 to 481 of the Civil Code; and 
 
3. An action to consolidate ownership 
required by Article 1607 of the CivilCode 
in a sale with a right to repurchase 
(Malana v. Tappa,  G.R. No.181303 
(2009). 
 
Note: A distinction must be made between 
these proceedings and an action for 
declaratory relief because of Sec. 5, Rule 63 
on when the court’s action on such a petition 
is discretionary. 
 
Reformation of an Instrument 
 
Reformation is a remedy in equity, whereby 
a written instrument is made or construed so 
as to express or conform to the real intention 
of the parties, where some error or mistake 
has been committed. 
 
Nature: In personam 
 
Jurisdiction: RTC has exclusive original 
jurisdiction. 
 
Requisites 
 
1. 
There must have been a meeting of 
the minds of the parties to the contract; 
2. 
The instrument does not express the 
true intention of the parties; and 
3. 
The failure of the instrument to 
express the true intention of the parties is 
due 
to 
mistake, 
fraud, 
inequitable 
conduct, 
or 
accident 
(multi-Ventures 
Capital v. Stalwart Management Services 
Corp., G.R. No. 157439, 2007). 
 
Prescriptive Period 
 
In an action for reformation, the plaintiff has 
10 years within which to bring it from the time 
the right of action accrued.  
When Reformation Not Applicable under 
the Civil Code 
 
There shall be no reformation in the following 
cases: 
 
a. Simple donations inter vivos wherein 
no 
condition is imposed, 
b. Wills, or 
c. When the real agreement is void [Art. 
1366, Civil Code]. 
 
When one of the parties has brought an 
action to enforce the instrument, he cannot 
subsequently ask for its reformation (Art. 
1367, Civil Code). 
 
Quieting of Title to Real Property (Quasi 
In Rem) 
 
Whenever there is a cloud on title to real 
property or any interest therein, by reason of 
any of the following: 
 
 
PRICE  
 
1. Proceeding 
2. Record 
3. Instrument 
4. Claim 
5. Encumbrance 
 
Which is apparently valid or effective but 
is in truth and in fact invalid, ineffective, 
voidable, or unenforceable, and may be 
prejudicial to said title, an action may be 
brought to remove such cloud or to quiet the 
title. 


<!-- PAGE 151 -->

 
 
139 
 
An action may also be brought to prevent a 
cloud from being cast upon title to real 
property or any interest therein.  
Jurisdiction:  
 
MeTC/MCTC/MTC or RTC, depending on 
the assessed value of the property. 
 
Requisites: 
 
1. The plaintiff or complainant has a legal or 
an equitable title to or interest in the real 
property subject of the action, and 
 
 
 
2. The deed, claim, encumbrance, or 
proceeding (DCEP) claimed to be casting 
cloud on his title must be shown to be in fact 
invalid or inoperative despite its prima facie 
appearance of validity or legal efficacy 
(Mananquil v. Moico, G.R. No. 180076 
(2012). 
 
 
Consolidation of Ownership 
 
In cases involving real property, the 
consolidation of ownership in favor of the 
vendee due to the vendor's failure to exercise 
the right of redemption under Article 1616 of 
the Civil Code requires a judicial order. This 
judicial order is issued only after the vendor 
has been given the opportunity to be heard, 
as mandated by Article 1607 of the Civil 
Code. 
 
The vendor can only exercise the right of 
repurchase under Article 1616 by returning 
the purchase price to the vendee, along with: 
 
a. The expenses of the contract and other 
legitimate payments made by reason of the 
sale; and 
 
b. The necessary and useful expenses 
incurred on the property sold. 
These provisions safeguard both parties' 
rights and ensure fairness in transactions 
involving the redemption of real property. 
 
Applicability: 
 
It applies only to conventional redemption 
under Article 1607, in relation to Article 1616, 
of the Civil Code.  
 
Jurisdiction: MeTC/MCTC/MTC or RTC, 
depending on the assessed value of the 
property. 
 
Declaratory Relief 
 
The subject matter in a petition for 
declaratory relief is any of the following 
(EXCLUSIVE LIST): 
 
Will, written Instrument, Deed, Contract, 
Executive order or resolution, 
 
A declaratory relief is an action by any 
person interested in a deed, will, contract 
or other written instrument, executive 
order or resolution, to determine any 
question of construction or validity arising 
from the instrument, executive order or 


<!-- PAGE 152 -->

 
 
140 
regulation, or statute, and for a declaration of 
his rights and duties thereunder. 
 
 
 
The only issue that can be raised in such a 
petition is the question of construction or 
validity of provisions in an instrument or 
statute. Corollary is the general rule that such 
an action must be justified, as no other 
adequate relief is available. 
 
Purpose 
 
To secure an authoritative statement of the 
rights and obligations of the parties under a 
statute, deed, contract, etc. for their guidance 
in its enforcement or compliance and not to 
settle issues arising from its alleged breach. 
 
Where to File Declaratory Relief 
 
GR: Exclusive and original jurisdiction is with 
the RTC since the subject in a petition for 
declaratory relief is incapable of pecuniary 
estimation (Sec. 19, B.P.129, as amended by 
R.A. 7691). 
 
XPN: Where the action is a proceeding 
similar to declaratory relief (e.g. quieting of 
title to real property), jurisdiction will depend 
on the assessed value of the property 
(Malana v.Tappa, G.R. No. 181303 (2009). 
 
Parties to the Action 
 
1. 
All persons who have or claim any 
interest which would be affected by the 
declaration must be impleaded (Sec. 2, Rule 
63). 
 
2. 
In actions questioning the validity of a 
statute, executive order, or governmental 
regulation, the Solicitor General must be 
notified and is entitled to be heard (Sec. 3, 
Rule 63). 
 
3. 
For actions involving the validity of a 
local government ordinance, the prosecutor 
or 
attorney 
of 
the 
concerned 
local 
government unit must also be notified and 
given the opportunity to be heard. 
 
Note: The non-joinder of interested 
persons is not a jurisdictional defect, but 
unjoined persons will not be bound or 
prejudiced by the decision unless the Rules 
provide otherwise (Sec. 2, Rule 63). 
 
Requisites 
 
a. The subject matter of the controversy must 
be a Will, written Instrument, Deed, Contract, 
Executive order or resolution (WIDE C Ex) 
 
b. The terms of said documents and the 
validity thereof are doubtful and require 
judicial construction; 
 
c. There must have been no breach of the 
documents in question;  
 
A petition for declaratory relief is filed 
BEFORE the occurrence of any breach or 
violation of the deed, contract, statute, 
ordinance 
or 
executive 
order 
or 
regulation. It will not prosper when brought 
after a contract or a statute has already been 
breached or violated. 
 
If there has already been a breach, the 
appropriate ordinary civil action and NOT 
declaratory relief should be filed [City of 
Lapu-Lapu 
v. 
PEZA, 
G.R. 
No. 
184203(2014)]. 


<!-- PAGE 153 -->

 
 
141 
d. There must be an actual justiciable 
controversy or the “ripening seeds” of one 
between persons whose interests are 
adverse; 
 
A justiciable controversy refers to an 
existing case or controversy appropriate or 
ripe for judicial determination, not one that is 
conjectural or merely anticipatory. 
 
e.  Adequate relief is not available through 
other means or other forms of action or 
proceeding. 
 
 
D. Certiorari, Prohibition, and 
Mandamus – Rule 65 
 
Certiorari 
A writ emanating from the 
proper court directed against 
any tribunal, board or officer 
exercising judicial or quasi-
judicial functions, the purpose 
of which is to correct errors of 
jurisdiction - i.e. without or in 
excess of jurisdiction, or with 
grave abuse of discretion 
amounting to the same 
Prohibition 
A writ issued by the proper 
court and directed against any 
tribunal, corporation, board, 
officer or person, whether 
exercising 
judicial, 
quasi-
judicial or ministerial functions, 
commanding the respondent 
to 
desist 
from 
further 
proceedings in the action or 
matter specified therein 
Mandamus 
A writ to compel a tribunal, 
corporation, board, officer or 
person to do the act required to 
be done to protect the rights of 
the 
petitioner 
when 
the 
respondent 
unlawfully 
neglects the performance of an 
act which the law specifically 
enjoins as a duty resulting from 
an office, trust, or station, or 
excludes another from the use 
and enjoyment of a right or 
office to which such other is 
entitled, and there is no other 
plain, speedy and adequate 
remedy in the ordinary course 
of law [Sec. 3, Rule 65]. 
(See Certiorari: Rule 45 v. Rule 65 – 
Discussion on Appeals) 
 
The remedies of appeal and certiorari are 
mutually exclusive and not alternative or 
successive. Thus, a petitioner must show 
valid reasons why the issues raised in his 
petition for certiorari could not have been 
raised on appeal.
