1. Requisites, when and where to file  
Requisites: 
1. Respondent (BOT – Board, Officer, 
Tribunal) is exercising judicial or quasi- 
judicial functions; 
 
2. Respondent acted without or in excess of 
its jurisdiction or acted with grave abuse of 
discretion (GAD) amounting to lack of 
jurisdiction; and 
Mere abuse of discretion is not 
enough 
 
The abuse of discretion must be grave, 
which means either that the judicial or 
quasi-judicial power was exercised in an 
arbitrary or despotic manner by reason of 
passion or personal hostility, or that the 
respondent judge, tribunal or board 
evaded a positive duty, or virtually 
refused to perform the duty enjoined or to 
act in contemplation of law, such as when 
such judge, tribunal or board exercising 
judicial or quasi-judicial powers acted in 
a capricious or whimsical manner as to 
be equivalent to lack of jurisdiction. 
Grave abuse of discretion under Rule 
65 is the arbitrary or despotic exercise of 
power due to passion, prejudice or 
personal hostility;  
 
or 
the 
whimsical, 
arbitrary, 
or 
capricious exercise of power that 
amounts to an evasion or refusal to 
perform a positive duty enjoined by 
law or to act at all in contemplation of 
law. The abuse of discretion must be 
patent and gross. (★Jesus Caballes v. 
CA, G.R. No. 263481, February 8, 2023, 
as penned by J. Gaerlan) 
3. There must be no (APSA) appeal or no 
other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy. 
A petition for review under Rule 65 requires 
that there be NO APPEAL OR OTHER 
PLAIN, 
SPEEDY, 
AND 
ADEQUATE 
REMEDY AVAILABLE TO CORRECT THE 
ERROR. Thus, certiorari may not be issued 
if the error can be the subject of an ordinary 
appeal. 
 
The petitioners resorted to certiorari, by 
alleging that the Court of Appeals acted in 
grave abuse of discretion when it rendered 
the rulings against them. Yet, a plain, 
speedy, and adequate remedy was still 
available to petitioners for purposes of 
challenging the dispositions of the Court of 
Appeals – a petition for review on certiorari 
under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court. 
(RELIABLE INDUSTRIAL v. CAL, GR No. 
190924 | 2021-09-14) 
GR: Where an appeal is available, certiorari 
will not lie. 


<!-- PAGE 155 -->

 
 
143 
XPNs:  
a. Where appeal does not constitute a 
speedy and adequate remedy;  
 
b. Where orders were also issued either in 
excess of or without jurisdiction; 
 
c. For certain special considerations, as 
public welfare or public policy;  
 
d. Where, in criminal actions, the court 
rejects the rebuttal evidence 
for 
the 
prosecution as, in the case of acquittal, there 
could be no remedy;  
 
e. Where the order is a patent nullity; and  
 
f. Where the decision in the certiorari case 
will avoid future litigations. 
 
 
The writ of certiorari or prohibition may be 
issued to correct errors of jurisdiction (not 
errors of judgment) committed not only by a 
tribunal, 
corporation, 
board 
or 
officer 
exercising 
judicial, 
quasi-judicial 
or 
ministerial functions but also to set right, 
undo and restrain any act of grave abuse of 
discretion amounting to lack or excess of 
jurisdiction by any branch or instrumentality 
of the Government, even if the latter does not 
exercise judicial, quasi-judicial or ministerial 
functions (Araullo v. Aquino, G.R. No. 
209287 (2014). 
Errors of judgment 
 
Errors of judgement are those errors arising 
from erroneous conclusions of law. 
 
What cannot be raised a certiorari 
 
Questions of fact cannot be raised in an 
original action for certiorari. Only established 
or admitted facts may be considered. 
II. Prohibition 
 
Prohibition is a preventive remedy. However, 
to prevent the respondent from performing 
the act sought to be prevented during the 
pendency of the proceedings for the writ, the 
petitioner should obtain a restraining order 
and/or a writ of preliminary injunction. 
 
Function of prohibition 
 
The office of prohibition is not to correct 
errors of judgment but to prevent or restrain 
usurpation by inferior tribunals and to compel 
them to observe the limitation of their 
jurisdictions. 
 
Requisites:  
 
1. Respondent (BOT – Board, Officer, 
Tribunal) is exercising judicial or quasi- 
judicial functions;  
 
2. Respondent acted without or in excess of 
its jurisdiction or acted with grave abuse of 
discretion (GAD) amounting to lack of 
jurisdiction; and 
 
 
3. There must be no (APSA) appeal or no 
other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy 
  
GR: Prohibition, as a rule, does not lie to 
restrain an act which h already been done. 
 
XPN: A writ of prohibition will lie to prevent 
the unlawful creation of a new province by 
those in the corridors of power who could 
avoid judicial intervention and review by 
merely speedily and stealthily completing the 
commission of such illegality. 
 
 
 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 156 -->

 
 
144 
III. Mandamus 
 
Requisites: 
 
1. Respondent unlawfully:  
 
a. Neglects the performance of an act which 
the law specifically enjoins as a duty resulting 
from an office, trust, or station; or  
 
b. Excludes another from the use and 
enjoyment of a right or office to which such 
other isentitled; and 
 
2. There is no other plain, speedy, and 
adequate (PSA) remedy in the ordinary 
course of law. 
 
There must be a well-defined, clear legal 
right or duty which is enjoined by law; 
hence, a contractual duty cannot be enforced 
by mandamus. 
 
Note: If the respondent claims any right to the 
office and usurps, intrudes into or unlawfully 
holds it against the petitioner, quo warranto 
is the proper remedy (Sec. 1, Rule 66). 
3. 
Mandamus 
is 
available 
against 
respondents who exercise judicial and/or 
non-judicial functions. 
 
Ministerial Duty 
 
The respondent must be exercising a 
ministerial duty. As such, mandamus “will lie 
to compel discharge of the discretionary duty 
itself but not to control the discretion to be 
exercised. In other words, a mandamus can 
be issued to require action, but not specific 
action”.

When to file 
 
The petition for certiorari, prohibitions or 
mandamus shall be filed before the proper 
court:  
 
(1) Not later than 60 days from notice of 
the judgment, order or resolution; or  
 
 
 
(2) In case a motion for reconsideration or 
new trial is timely filed, whether such motion 
is required or not, the petition shall be filed 
not later than 60 days counted from the 
notice of the denial of the motion. 
 
 
 
Period is now inextendible 
 
GR: Petitions for certiorari must be filed 
strictly within 60 days from notice of 
judgment or from the order denying a motion 
for reconsideration. 
 
The last paragraph of Section 4 provides that 
"No extension of time to file the petition shall 
be granted except for compelling reasons 
and in no case exceeding fifteen (15) days" 
has been deleted by A.M. No. 07-7-12- SC, 
effective December 27, 2007. 
 
XPN: To serve substantial justice or to 
protect strong public interest. (Republic vs.

145 
St. Vincent de Paul Colleges, Inc., G.R. No. 
192908, August 22, 2012). 
 
Rule 65 is NOT a remedy for lost appeal 
 
GR: It is settled that an extraordinary remedy 
of certiorari will not lie if there is a plain, 
speedy, and adequate remedy in the 
ordinary course of law. It is not and cannot 
be a substitute for an appeal, where the latter 
remedy is available. 
 
XPNs:  
 
(a) 
when 
public 
welfare 
and 
the 
advancement of public policy dictates;  
 
(b) when the broader interest of justice so 
requires; 
 
(c) when the writs issued are null and void; or 
 
(d) when the questioned order amounts to an

Where to File  
 
Supreme Court 
 
Subject to the doctrine of hierarchy of courts 
and only when compelling reasons exist for 
not filing the same with the lower courts (Uy 
v. Contreras, G.R. No.111416-17 (1994]. 
 
RTC 
 
If the petition relates to an act or an omission 
of an MTC, corporation, board, officer or 
person (Sec. 4, Rule 65, as amended by

Court of Appeals 
 
If the petition involves an act or an omission 
of a quasi-judicial agency, unless otherwise

Court of Appeals or Sandiganbayan 
 
Whether or not in aid of appellate jurisdiction 
(Sec. 4, A.M. No. 07-7- 12-SC) 
 
Commission on Elections 
 
In election cases involving an act or an  
omission of an MTC or RTC (Sec. 4, A.M. No. 
07-7-12-SC) 
 
Effects of filing of an unmeritorious 
petition  
 
Under Section 8, Rule 65, the court may 
dismiss the petition if it finds the same to be 
“patently 
without 
merit, 
prosecuted 
manifestly for delay, or that the questions 
raised therein are too unsubstantial to 
require consideration.”  
 
The Supreme Court has consistently ruled 
that abuse of certiorari petitions undermines 
the judicial system and should be penalized, 
as held in Mendoza v. Mayor Villas (G.R. No. 
187256, March 21, 2012), emphasizing the 
need for candor and good faith in all judicial 
pleadings. 
 
 
E. Quo Warranto – Rule 66 
Quo Warranto - “by what authority” 
A quo warranto proceeding is the proper 
legal remedy to determine the right or title to 
the contested public office and to oust the 
holder from its enjoyment. 
It is brought against the person who is 
alleged to have usurped, intruded into, or 
unlawfully held or exercised the public office, 
and may be commenced by the Solicitor 
General or a public prosecutor, as the case 
may be, or by any person claiming to be 
entitled to the public office or position 
usurped or unlawfully held or exercised by 
another. (Aguinaldo v. Aquino III, G.R. No. 
224302, November 29, 2016) 
A Quo Warranto proceeding may be 
commenced by a verified petition brought 


<!-- PAGE 158 -->

 
 
146 
in the name of the Republic of the Philippines 
against: 
(a) A person who usurps, intrudes into, or 
unlawfully holds or exercises a public 
office, position or franchise;  
(b) A public officer who does or suffers an 
act which, by the provision of law, 
constitutes a ground for the forfeiture of 
his office; or  
(c) An association which acts as a 
corporation within the Philippines without 
being legally incorporated or without 
lawful authority so to act. (Rule 66, 
Sec.1). 
 
F. Expropriation – Rule 67; R.A. No. 
8974, Sec. 4 
 
1. Stages of Expropriation 
Two 
(2) 
Stages 
in 
an 
Action 
for 
Expropriation 
1. The determination of the authority of the 
plaintiff to exercise the power of eminent 
domain and the propriety of its exercise in the 
context of the facts involved in the suit. 
 
2. The determination by the Court of just 
compensation for the property sought to be 
taken. 
 
Note: A final order sustaining the right to 
expropriate the property may be appealed by 
any party aggrieved thereby. Such appeal, 
however, shall not prevent the court from 
determining the just compensation to be paid 
2. Immediate Possession of 
Expropriated Land – R.A. No. 
10752 
Under R.A. No. 10752 (The Right-of-Way 
Act), a plaintiff can immediately enter into 
possession of real property for a government 
infrastructure project after complying with the 
requirements under Section 6. 
Section 6 of R.A. No. 10752 (Right-of-Way 
Act) 
"Upon the filing of the complaint or at any 
time thereafter, and after due notice to the 
defendant, the implementing agency shall 
immediately pay the property owner the 
amount equivalent to the sum of: (a) the 
current market value of the property as 
determined by the Bureau of Internal 
Revenue (BIR) zonal valuation, and (b) the 
value of improvements and/or structures 
using the replacement cost method." 
The government must first offer the property 
owner compensation based on current 
market value determined by a government 
financial institution or an independent 
property 
appraiser. 
Upon 
acceptance, 
payment is made in cash, or, in cases of 
refusal or failure to agree, the government 
deposits the amount equivalent to the current 
zonal value of the property and other relevant 
valuations, as supported by jurisprudence 
such as Republic v. Sarabia (G.R. No. 
157847, October 13, 2009). 
To reiterate, if the property owner refuses or 
fails to accept payment, the amount shall be 
deposited in court, allowing the government 
to immediately take possession of the 
property. 


<!-- PAGE 159 -->

 
 
147 
Once the required compensation is paid or 
deposited, the government, through the 
implementing agency, is granted immediate 
possession to prevent delays in public 
infrastructure projects, subject to judicial 
oversight to protect the property owner's 
constitutional right to due process. 
3. Ascertainment of Just 
Compensation 
 
Just compensation is defined as the FULL 
AND FAIR EQUIVALENT of the property 
taken from its owner by the expropriator.  
1. The determination by the Court of 
“the just compensation for the property 
sought to be taken” should be done with 
the assistance of not more than three (3) 
commissioners. 
2. The 
order 
fixing 
the 
just 
compensation on the basis of the 
evidence before, and the findings of, the 
commissioners would be final. 
Effect 
of 
Failure 
to 
Pay 
Just 
Compensation 
GR: Non-payment of just compensation does 
not entitle the private landowner to recover 
possession of the expropriated lots. 
 
XPN: In cases where the government failed 
to pay just compensation within 5 years from 
the finality of judgment in the expropriation 
proceedings, the owners concerned shall 
have the right to recover possession of their 
property (Yujuico v. Atienza, G.R. No. 
164282 (2005). 
 
 
G. Foreclosure of Real Estate Mortgage 
– Rule 68; R.A. No. 8791, Sec. 47 
 
1. Judicial 
Judicial foreclosure is a mode of foreclosure 
that is done pursuant to Rule 68 of the Rules 
of Court. 
Jurisdiction 
Where the action is one involving title to, or 
possession of, real property or any 
interest 
therein 
(real 
action), 
the 
determination of jurisdiction shall be made by 
inquiring into the assessed value of the 
property. Exclusive original jurisdiction would 
fall either in the MTC or the RTC depending 
on the assessed value. 
Sale 
 
When the defendant fails to pay the amount 
of the judgment ascertaining the amount due 
to the plaintiff upon the mortgage debt, the 
court, upon motion, shall order the property 
to be sold in the manner and under the 
provisions of Rule 39 and other regulations 
governing sales of real estate under 
execution [Sec. 3, Rule 68]. 


<!-- PAGE 160 -->

 
 
148 
Under Rule 39, the notice of sale shall 
specify the place, date, and exact time of the 
sale. The place of the sale may be agreed 
upon by the parties. 
In the absence of such agreement, the sale 
of real property shall be held in the office of 
the clerk of court in the RTC or MTC which 
issued the writ, or which was designated by 
the appellate court [Sec. 15, Rule 39].  
Posting Requirement 
Before the sale of real property, it is required 
that there be posting for 20 days in 3 public 
places, preferably in conspicuous areas of 
the municipal or city hall, post office, and 
public market in the municipality or city where 
the sale is to take place. 
Such notice must particularly describe the 
property and state where the property is to 
be sold (Sec 15(c), Rule 39). 
Effect of Failure to Post Notice 
The failure to post a notice is not per se a 
ground for invalidating the sale provided that 
the notice thereof is duly published in a  
newspaper of general circulation [DBP v. 
Aguirre, G.R. No. 144877 (2001)]. 
Publication 
If the assessed value of the property exceeds 
P50,000, one must also publish a copy of the 
notice once a week for 2 consecutive weeks 
in one newspaper having general circulation 
in the province or city [Sec. 15 (c), Rule 39]. 
Personal Notice to Mortgagor 
The mortgagor is notified through the service 
of summons [Sec. 1, Rule 68]. 
Possession of Property 
GR: Upon the finality of the order of 
confirmation or upon the expiration of the 
period of redemption, the purchaser at the 
auction sale or the last redemptioner, if any, 
shall be entitled to the possession of the 
property. 
Order of confirmation; 
 
After the foreclosure sale, the mortgagee 
should file a motion for the confirmation of 
the sale. Such requires notice and hearing. 
During the hearing, the mortgagor will be 
allowed to show why the sale should not be 
confirmed. 
If, after such, the court finds ground to 
confirm, 
it 
shall 
issue 
the 
order 
of 
confirmation. 
Such order removes from the parties the right 
to the property and grants such right to the 
purchaser, subject to redemption. 
Such order of confirmation is appealable. 
XPN: When a third party is actually holding 
the same adversely to the judgment obligor. 
In such a case, the purchaser or the last 
redemptioner 
may 
secure 
a 
writ 
of 
possession, upon motion, from the court 
(Sec. 3, Rule 68). 
Remedy of Debtor If Foreclosure Not 
Proper  
The 
debtor-mortgagor 
is 
allowed 
the 
opportunity to show why the sale should not 
be confirmed during the hearing on the 
motion of confirmation of the sale [2 Riano 
318, 2016 Bantam Ed.]. 
A failure to give notice of the hearing for 
motion of confirmation is good cause for 


<!-- PAGE 161 -->

 
 
149 
setting aside the sale [Grimalt v. Velasquez, 
36 Phil 936 (1917)] 
Redemption 
 
GR: There is no right of redemption in a 
judicial foreclosure under Rule 68. 
In judicial foreclosure, there is only an equity 
of redemption, which can be exercised prior 
to the order of confirmation of the foreclosure 
sale. This means that after the foreclosure 
sale 
but 
before 
its 
confirmation, 
the 
mortgagor may exercise his right to pay the 
proceeds of the sale and prevent the 
confirmation of the sale. 
XPN: There is a right of redemption in a 
judicial foreclosure if the foreclosure is in 
favor of banks, as provided for in the General 
Banking Law (See discussion on R.A. No. 
8791, Section 47 – Bank Foreclosure). 
 
Note: What Secs. 2-3, Rule 68 provide for is 
the mortgagor’s equity of redemption. This 
may be exercised by him even beyond the 
period to pay the judgment obligation (i.e. 90-
120 days) and even after the foreclosure sale 
itself, provided it be before the order of the 
confirmation of sale [Rosales v. Alfonso, 
G.R. No. 137792 (2003)]. 
The equity of redemption is the mortgagor’s 
equity to be able to extinguish the mortgage 
and retain ownership of the property [2 Riano 
316, 2016 edition]. 
Amount 
In equity of redemption, the price that needs 
to be paid in order to retain ownership of the 
property and extinguish the mortgage would 
be the debt amount (2 Riano 317, 2016 
Bantam Ed) 
2. Extrajudicial – Act No. 3135 
Extrajudicial foreclosure is a mode of 
foreclosure that is done pursuant to Act 
3135, as amended by Act 4118. 
It is the mode to be used if there is a special 
power inserted in the real estate mortgage 
contract allowing an extrajudicial foreclosure 
sale. Where there is no such special power, 
the foreclosure shall be done judicially 
following Rule 68. 
 
Without the required authority, extrajudicial 
foreclosure proceedings cannot be inititated  
under Act No. 3135. It may only enforce its 
lien through an ordinary collection suit or 
judicial foreclosure proceedings as provided 
under Rule 68 of the Rules of Court (Sps. 
Baysa v. Sps. Plantilla, 763 Phil. 562, 570 
(2015) 
Sale 
Said sale cannot be made legally outside of 
the province in which the property sold is 
situated; and in case the place within said 
province in which the sale is to be made is 
subject to stipulation, such sale shall be 
made in said place or in the municipal 
building of the municipality in which the 
property or part thereof is situated (Sec. 2, 
Act 3135). 
 


<!-- PAGE 162 -->

 
 
150 
Notice 
 
Notice shall be given by posting notices of 
the sale for not less than 20 days in at least 
3 public places of the municipality or city 
where the property is situated (Sec. 3, Act 
3135). 
Publication 
If such property is worth more than P400, 
such notice shall also be published once a 
week for at least three consecutive weeks in 
a newspaper of general circulation in the 
municipality or city (Sec. 3, Act 3135). 
Republication 
During extrajudicial foreclosure proceedings 
under Act 3135, republication as well as 
reposting of the notice of sale is required if 
the foreclosure does not proceed on the date 
originally intended. The lack of republication 
of the notice of the foreclosure sale renders 
it void (Metrobank v. Nikko, G.R. No. 178479 
(2009). 
Personal Notice to Mortgagor 
GR: Personal notice to the mortgagor in 
extrajudicial foreclosure proceedings is not 
necessary, and posting and publication will 
suffice. 
XPN: When the parties stipulate that 
personal notice is additionally required to be 
given the mortgagor. Failure to abide by the 
general rule, or its exception, renders the 
foreclosure proceedings null and void 
(Paradigm v. BPI, G.R. No. 191174 (2017]. 
Remedy of Debtor If Foreclosure is Not 
Proper 
 
The debtor may, in the proceedings in which 
possession was requested, but not later than 
30 days after the purchaser was given 
possession, petition that the sale be set 
aside and the writ of possession cancelled, 
specifying the damages suffered by him, 
because the mortgage was not violated or 
the sale was not made in accordance with 
the (Sec. 8, Act 3135). 
Right of Redemption (ROR) 
 
This right exists only in extrajudicial 
foreclosure where there is always a right of  
redemption within one year from the date of 
sale, but interpreted by the court to mean one 
year from the registration of the sale. 
Who May Redeem 
The debtor, his successors in interest or any 
judicial creditor or judgment creditor of said 
debtor, or any person having a lien on  
property subsequent to the mortgage or deed 
of trust under which the property is sold, may 
redeem the same (Sec. 6, Act 3135). 
Note: 
The 
period 
for 
redemption 
in 
extrajudicial foreclosure is shortened when 
the mortgagor is a juridical person. The 
period of redemption is “until but not after” 
the registration of certificate of sale with the 
Register of Deeds, “which in no case shall be 


<!-- PAGE 163 -->

 
 
151 
more than 3 months after foreclosure, 
whichever is earlier”. 
 
H. Partition – Rule 69 
 
Definition 
Partition is the separation, division and 
assignment of a thing held in common 
among those to whom it may belong. Every 
act which is intended to put an end to 
indivision among co-heirs and legatees or 
devisees is deemed to be a partition (Marcos 
v. Heirs of Isidro Bangi, G.R. No. 185745 
(2014). 
Partition may be: 
 
a. Judicial – Procedure is Rule 69 
b. Extrajudicial – No court intervention is 
required 
Nothing in Rule 69 contained shall be 
construed to restrict or prevent persons 
holding real estate jointly or in common from 
making an amicable partition by agreement 
and suitable instruments of conveyance 
without recourse to an action (Sec. 12, Rule 
69). 
 
Partition by Commissioners  
When Proper 
When the parties are unable to agree upon 
the partition [Sec. 3, Rule 69]. 
Action of the Court 
1. The court shall appoint not more than 3 
competent and disinterested persons as 
commissioners to make the partition, 
2. Commanding them to set off to the plaintiff 
and to each party in interest such part and 
proportion of the property as the court shall 
direct (Sec. 3, Rule 69). 
Partition of Personal Property  
The provisions of Rule 69 shall apply to 
partitions of estates composed of personal 
property, or both real and personal property, 
in so far as the same may be applicable [Sec. 
13, Rule 69]. 
When Partition is Not Allowed 
The following instances are cases when a 
co-owner cannot demand partition, to wit: 
1. There is an agreement among the co-
owners to keep the property undivided for a   
certain period of time not exceeding 10 
years. The term may however be extended 
by a new agreement [Art. 494, Civil Code]. 
2. When partition is prohibited by the donor 
or testator for a period not exceeding 20 
years [Art. 494, Civil Code]. 
3. When a partition is prohibited by law [Art 
494, Civil Code]. 
4. When the property is not subject to a 
physical division and to do so would render it 


<!-- PAGE 164 -->

 
 
152 
unserviceable for the use for which it is 
intended [Art. 495, Civil Code]. 
5. When the condition imposed upon 
voluntary heirs before they can demand 
partition has not yet been fulfilled [Art. 1084, 
Civil Code]. 
Two Stages in Every Action for Partition: 
I. First Stage 
 
Determination of the Propriety of Partition  
This involves a determination of whether the 
subject property is owned in common and 
whether all the co-owners are made parties 
in the case (Lacbayan v. Samoy, G.R. 
No.165427 (2011). 
Remedy 
A final order decreeing partition and 
accounting may be appealed by any party 
aggrieved thereby [Sec. 2, Rule 69]. 
If not appealed, then the parties may partition 
the common property in the way they want. If 
they cannot agree, then the case goes into 
the second stage. However, the order of 
accounting may in the meantime be 
executed [De Mesa v. CA, G.R. No.109387 
(1994)] 
II. Second Stage 
 
 
Actual 
Partitioning 
of 
the 
Subject 
Property  
Partition, in general, is the separation, 
division  and assignment of a thing held in 
common  among those to whom it may 
belong. [Noceda  v. CA, G.R. No. 119730 
(1999)].  
The action for partition is subject to multiple 
appeals and would require a record on 
appeal  [Roman Catholic Archbishop of 
Manila v. CA, G.R. No. 77425 (1991)]. 
Order 
of 
Partition 
and 
Partition 
Agreement 
A. 
Order of Partition 
 
If after the trial the court finds that the plaintiff 
has the right thereto, it shall order the 
partition of the real estate among all the 
parties in interest [Sec. 2, Rule 69]. 
B. 
Partition by Agreement 
 
1. The parties may, if they are able to agree, 
make the partition among themselves by  
proper instruments of conveyance, 
 
2. The court shall confirm the partition so 
agreed upon by all the parties, and 
 
3. Such partition, together with the order of 
the court confirming the same, shall be 


<!-- PAGE 165 -->

 
 
153 
recorded in the registry of deeds of the place 
in which the property is situated (Sec 2, Rule 
69).

J. Contempt – Rule 71 
 
Definition 
Contempt of court is disobedience to the 
court by acting in opposition to its authority, 
justice, and dignity. It signifies not only a 
willful disregard or disobedience to the 
court’s orders  but also conduct tending to 
bring the authority of the court and 
administration of law into disrepute, or,in 
some 
manner, 
to 
impede 
the 
due 
administration of justice [Siy v. NLRC, G.R. 
No. 158971 (2012)]. 
Nature 
The power to declare a person in contempt 
of  court and in dealing with him accordingly 
is an inherent power of the court. It is used 
as a means to protect and preserve the 
dignity of the court, the solemnity of the 
proceedings, and administration of justice. 
[Sison v. Caoibes, A.M. No. RTJ-03-1771 
(2004]. 
Kinds of contempt 
Contempt, whether direct or indirect, may be 
civil or criminal depending on the nature and 
effect of contemptuous act [Montenegro v. 
Montenegro, G.R. No. 156829 (2004)]. 
Criminal contempt 
Civil contempt 
It 
is

of the court or a

acting

or 
disrespect.

A. 
Direct contempt  


<!-- PAGE 167 -->

 
 
155 
For a person to be adjudged guilty of direct 
contempt, he must commit a misbehavior in 
the presence of or so near a judge as to 
interrupt the administration of justice (SBMA 
v. Rodriguez, G.R. No. 160270 (2010). 
 
Grounds: 
1.Misbehavior in the presence of or so near  
 
2.court as to obstruct or interrupt the 
proceedings before the same 
 
3.Disrespect toward the court 
 
4.Offensive personalities toward others, or 
 
5.Refusal to be sword or to answer as  
 
6.witness, or to subscribe to an affidavit or  
 
7.deposition when lawfully required to do so 
 
Other examples: 
 
1. Willful and deliberate forum shopping 
 (Sec. 5, Rule 7) 
 
2.Submission 
of

containing

offensive, 
and 
malicious 
statements submitted to the court (Re: Letter 
of Atty. Noel Sorreda, A.M. No. 05-3-4-SC 
(2005) 
 
 
B. Indirect contempt 
 
Grounds (sec. 3, Rule 71): 
 
1. Misbehavior of an officer of a court in the 
performance of his official duties or in his 
official transactions. 
 
2. Disobedience of or resistance to a lawful  
process, order, or judgment of court,  
including the act of a person who, after being 
dispossessed or ejected from any real 
property by the judgment or process of any 
court of competent jurisdiction, enters or 
attempts or induces another to enter into or 
upon such real property, for the purpose of 
executing acts of ownership or possession, 
or in any manner disturbs the possession 
given to the person adjudged to be entitled 
thereto. 
 
3. Any abuse of or any unlawful interference 
with the processes or proceedings of a court 
not constituting direct contempt. 
 
4. Any improper conduct tending, directly or 
indirectly, to impede, obstruct, or degrade  
the administration of justice. 
 
5. Assuming to be an attorney or an officer of 
a court, and acting as such without authority. 
 
6. Failure to obey a subpoena duly served. 
 
7. The rescue, or attempted rescue, of a 
person or property in the custody of an officer 
by virtue of an order or process of a court 
held by him (Sec. 3, Rule 71) 
 
Other examples 
 
1. Submission, of a false certification of non 
forum shopping or non- compliance with any 
of the undertakings [Sec. 5, Rule 7]. 
 
2. Upon a judgment obligor’s failure to pay 
any such installment when due without good 


<!-- PAGE 168 -->

 
 
156 
excuse, if the court orders him to pay the 
judgment in fixed monthly installments [Sec. 
40, Rule 39]. 
 
Unlike 
direct 
contempt, 
court 
cannot  
summarily adjudge a person guilty of indirect  
contempt. There has to be a charge filed in 
writing, with opportunity on the part of the 
respondent to be heard via comment within 
such 
period 
as 
fixed 
by 
the 
court. 
Respondent may be heard by himself or 
counsel. [Sec. 3, Rule 71] 
 
How contempt proceedings commenced/ 
where to file  
 
1. Where to File Charge (Direct & 
Indirect Contempt) 
 
a. Where committed against a RTC or a court 
of equivalent or higher rank, or against an  
officer appointed by it - the charge may be 
filed with such court. 
 
b. Where committed against a lower court – 
the charge may be filed with the RTC of the 
place in which the lower court is sitting; but 
the proceedings may also be instituted in 
such lower court subject to appeal to the 
RTC of such place in the same manner as 
provided in Sec. 11 of Rule 71. 
 
c. Where committed against persons or 
entities exercising quasi-judicial functions – 
the charge shall be filed in the RTC of the 
place  wherein contempt was committed 
(Sec. 12, Rule 71) 
 
2. By Whom Initiated: 
 
 
 
a. Generally, civil contempt proceedings 
should be instituted by an aggrieved party, or 
his successor, or someone who has 
pecuniary interest in the right to be protected. 
 
b. In criminal contempt proceedings, it is 
generally held that the State is the real 
prosecutor (People v. Godoy, G.R. Nos. 
115908-09 (1995).

indirect contempt

Contempt against quasi-judicial bodies  
 
Under Section 12, Rule 71, contempt 
committed against quasi-judicial entities is 
governed by the same rule unless their 
specific laws provide otherwise. Quasi-
judicial bodies like the NLRC or SEC, 
empowered by statutes (e.g., Labor Code, 
Article 218(d); Securities Regulation Code, 
Section 5.1[l]), may punish for contempt 
within their jurisdiction.  
 
Charges are filed before the Regional Trial 
Court of the place where contempt occurred. 
In Garcia v. De Vera (G.R. No. 165961, 
February 11, 2010), the Supreme Court 
reiterated that Rule 71 applies suppletorily, 
ensuring due process and jurisdictional 
compliance in contempt cases before such 
entities.

VI. SPECIAL PROCEEDINGS AND WRITS 
 
A special proceeding is a remedy by which a 
party seeks to establish a status, a right, or a 
particular fact. (Rule 1, Sec.3c, ROC) 
 
GR: A Special Proceeding is non-adversarial 
in nature. (No definite adverse party because 
it is directed against the whole world). 
 
XPN: May become adversarial in the course 
of 
the 
proceedings 
when 
there 
are 
oppositions to the petition. 
 
Rules in civil actions applicable to special 
proceedings. 
Special 
proceedings 
are 
primarily governed by the special provisions 
applicable to them. In the absence of special 
provisions, the rules provided for in ordinary 
actions shall be, as far as practicable, 
applicable in special proceedings. (Rule 72, 
Sec. 2, ROC). 
A. 
SETTLEMENT 
OF 
ESTATE 
OF 
DECEASED PERSONS 
 
1. Venue and Process – Rule 73 
Jurisdiction of Probate Courts 
A. MTC, MTCC, MCTC, MetC 
Metropolitan Trial Courts, Municipal Trial 
Courts in Cities, Municipal Trial Courts, and 
Municipal Circuit Trial Courts shall exercise 
exclusive original jurisdiction over civil 
actions and probate proceedings, testate 
and 
intestate 
including 
the 
grant 
of 
provisional remedies in proper cases, where 
the value of the personal property, estate, or 
amount of demand DOES NOT EXCEED 
Two Million Pesos (P2,000,000.00). 
B. RTC 
Regional 
Trial 
Courts 
shall 
exercise 
exclusive original jurisdiction in all matters of 
probate, both testate and intestate, where 
the gross value of the estate EXCEEDS Two 
Million Pesos (P2,000,000.00). (BP Blg.129, 
as amended by R.A. No. 11576)  
The court first taking cognizance of the 
settlement of estate of a decedent shall 
exercise jurisdiction to the exclusion of all 
other courts (Sec. 1, Rule 73). 
Relevant Rules on Special Proceedings 
1. If the decedent is an inhabitant of the 
Philippines at the time of his death, whether 
a citizen or an alien 
 


<!-- PAGE 171 -->

 
 
159 
His will shall be proved, or letters of 
administration granted, and his estate 
settled, in the RTC of the province in which 
he resides at the time of his death. 
2. 
If the decedent is an inhabitant of a 
foreign country 
 
His will shall be proved, or letters of 
administration granted, and his estate 
settled, in the RTC of any province in which 
he had estate.  (Section 1, Rule 73). 
Meaning of “residence” 
 
For purposes of settlement of estate, 
"residence," in the context of venue 
provisions, means nothing more than a 
person’s actual residence or place of abode, 
provided he resides therein with continuity 
and consistency. (Garcia-Quiazon vs. Belen, 
GR No.189121, July 31, 2013) 
The jurisdiction assumed by a court, so far as 
it depends on the place of residence of the 
decedent, or of the location of his estate, 
shall not be contested in a suit or proceeding, 
except in an appeal from that court, in the 
original case, or when the want of jurisdiction 
appears on the record. (Sec. 1, Rule 73) 
2. Extrajudicial – Rule 74, Secs. 1, 
4, and 5 
Extrajudicial settlement refers to a procedure 
where the heirs of a deceased person who 
died intestate (without a will) agree to divide 
and distribute the decedent’s estate without 
judicial intervention.  
Section 1 allows for this procedure provided 
there is no will, no outstanding debts, and the 
heirs are all of legal age or, if minors are 
involved, they are duly represented. The 
heirs must execute a public instrument, such 
as an affidavit of extrajudicial settlement, 
which must be published once a week for 
three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of 
general circulation pursuant to Section 1. 
Additionally, Section 2 requires the filing of a 
bond equivalent to the value of the personal 
property of the estate to protect potential 
creditors. 
If debts exist, creditors must be notified and 
paid before the estate is distributed. Non-
compliance with these requirements can lead 
to liabilities, as clarified in Heirs of Gregorio 
Lopez 
v. 
Development 
Bank 
of 
the 
Philippines (G.R. No. 150810, May 28, 
2004), where the Supreme Court held that 
heirs who fail to comply with the formalities of 
Rule 74 are solidarily liable for obligations 
and claims against the estate. 
3. Judicial 
 
a. Summary Settlement – Rule 74, Secs. 
2-5 
When allowed 
Allowed whenever the gross value of estate 
of the decedent does not exceed P10,000.

160 
How 
(1) Petition shall be filed by an interested 
person; 
(2) Notice which shall be published once a 
week for 3 consecutive weeks in a 
newspaper of general circulation in the

persons as the court may direct; 
(3) Hearing which shall be held not less than 
1 month nor more than 3 months from the 
date of the last publication of the notice; 
(4) The complaint must allege that the gross 
value of the estate of the deceased does not 
exceed Php 10,000.00; and 
 
(5) A bond duly filed in an amount fixed by 
the court. (Rule 74, Sec. 2)

Upon fulfillment of the requisites, the court 
may 
proceed 
summarily 
without 
the 
appointment of an executor/administrator 
and without delay  
 
1. to grant, if proper, allowance of the will, if 
there be any; 
2. to determine who are persons legally 
entitled to participate in the estate; and 
3. to apportion and divide the estate among 
them after the payment of such debts of the 
Estate.

If it shall appear at any time within two (2)

participation payable in money- 
 
The court having jurisdiction of the estate

b. Intestate – Petition for Letters of 
Administration – Rules 78-79 
Letters of Administration are issued in 
intestate 
succession 
to 
authorize 
an 
administrator to manage and settle the estate 
of a deceased person who died without a will.  
Section 2 specifies that a petition for letters 
of administration must be filed by an 
interested party in the Regional Trial Court 
(RTC) of the province where the deceased 
resided at the time of death or, if they had no 
fixed residence, where they had property. 
The petition must contain the following 
essential information as provided under 
Section 2: 
1. The decedent's name, age, and place 
of residence at the time of death; 
2. The value and nature of the estate; 
3. The 
names, 
addresses, 
and 
relationships of the heirs, legatees, and 
devisees; 
4. The 
name 
of 
the 
proposed 
administrator and their qualifications. 
The priority for appointing an administrator is 
established under Section 6, with preference 
given to the surviving spouse or next of kin, 
barring disqualification due to incompetence 
or conflict of interest, as upheld in Reyes v. 
RTC of Oriental Mindoro (G.R. No. 156711, 
March 31, 2005). 
The administrator is tasked with preserving 
the estate, paying debts, and distributing the 
remainder to the heirs, following the order of 
intestate succession outlined in Articles 961-
1014 of the Civil Code. 
To illustrate: 
If a decedent dies intestate leaving 
behind real property and a surviving 
spouse with minor children, the 
spouse may petition for letters of 
administration. 
The 
court 
will 
evaluate the spouse’s qualifications 
and issue the letters, empowering 
them to manage the estate. 
However, creditors or other heirs may 
oppose 
the 
appointment 
if 
they 
can 
demonstrate the spouse’s unfitness or 
conflict of interest. 
Who 
are 
disqualified 
to 
serve 
as 
executors or administrators 
1. Minor; 
2. Is not a resident of the Philippines; and 
3. Is in opinion of the court unfit to execute 
the duties of the trust by reason of 
drunkenness, improvidence, or want of 
understanding or integrity, or by reason 
of conviction of an offense involving 
moral turpitude. 
When and to whom letters of administration 
granted 
 
If no executor is named in the will, or the 
executor or executors are incompetent, 
refuse the trust, or fail to give bond, or a 
person dies intestate, administration shall be 
granted: 
(a) To the surviving husband or wife, as the 
case may be, or next of kin, or both, in the 
discretion of the court, or to such person as 


<!-- PAGE 174 -->

 
 
162 
such surviving husband or wife, or next of 
kin, requests to have appointed, if competent 
and willing to serve; 
(b) If such surviving husband or wife, as the 
case may be, or next of kin, or the person 
selected by them, be incompetent or 
unwilling, or if the husband or widow, or next 
of kin, neglects for thirty (30) days after the 
death 
of 
the 
person 
to 
apply 
for 
administration 
or 
to 
request 
that 
administration be granted to some other 
person, it may be granted to one or more of 
the principal creditors, if may be granted to 
one or more of the principal creditors, if 
competent and willing to serve; 
(c) If there is no such creditor competent and 
willing to serve, it may be granted to such 
other person as the court may select. 
 
c. Testate – Probate Proceedings 
i. Allowance or Disallowance of Will – 
Rules 76-77 
Allowance of will; Necessary 
 
Any executor, devisee, or legatee named in 
a will, or any other person interested in the 
estate, may, at any time after the death of the 
testator, petition the court having jurisdiction 
to have the will allowed, whether the will is in 
his possession or not, or is lost or destroyed. 
The testator himself may, during his lifetime, 
petition the court for the allowance of his will. 
Mnemonics. The following are the persons 
who may petition for probate under Sec. 1, 
Rule 76 
 
a) Devisee 
(b) Executor 
(c) Legatee 
(d) Testator – during his lifetime 
(e) Any other interested person – heir; 
creditor 
An "interested person" has been defined 
as one who would be benefited by the 
estate,such as an heir, or one who has a 
claim against the estate, such as a creditor. 
The interest must be material and direct, and 
not merely indirect or contingent (San Luis 
vs. San Luis, G.R. No. 133743, February 6, 
2007). 
 
Contents of petition 
 
A petition for the allowance of a will must 
show, so far as known to the petitioner: 
1. Jurisdictional facts  
Refer to the fact of death of the decedent, his 
residence at the time of his death in the 
province where the court is sitting, or if he is 
an inhabitant of a foreign country, the estate 
he left in such province (Palaganas v. 
Palaganas, G.R. No. 169144 (2011)). 
 
2. Names, ages, and residences of the 
heirs, legatees, and devisees of the 
testator or decedent 


<!-- PAGE 175 -->

 
 
163 
3. Probate value and character of the 
property of the estate 
 
4. Name of the person for whom letters 
are prayed 
 
5. If the will has not been delivered to the 
court, the name of the person having 
custody of it (Sec. 2, Rule 76). 
 
Jurisdictional requirements for proving 
wills; Rules on Notice 
The following are the persons which may be 
notified by mail or personally, if their place of 
residences are known: 
(1) Heirs 
(2) Legatees 
(3) Devisees 
(4) Executor/co-executor, if they are not the 
one petitioning. 
Notice is jurisdictional 
 
Note: No defect in the petition shall render 
void the allowance of the will or the issuance 
of letters testamentary or of administration 
with the will annexed. 
 
Setting of hearing and publication of 
notice 
Upon delivery of the will or filing of the 
petition for allowance, the court shall: 
1. Fix a time and place for proving the 
will; 
2. Cause notice of such time and place 
to be published three (3) weeks 
successively in a newspaper of 
general circulation in the province, 
prior to the hearing. 
Note: No newspaper publication is required 
where the petition for probate is filed by the 
testator himself. 
Notice to heirs, devisees, legatees, and 
executors 
The court shall cause copies of the notice of 
hearing to be: 
1. Mailed to the designated or known 
heirs, 
legatees, 
and 
devisees 
residing in the Philippines, at least 
twenty (20) days before the hearing; 
2. Mailed to the executor or co-
executor, if not the petitioner; 
3. Personally served at least ten (10) 
days before the hearing, which is 
equivalent to mailing. 
If the testator petitions for the allowance of 
his own will, notice shall be sent only to his 
compulsory heirs. 


<!-- PAGE 176 -->

 
 
164 
Notice to designated heirs, legatees and 
devisees is jurisdictional when they are 
known and their place of residence are 
known (Racca v. Echague,G.R. No. 237133, 
January 20, 2021) 
Notice is required to be personally given to 
known heirs, legatees, and devisees of the 
testator (Rule 76, Sec. 4). 
Proof at hearing in absence of contest 
Before introduction of testimony, compliance 
with publication and notice requirements 
must be shown. All testimony shall be under 
oath and reduced to writing. 
Essence of Publication 
 
Publication of the notice of hearing brings in 
the whole world as a party in the case for 
probate and vests the court with jurisdiction 
to hear and decide it. Thus, parties not 
mentioned in the petition for probate 
eventually 
became 
parties 
as 
a 
consequence of publication (Alaban v. CA, 
G.R. No. 156021 (2005). 
The notice must be published 3 weeks 
successively, previous to the time set for 
hearing, 
in 
a 
newspaper 
of 
general 
circulation in the province (Sec. 3, Rule 76), 
except in an antemortem petition for probate 
filed by the testator herself (no publication 
required).  
If no contest is filed: 
1. For a notarial will, the testimony of 
one subscribing witness is sufficient if 
he testifies that the will was executed 
as required by law. 
 
2. For a holographic will, at least one 
witness must explicitly declare that 
the will and signature are in the 
handwriting of the testator. 
 
Note: In the absence of a competent 
handwriting witness, and if the court deems 
it necessary, expert testimony may be 
resorted to. 
Proof of lost or destroyed will 
A lost or destroyed will may be proved only 
if: 
1. Its 
execution 
and 
validity 
are 
established; 
2. It is shown to have been in existence 
at the time of the testator’s death, or 
fraudulently or accidentally destroyed 
during 
his 
lifetime 
without 
his 
knowledge; 
3. Its 
provisions 
are 
clearly 
and 
distinctly proved by at least two (2) 
credible witnesses. 
When proved, the provisions shall be 
distinctly stated and certified by the judge 
and recorded as other wills. 
Proof when subscribing witnesses do not 
reside in the province 


<!-- PAGE 177 -->

 
 
165 
If none of the subscribing witnesses resides 
in the province, but their depositions can be 
taken elsewhere, the court may: 
1. Order the taking of depositions; 
2. Authorize the presentation of a 
photographic copy of the will during 
examination. 
Proof when subscribing witnesses are 
dead, insane, or not residing in the 
Philippines 
If subscribing witnesses are dead, insane, or 
none resides in the Philippines, the court 
may admit: 
1. Testimony of other witnesses to 
prove the sanity of the testator and 
due execution of the will; 
2. Proof of handwriting of the testator 
and subscribing witnesses. 
Grounds for disallowance of will 
A will shall be disallowed if: 
1. It was not executed and attested as 
required by law; 
2. The testator was insane or mentally 
incapable at the time of execution; 
3. It was executed under duress, fear, or 
threats; 
4. It was procured by undue and 
improper pressure or influence; 
5. The signature was procured by fraud 
or trick, without intent that it be the 
testator’s will. 
Contest of will 
Any person contesting the will must: 
1. State in writing the grounds for 
opposing its allowance; 
2. Serve a copy upon the petitioner and 
other interested parties. 
Proof where will is contested 
If the will is contested: 
1. All subscribing witnesses and the 
notary 
must 
be 
produced 
and 
examined, 
if 
present 
in 
the 
Philippines and not insane; 
2. Their death, absence, or insanity 
must be satisfactorily shown if not 
produced; 
3. Depositions 
shall 
be 
taken 
if 
witnesses are outside the province. 
Even if subscribing witnesses testify against 
due execution, do not remember, or are of 
doubtful credibility, the will may still be 
allowed if the court is satisfied from other 
evidence that it was duly executed. 
For a contested holographic will, at least 
three (3) handwriting witnesses are required, 
unless expert testimony is resorted to. 
Proof 
where 
testator 
petitions 
for 
allowance of holographic will 
If the testator himself petitions: 
1. If uncontested, his affirmation that the 
will 
and 
signature 
are 
in 
his 
handwriting is sufficient; 
2. If contested, the burden of disproving 
genuineness lies with the contestant. 
Note: The testator may present rebuttal 
evidence. 
 
Certificate of allowance and recording 
If the court is satisfied that the will was duly 
executed and the testator was of sound mind 
and free from duress or fraud: 
1. A certificate of allowance shall be 
issued and attached to the will; 
2. The will and certificate shall be 
recorded by the clerk; 
3. Attested 
copies 
affecting 
real 
property shall be recorded in the 
Register of Deeds. 
Notice of hearing 


<!-- PAGE 178 -->

 
 
166 
Upon filing of: 
1. A duly authenticated copy of the will; 
and 
2. A duly authenticated decree of 
allowance abroad, 
the court shall fix a hearing and cause notice 
to 
be 
given 
as 
in 
original 
probate 
proceedings. 
Effect of allowance 
If allowed, the will shall: 
1. Be recorded with a certificate of 
allowance; 
2. Have the same effect as if originally 
proved 
and 
allowed 
in 
the 
Philippines. 
Administration of estate 
Upon allowance of the foreign will: 
1. Letters testamentary or letters of 
administration with the will annexed 
shall be granted; 
2. Such letters extend to all estate of the 
testator in the Philippines; 
3. After payment of just debts and 
expenses, 
the 
estate 
shall 
be 
disposed of according to the will; 
4. Any residue shall be disposed of as 
provided by law. 
ii. Letters Testamentary 
 
(a) Issuance – Rule 78 
Letters 
Testamentary 
and 
of 
Administration, When and to Whom  
Who are incompetent to serve as 
executors or administrators 
No person in competent to serve as executor 
or administrator who: 
(a) Is a minor; 
(b) Is not a resident of the Philippines; and 
(c) Is in the opinion of the court unfit to 
execute the duties of the trust by reason of 
drunkenness, improvidence, or want of 
understanding or integrity, or by reason of 
conviction of an offense involving moral 
turpitude. 
Executor of executor not to administer 
estate 
The executor of an executor shall not, as 
such, administer the estate of the first 
testator. 
Married women may serve 
A married woman may serve as executrix or 
administratrix, and the marriage of a single 
woman shall not affect her authority so to 
serve under a previous appointment. 
Letters testamentary issued when will 
allowed 
When a will has been proved and allowed, 
the court shall issue letters testamentary 
thereon to the person named as executor 
therein, if he is competent, accepts the 
trust, and gives bond as required by the 
Rules of Court. 
 
Where some coexecutors disqualified 
others may act 
When all of the executors named in a will can 
not act because of incompetency, refusal to 
accept the trust, or failure to give bond, on 


<!-- PAGE 179 -->

 
 
167 
the part of one or more of them, letters 
testamentary may issue to such of them as 
are competent, accept and give bond, and 
they may perform the duties and discharge 
the trust required by the will. 
When 
and 
to 
whom 
letters 
of 
administration granted 
If no executor is named in the will, or the 
executor or executors are incompetent, 
refuse the trust, or fail to give bond, or a 
person dies intestate, administration shall be 
granted: 
(a) To the surviving husband or wife, as the 
case may be, or next of kin, or both, in the 
discretion of the court, or to such person as 
such surviving husband or wife, or next of 
kin, requests to have appointed, if competent 
and willing to serve; 
(b) If such surviving husband or wife, as the 
case may be, or next of kin, or the person 
selected by them, be incompetent or 
unwilling, or if the husband or widow, or next 
of kin, neglects for thirty (30) days after the 
death 
of 
the 
person 
to 
apply 
for 
administration 
or 
to 
request 
that 
administration be granted to some other 
person, it may be granted to one or more of 
the principal creditors, if may be granted to 
one or more of the principal creditors, if 
competent and willing to serve; 
(c) If there is no such creditor competent and 
willing to serve, it may be granted to such 
other person as the court may select. 
 
 
(b) Opposition – Rule 79 
Opposition 
to 
issuance 
of 
letters 
testamentary; simultaneous petition for 
administration 
 
Any person interested in a will may state in 
writing the grounds why letters testamentary 
should not issue to the persons named 
therein as executors, or any of them. The 
court, after hearing upon notice, shall pass 
upon the sufficiency of such grounds. 
A petition may, at the same time, be filed for 
letters of administration with the will 
annexed. 
Contents 
of 
petition 
for 
letters 
of 
administration 
A petition for letters of administration must be 
filed by an interested person and must show, 
so far as known to the petitioner: 
1. The jurisdictional facts; 
2. The names, ages, and residences of 
the heirs, and the names and 
residences of the creditors, of the 
decedent; 
3. The probable value and character of 
the property of the estate; 
4. The name of the person for whom 
letters of administration are prayed. 
Note: No defect in the petition shall render 
void the issuance of letters of administration. 
Setting of hearing; notice 
When a petition for letters of administration is 
filed in the court having jurisdiction, the court 
shall fix a time and place for hearing the 
petition and shall cause notice thereof to be 
given to the known heirs and creditors of the 
decedent, and to any other persons believed 
to have an interest in the estate, in the 
manner provided in Rules on publication and 
personal notice. 


<!-- PAGE 180 -->

 
 
168 
Opposition to petition for administration 
Any interested person may, by filing a written 
opposition, contest the petition: 
1. On the ground of the incompetency of 
the person for whom letters are 
prayed; or 
2. On the ground of the contestant’s 
own right to the administration. 
The contestant may pray that letters issue to 
himself, or to any competent person named 
in the opposition. 
Hearing and order for issuance of letters 
At the hearing of the petition, it must first be 
shown that notice has been given as 
required. The court shall then hear the proofs 
of the parties in support of their respective 
allegations. 
If the court is satisfied that the decedent left 
no will, or that there is no competent and 
willing executor, it shall order the issuance of 
letters of administration to the party best 
entitled thereto. 
Grant of letters of administration to any 
applicant 
Letters of administration may be granted to 
any qualified applicant, even if there are 
other competent persons having a better 
right to the administration, provided such 
persons fail to appear when notified and 
claim the issuance of letters to themselves. 
 
d. Claims against Estate – Rule 86 
Claims refer to all demands or rights of 
action owed by the decedent at the time of 
death, whether arising from contract, tort, or 
obligation, including contingent claims. 
Claims against the estate of a deceased 
person must be presented and settled 
during the settlement proceedings to 
ensure the orderly distribution of the estate 
and the payment of debts. 
 
Presentation of Claims 
Section 1 mandates that creditors present 
their claims to the court within the period 
fixed in the notice to creditors, which cannot 
be less than six (6) months nor more than 
twelve (12) months from the date of the first 
publication of the notice. 
Claims not presented within the allowed 
period are barred, except as provided under 
Section 5, which allows contingent claims or 
claims arising after the expiration of the 
period to be filed with leave of court. 
Procedure for Filing Claims 
1. Written Statement: Creditors must file a 
written statement of their claim, under oath, 
specifying the nature and amount of the 
claim, as provided under Section 2. 
2. Hearing and Resolution: The executor or 
administrator may admit or contest the claim. 
If contested, the court resolves the matter 
through a hearing, as required by Section 3. 
Order of Payment of Claims 
The court determines the order of 
payment based on Section 7, prioritizing: 
1. Funeral expenses, 
2. Expenses of the administration, 
3. Debts and taxes, 
4. Judgments for accidents or illness 
before death, 
5. Other judgments, and 
6. All other claims. 
 
Effects of Non-Compliance 


<!-- PAGE 181 -->

 
 
169 
Failure 
to 
present 
claims 
within 
the 
prescribed 
period 
or 
to 
comply 
with 
procedural requirements results in the 
barring of claims.  
In Heirs of Valera v. Locsin (G.R. No. 
170728, February 22, 2012), the Supreme 
Court emphasized that creditors must strictly 
adhere 
to 
the 
procedural 
rules, 
and 
exceptions are granted only for valid and 
justifiable reasons. 
Time within which claims shall be filed 
Immediately 
after 
granting 
letters 
testamentary or of administration, the court 
shall issue a notice requiring all persons 
having money claims against the decedent to 
file them in the office of the clerk of said court. 
(Sec. 1, Rule 86) 
GR: Claims must be filed within the time 
specified by the court in its notice which shall 
not be less than 6 months nor more than 12 
months from the date of the first publication 
of the notice (Sec. 2, Rule 86). 
 
Note: Such period once fixed by the court is 
mandatory and it cannot be shortened. 
XPN: Tardy Claims 
At any time before an order of distribution is 
entered, on application of a creditor who has 
failed to file his claim within the time 
previously limited, the court may, for cause 
shown and on such terms as are equitable, 
allow such claim to be filed within a time not 
exceeding one (1) month. (Sec. 2, Rule 86). 
Statute of Non-Claims 
The statute of non-claims is a period fixed by 
the rule for the filing of claims against the 
estate for examination and allowance. It 
supersedes the statute of limitations. 
Publication of Notice to Creditors 
 
Immediately after the notice to the creditors 
is issued, the executor or administrator shall 
cause the same to be published 3 weeks 
successively in a newspaper of general 
circulation in the proving. It shall also be 
posted for the same period in 4 public places 
in the province and in 2 public places 
in the municipality where the decedent last 
resided. (Rule 86, Sec. 3) 
Printed copy of the published notice shall be 
filed in court within 10 days after its 
publication 
accompanied 
with 
affidavit 
setting forth the dates of first and last 
publication and name of newspaper where it 
was printed (Sec. 4, Rule 86) 
Claims that must be presented under the 
statute of non-claims (EXCLUSIVE) 
(1) All claims for money against the 
decedent, arising from contract, express or 
implied, whether due, not due, or contingent. 
 
(2) All claims for funeral expenses. 
 
(3) Expenses for the last sickness of the 
decedent. 
 
(4) Judgment for money against the 
decedent. (Rule 86, Sec. 5) 
Contingent Claim 
 


<!-- PAGE 182 -->

 
 
170 
One which by its nature, is necessarily 
dependent upon an uncertain event for 
existence or validity, which may or may not 
develop into an enforceable claim (Buan v. 
Laya, G.R. No. L-7593 (1957)) 
 
When allowed 
1. When it becomes absolute; 
2.Presented 
to 
the 
court 
or 
executor/administrator within 2 years from 
the time limited for other creditors to present 
their claims; and 
3. Not disputed by executor/administrator 
(Sec. 5, Rule 88). 
If disputed, it may be proved and allowed or 
disallowed by the court as the facts 
maywarrant (Sec. 5, Rule 88). 
Favorable judgment 
If the debtor obtains a favorable judgment, 
the amount shall be considered the true 
balance against the estate, as though the 
claim had been presented directly before the 
court in the administration proceedings (Sec. 
5, Rule 86). 
Joint or Solidary Obligations 
If obligation is solidary - file claim against 
decedent as if he is the only debtor. 
 
If obligation is joint - claim confined to the 
portion belonging to the decedent (Sec. 6, 
Rule 86) 
Options Available to a Secured Creditor 
(1) Abandon or waive the mortgage and 
claim the entire debt from the estate of the 
mortgagor as an ordinary claim. 
(2) Foreclose the mortgage judicially and if 
there is judgment for deficiency, he may file 
a claim against the estate within the statute 
of non-claims. 
(3) Rely on the mortgage exclusively, 
foreclosing the same judicially or extra-
judicially at any time before it is barred by 
prescription without the right to claim for any 
deficiency. 
Note: The mortgage creditor can avail of only 
one of the three remedies and if he fails to 
recover under that remedy, he cannot avail 
of any of the other two remedies. (Bachrach 
Motor Co. Inc., vs. Icarangal, G.R. No. L-
45350, May 29, 1939) 
Claim of Executor or Administrator 
Against the Estate; Procedure 
 
(1) The executor or administrator shall give 
Notice in writing, to the court. 
(2) The court shall then appoint a special 
administrator who shall have the same 
powers and liabilities as the general 
executor/administrator in the adjustment of 
such claim. 
(3) The court may order the executor or 
administrator 
to 
pay 
to 
the 
special 
administrator necessary funds to defend 
such claim. (Rule 86, Sec. 8) 


<!-- PAGE 183 -->

 
 
171 
How to file for claim 
 
1. Deliver the claim with the necessary 
vouchers to the clerk of court, and 
2. 
Serve 
a 
copy 
thereof 
on 
the 
executor/administrator (Sec. 9, Rule 86). 
Answer by Executor/Administrator 
Shall be filed within 15 days after a copy of 
the claim has been served upon him.  
The executor/administrator may interpose 
any counterclaim. Said counterclaim is 
regarded as compulsory, as the failure to file 
the same shall bar the claim forever (Sec. 10, 
Rule 8). 
Executor/Administrator Entirely Admits 
Claim 
 
The claim shall be submitted by the clerk to 
the court who may approve the same without 
hearing, but the court in its discretion before 
approving the claim, may order that known 
heirs, legatees, or devisees be notified and 
heard. If the latter oppose upon hearing, the 
court may allow 15 days to file an answer 
(Sec. 11, Rule 86). 
Executor/Administrator Disputes Claim 
OR Fails to File Answer 
 
Clerk of court shall set the claim for trial with 
notice to both parties (Sec. 12, Rule 86). 
Judgment of court approving or disapproving 
a claim shall be appealable as in ordinary 
cases (Sec. 13, Rule 86). 
 
e. Payment of the Debts of the Estate – 
Rule 88 
Debts Paid in Full if Estate Sufficient 
1. After all money claims heard and 
their amount ascertained; and 
2. It appears there are sufficient 
assets to pay the debts (Sec. 1, Rule 
88). 
The executor/administrator shall pay 
the same within the time limited for 
that purpose (Sec. 1, Rule 88).   
Requisites before executor or administrator 
may pay a claim against the estate 
(1) Hearing is conducted; 
 
(2) 
Amounts 
of 
claims 
are 
ascertained; and, 
 
(3) There are sufficient assets to pay 
the claims. (Rule 88, Sec. 1) 
The provision in a will for the payment of a 
specific debt does not dispense with the 
requirement that a claim should be filed 
against the estate. (Special Proceedings 
Essentials for Bench and Bar, De Leon and 
Wilwayco, 2020). 
Note: In any case where the provision in the 
will is insufficient to cover the entire debt, that 


<!-- PAGE 184 -->

 
 
172 
part of the decedent’s estate not disposed of 
by will shall answer for such deficiency (Sec. 
2). 
 
 
Order of Preference for Payment of Debts 
 
1. Portion of property designated in the will  
a. If testator makes provision by will, 
or designates the estate for the 
payment of debts, expenses of 
administration, or family expenses, 
they shall be paid according to such 
provisions 
b. If not sufficient – part of the estate 
not disposed of by will shall be 
appropriated (Sec. 2, Rule 88). 
 
2. Personal property (Sec. 3, Rule 88). 
3. Real property (Sec. 2, Rule 89). 
If there is still a deficiency, the debt shall be 
satisfied through the contributive shares of 
the devisees, legatees, or heirs who have 
been in possession of portions of the estate 
before debts and expenses have been 
settled and paid (Sec. 6, Rule 88). 
GR: Personal estate not disposed of by will 
shall be first chargeable. 
XPNs: (Real properties are charged first) 
1. When the sale of personal property is 
insufficient (Sec. 3, Rule 88) 
2. When its sale will redound to the detriment 
of the participants for the estate (Id.) 
3. When its sale may injure the business or 
other interests of those interested in the 
estate (Sec. 2, Rule 89) 
4. When the testator has not made sufficient 
provision for payment of such debts, 
expenses, and legacies. 
5. When the decedent was, in his lifetime, 
under contract, binding in law, to deed real 
property, or an interest therein, to beneficiary 
(Id., Sec. 8) 
6. When the decedent during his lifetime held 
real property in trust for another (Id., Sec. 9) 
Requisites before any of the exceptions 
apply: 
 
1. The executor or administrator makes an 
application with the court 
 
2. Written notice is given to the persons  
interested 
 
3. Hearing by the court 
 
f. Distribution and Partition of the 
Estate – Rule 90 
Before there could be a distribution of the 
estate, the following stages must be 
followed: 


<!-- PAGE 185 -->

 
 
173 
1. Liquidation of estate (i.e., payment of 
obligations of deceased) 
2. Declaration of heirs - to determine to 
whom the residue of the estate should be 
distributed 
a. Determination of the right of a natural child 
b. Determination of proportionate shares of 
distributees. 
Afterwards, the residue may be distributed 
and delivered to the heirs. 
 
The courts may make a declaration of heirs 
at any stage of the proceedings before the 
order of distribution. 
Payment of the inheritance tax, per se, does 
not settle the estate of a deceased person 
(Agtarap v. Agtarap, G.R. Nos. 177099 and 
177192 , 2011). 
a. Liquidation 
GR: Before an order of distribution or 
assignment, it must be shown that the debts, 
funeral 
expenses, 
and 
expenses 
of 
administration, allowance to widow, and 
inheritance tax chargeable to the estate have 
been paid. 
XPN: If the distributees give a bond 
conditioned 
for 
the 
payment 
of 
said 
obligations (Sec. 1, Rule 90; Estate of Ruiz 
v. CA, G.R. No. 118671, 1996) 
The part distributed must not be subject to 
any controversy or appeal [Sec. 2, Rule 109]. 
Project of Partition 
 
A project of partition is a document 
prepared by the executor or administrator 
setting forth the manner in which the estate 
of the deceased is to be distributed among 
the heirs. It is a proposal for distribution of the 
hereditary estimates and determines the 
persons entitled thereto. 
Towards the end of the proceedings in a 
settlement of estate petition, a project of 
partition is usually prepared and presented to 
the court. 
 
If the estate is a testate estate, the project of 
partition must conform to the terms of the will; 
if intestate, the project of partition must be in 
accordance with the provisions of the Civil 
Code (Camia de Reyes vs. Reyes de Ilano, 
G.R. No. 42092, October 28, 1936) 
Approval of Project of Partition 
(1) Finality of the approval of project of 
partition, by itself, does not terminate probate 
proceeding (Timbol vs. Cano, G.R. No. L- 
15445, April 29, 1961). 
As long as the order of the distribution of the 
estate has not been complied with, the 
probate proceedings cannot be deemed 
closed and terminated (Treyes v. Larlar, G.R. 
No. 232579, September 8, 2020) 
(2) A judicial partition is not final and 
conclusive and does not prevent the heir 


<!-- PAGE 186 -->

 
 
174 
from bringing an action to obtain his share, 
provided the the prescriptive period has not 
closed (ibid.) 
\ 
Court may determine questions as to 
advancement made by decedent (Sec. 2, 
Rule 90) 
Although it is within the jurisdiction of the 
court whether or not to permit the advance 
distribution of the estate, its exercise should 
be qualified by the following: 
1. Only part of the estate that is not affected 
by any pending controversy or appeal may 
be subject of advance distribution (Sec. 2, 
Rule 109); and 
2. The distributees must post a bond, fixed 
by the court, conditioned for the payment of 
outstanding obligations of the estate (par. 2, 
Sec. 1, Rule 90, Quasha Ancheta Peña & 
Nolasco Law Office v. LCN Construction 
Corp., G.R. No. 174873, 2008) 
Effect of Final Decree of Distribution 
Title to the property of the estate vests in the 
distributees (De Kilayko v. Tengco, G.R. No. 
45425 (1992)). 
The only instance where a party interested in 
a probate proceeding may have a final 
liquidation set aside is when he is left out by 
reason of circumstances beyond his control 
or through mistake or inadvertence not 
imputable to negligence (Vda. De Alberto v. 
CA, G.R. No. L- 29759, 1989). 
Remedy of Heir Entitled to Residue But 
Not Given His Share 
If there is a controversy before the court as 
to who are the lawful heirs of the deceased 
person or as to the distributive shares to 
which each person is entitled under the law, 
the controversy shall be heard and decided 
as in ordinary cases (Rule 90, Sec. 1) 
The better practice for the heir who has not 
received his share is to 
1. Demand his share through a proper 
motion in the same probate or administrative 
proceedings, or 
2. Motion for reopening of the probate or 
administrative proceedings if it had already 
been 
closed, 
and 
not 
through 
an 
independent action (Guilas v. Judge of CFI of 
Pampanga, G.R. No. L-26695, 1972). 
When 
does 
a 
probate 
court 
lose 
jurisdiction 
of 
an 
estate 
under 
administration? 
The probate court loses jurisdiction of an 
estate 
under 
administration 
only 
after 
payment of all debts, and the remaining 
estate delivered to the heirs entitled to 
receive the same (Guilas v.Judge of CFI of 
Pampanga, supra)

Petition that competency of ward be 
adjudged; proceedings 
 
A 
person 
who

incompetent for any reason, or his guardian,

On the trial, the guardian or relatives of the

on its own motion.

adjudged and the guardianship shall cease.

Removal or resignation of guardian; new 
appointment 
 
When a guardian becomes insane or 
otherwise incapable of discharging his trust, 
or is unsuitable therefor, or has wasted or 
mismanaged the estate, or has failed for 
thirty (30) days after it is due to render an 
account or make a return, the court may, 
upon reasonable notice to the guardian, 
remove him and compel him to surrender the 
estate of the ward to the person lawfully 
entitled thereto. 
 
A guardian may resign when it appears 
proper to allow the same. Upon resignation 
or removal, the court may appoint another 
guardian in his place. 
 
Other 
modes 
of 
termination 
of 
guardianship 
 
The marriage or voluntary emancipation of a 
minor ward terminates the guardianship of 
the person of the ward and enables the minor 
to administer his property as though he were 
of age. 
However, the minor cannot borrow money or 
alienate or encumber real property without 
the consent of his father or mother, or 
guardian. He can sue and be sued only with 
the assistance of his father, mother, or 
guardian. 
The guardian of any person may be 
discharged by the court when it appears, 
upon application of the ward or otherwise, 
that the guardianship is no longer necessary.

The court may, upon :

A guardian may resign when it appears

4. Discharge  
 
The guardian of any person may be

upon application of the ward or otherwise,

(Sec. 3, Rule 97).

RULE ON GUARDIANSHIP OF MINORS – 
A.M. NO. 03-02-05-SC  
Applicability of the Rule  
This Rule shall apply to petitions for 
guardianship over the person or property, or 
both, of a minor. 
 
The father and the mother shall jointly 
exercise legal guardianship over the person 
and 
property 
of 
their 
unemancipated 
common child without the necessity of a 
court appointment.  
Who 
may 
file 
a 
petition 
for 
the 
appointment of a guardian 
Any relative or other person on behalf of a 
minor, or the minor himself if fourteen years 
of age or over, may petition the Family Court 
for the appointment of a general guardian 
over the person or property, or both, of such 
minor.  
The petition may also be filed by the 
Secretary 
of 
Social 
Welfare 
and 
Development and by the Secretary of Health 
in the case of an insane minor who needs to 
be hospitalized. 
Where to file the petition 
It may be filed in the Family Court of the 
province or city where the minor actually 
resides. If he resides in a foreign country, the 
petition shall be filed with the Family Court of 
the province or city where his property or any 
part thereof is situated.
