 (j) That a person found in possession of a

 (k) That a person in possession of an order

3. Presumptions in Civil Actions 
and Proceedings – Rule 131, Sec. 
5 
 
In all civil actions and proceedings not 
otherwise provided for by the law or these 
Rules, a presumption imposes on the party 
against whom it is directed the burden of 
going forward with evidence to rebut or meet 
the presumption. 
If presumptions are inconsistent, the 
presumption that is founded upon weightier 
considerations of policy shall apply. If 
considerations of policy are of equal weight, 
neither presumption applies. 
 
4. Presumption against an 
Accused in Criminal Cases – Rule 
131, Sec. 6 
If a presumed fact that establishes guilt, is an 
element of the offense charged, or negates a 
defense, the existence of the basic fact must 
be proved beyond reasonable doubt and the 
presumed fact follows from the basic fact 
beyond reasonable doubt.

FOR TAKING OF EVIDENCE IN CIVIL OR

A.M. NO. 25-02-17-SC 
 
1. Scope and Applicability – Sec. 
1 
A.M. No. 25-02-17-SC shall govern the 
request, 
preparation, 
transmission, 
execution, and return of Letters of Request 
under Chapter I of the Hague Evidence 
Convention involving civil or commercial 
matters for the purpose of obtaining 
evidence, or the performance of some other 
related judicial act, provided that the Hague 
Evidence Convention has entered into force 
between the Philippines and the other 
Contracting State. 
The rules shall not preclude the filing of 
requests for deposition under the Rules of 
Court to be taken in foreign countries which 
are not Contracting States to the Hague

2. Definition of Terms – Sec. 2 
The following terms shall have the meaning 
given to them below: 
(a) “Central Authority” refers to an entity

another Contracting State and cause its

execute the same. The Office of the Court 
Administrator (OCA) is designated as the 
Philippine Central Authority for the Hague 
Evidence Convention. 
(b) “Evidence” that may be obtained under

of

(e) 
“Hague 
Conference 
on 
Private 
International Law” or the HCCH is an

to work for the progressive unification of the 
rules of private international law. The 
Philippines became a member of the HCCH 
on July 14, 2010. 
(f) “Hague Evidence Convention” refers to 
the Convention of March 18, 1970 on the 
Taking of Evidence Abroad in Civil or

the procedure of taking evidence whereby

3. Use of Evidence Taken Abroad 
– Sec. 18 
At the trial or upon the hearing of a motion or 
an interlocutory proceeding, any part or all of 
the evidence taken abroad, so far as 
admissible under the Rules of Evidence, may 
be used against any party who was present 
or represented at the taking of the evidence 
or who had due notice thereof, in accordance 
with any one of the following provisions: 
(a) The evidence taken abroad may be used 
by any party for the purpose of contradicting 
or impeaching the testimony of the person 
examined if presented as a witness; 
(b) The evidence taken abroad of a party or 
of any one who at the time of the taking was 
an officer, director, or managing agent of a 
public or private corporation, partnership, or 
association which is a party may be used by 
an affected party for any purpose; 
(c) The evidence taken may be used by any 
party for any purpose if the court finds:  
(i) that the person examined is dead; or  
(ii) that the person examined is out of the 
Philippines, unless it appears that his 
absence was procured by the party 
offering the evidence taken; or  
(iii) that the person examined is unable to 
attend or testify because of age, 
sickness, infirmity, or imprisonment; or  
(iv) that the party offering the evidence 
taken has been unable to procure the 
attendance of the person examined by 
subpoena; or  


<!-- PAGE 345 -->

 
 
333 
(v) upon application and notice, that such 
exceptional circumstances exist as to 
make it desirable, in the interest of justice 
and with due regard to the importance of 
presenting the testimony of the person 
examined orally in open court, to allow 
the evidence taken to be used; and 
(d) If only part of the evidence taken is 
offered in evidence by the Requesting Party, 
the affected party may require him to 
introduce all of it which is relevant to the part 
introduced. 
 


<!-- PAGE 346 -->

 
 
334 
Illustrative Chart: Use of Evidence Taken Abroad – Sec. 18 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 347 -->

 
 
335 
4. Effect of Using Evidence Taken 
Abroad – Sec. 19 
The use of evidence taken abroad or any part 
thereof for any purpose other than that of 
contradicting or impeaching the person 
examined makes the person the witness of 
the party offering it. However, this shall not 
apply to the use by an adverse party of the 
evidence taken as described in paragraph (b) 
of Section 18 of this Rule. 
Any party may rebut any relevant evidence 
taken abroad whether introduced by them or 
by any other party. 
5. Admissibility of Evidence 
Taken Abroad – Sec. 20 
In determining the admissibility of evidence 
taken, the court shall consider the following: 
(a) The person from whom the evidence was 
taken is present in the Philippines and is 
reasonably able to testify in person during 
the hearing; 
(b) The evidence fails to meet the standards 
of admissibility under the Rules of Court; or 
(c) The evidence is a privileged matter or was 
obtained in contravention of due process, 
including 
coercive 
measures 
that 
are 
incompatible with the fair administration of 
justice 
or 
the 
procedural 
safeguards 
recognized under Philippine law. 
6. Privileges – Sec. 33 
In the execution of a Letter of Request, the 
person examined may refuse to give 
evidence insofar as he or she has a privilege 
or duty to refuse to give the evidence: 
 
(a) under Philippine law, rules, or regulation; 
or 
(b) under the law of the Requesting Authority, 
and the privilege or duty has been specified 
in the Letter of Request. 
7. Interpretation of the Rules – 
Sec. 34 
A.M. No. 25-02-17-SC shall be liberally 
construed in order to promote their objective 
of mutual judicial co-operation by securing a 
just, speedy, and inexpensive taking of 
evidence.

IX. LEGAL AND JUDICIAL ETHICS 
 
 
A. 
LEGAL 
ETHICS 
– 
CODE 
OF 
PROFESSIONAL RESPONSIBILITY AND 
ACCOUNTABILITY (CPRA), A.M. NO. 22-
09-01-SC 
 
1. Practice of Law 
 
a. Definition and Nature – CPRA, Canon 
III, Sec. 1 
 
It refers to any activity, in and out of court, 
that requires the application of the law, 
legal procedure, knowledge, training, and 
experience.  (Cayetano vs. Monsod, G.R. 
No. 100113 – 278 Phil. 235 – 201 SCRA 210) 
 
 
 
The practice of law is the rendition of legal 
service or performance of acts or the 
application of law, legal principles, and 
judgment, in or out of court, with regard to the 
circumstances or objectives of a person or a 
cause, and pursuant to a lawyer-client 
relationship or other engagement governed 
by the Code of Professional Responsibility 
and Accountability for lawyers. It includes 
employment in the public service or private 
sector and requires membership in the 
Philippine bar as qualification. (Sec. 1, 
Canon III) 
 
A Mere Privilege and Not a Right 
 
The privilege to practice law is not an 
inherent right but a privilege granted by 
the State under its regulatory powers. Rule 
138, Section 2 of the Rules of Court explicitly 
states that admission to the practice of law 
requires fulfilling the Supreme Court’s 
stringent requirements. 
 
Law as a Profession Not a Business or 
Trade 
 
Law is a profession imbued with public 
interest and not a business or trade. In 
Sebastian v. Calis (G.R. No. 195137, 
September 19, 2012), the Supreme Court 
emphasized that the practice of law is 
primarily 
a 
service-oriented 
profession 
requiring lawyers to uphold justice and serve 
the public good. This distinction is crucial 
because it imposes ethical obligations on 
lawyers, such as prioritizing client welfare 
over profit motives, as embodied in the Code 
of 
Professional 
Responsibility 
and 
Accountability 
 
Supreme 
Court’s 
Administrative 
Supervision and Control over members of 
the Philippine Bar – 1987 CONST. art. VIII, 
sec. 5 (5) 
 
The Supreme Court shall have the following 
powers: 
 
Promulgate rules concerning: 
 
 
 
1. The protection and enforcement of 
constitutional rights, (PEC) 
 
2. Pleading, practice, and procedure in all 
courts (PPP) 
 
3. The admission to the practice of law, the 
integrated bar (AB) 
 
4. Legal assistance to the under-privileged 
(LAU) 
 
Such rules shall provide a simplified and 
inexpensive procedure for the speedy 
disposition of cases, shall be uniform for all 


<!-- PAGE 349 -->

 
 
337 
courts of the same grade, and shall not 
diminish, increase, or modify substantive 
rights. 
 
 
 
Rules of procedure of special courts and 
quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective 
unless disapproved by the Supreme 
Court. 
 
2. Admission to the Practice of Law 
 
The requirements for admission to the 
practice of law in the Philippines are as 
follows: 
 
 
1. Residency: Applicants must be 
residents of the Philippines. 
2. Took the Lawyer’s Oath 
3. Passed the Bar Examination 
4. Education: All applicants, except those 
with specific exemptions, must have: 
a. Completed a bachelor’s degree 
b. Completed a Juris Doctor degree in 
an authorized and recognized 
university 
5. Signed the Roll of Attorneys 
6. No charges involving moral Turpitude 
should be pending against the applicant 
in any court in the Philippines. 
7. Age: Applicants must be at least 21 
years old. 
8. Good Moral Character: Satisfactory 
evidence of good moral character is 
essential.  
9. Citizenship: Every applicant must be a 
citizen of the Philippines. 
 
a. Legal Education 
 
i. Pre-law 
 
Applicant must present a certificate that he or 
she 
had 
pursued 
and 
satisfactorily 
completed in an authorized and recognized 
university or college, the course of study 
prescribed therein for a bachelor's degree in 
arts or sciences. 
 
The university or college must require for 
admission the completion of a 4-year high 
school course. 
 
If a Filipino citizen completed and obtained 
his or her Bachelor of Laws degree or its 
equivalent in a foreign law school, he must 
also present proof of completion of a 
separate bachelor’s degree course. 
 
ii. Law Proper 
 
Applicant must satisfactorily show that they 
completed all the prescribed courses for a 
degree of Bachelor of Laws (or its 
equivalent). 
 
In a law school or university recognized by 
the government or the proper authority in the 
foreign jurisdiction where the degree has 
been granted. 
 
A Filipino citizen who graduated from a 
foreign law school must submit to the SC 
certifications showing: 
 
a. Completion of all courses leading to the 
degree of Bachelor of Laws or its equivalent 
degree; 
b. Recognition or accreditation of the law 
school by the proper authority; and 
 
c. Completion of all the fourth year subjects 
in the Bachelor of Laws academic program in 
a law school duly recognized by the 
Philippine Government. 


<!-- PAGE 350 -->

 
 
338 
 
iii. R.A. No. 7662 (Legal Education Reform 
Act) 
 
R.A. No. 7662 created the Legal Education 
Board to uplift the standards of legal 
education 
by 
undertaking 
appropriate 
reforms in the legal education system, 
requiring proper selection of law students, 
maintaining quality among law schools, and 
requiring legal apprenticeship and continuing 
legal education. 
 
PhilSAT Case 
 
In Dec. 2016, LEB promulgated LEB 
Memorandum Order No. 7, Series of 2016 
which required the Philippine Law School 
Admission Test (PhilSAT) as a prerequisite 
for admission to the basic law courses 
leading either to a Bachelor of Laws or Juris 
Doctor degree beginning school year 2017-
2018. 
 
However, 
the 
SC 
declared 
LEB 
Memorandum 
Order 
No. 
7 
as 
unconstitutional, as it “usurps the right and 
duty of the law school to determine for itself 
the criteria for the admission of students and 
thereafter, to apply such criteria on a case-
to-case basis.” [Pimentel v. Legal Education 
Board, G.R. Nos. 230642 & 242954 (2019)] 
 
b. Citizenship 
 
Filipino Citizenship 
 
Rule 138, Section 2 of the Rules of Court 
mandates that only Filipino citizens may be 
admitted to the Bar. 
 
This requirement is consistent with the 
concept of the practice of law as a privilege 
tied to national interest and loyalty. 
 
1. 1987 CONSTITUTION 
 
The 
citizenship 
requirement 
is 
further 
reinforced by Rule 138, Section 2 of the 
Rules of Court, which mandates that only 
Filipino citizens may be admitted to the Bar. 
Lawyers, as officers of the court, are 
instrumental in safeguarding constitutional 
rights, administering justice, and promoting 
the rule of law, making Filipino citizenship a 
non-negotiable prerequisite. 
 
The rationale for this limitation includes: 
 
a. Ensuring loyalty to the Philippines and its 
Constitution. 
b. Promoting familiarity with the country's 
unique legal and cultural context. 
c. Safeguarding 
the 
legal 
profession's 
integrity and independence from foreign 
influence. 
 
2. R.A. NO. 9225 (DUAL CITIZENSHIP 
ACT) 
 
Under R.A. No. 9225 (Citizenship Retention 
and Re-acquisition Act of 2003), individuals 
with dual citizenship who retain or reacquire 
Filipino citizenship are eligible for admission 
to the Bar. 
 
The Supreme Court in Republic v. Manalo 
(G.R. No. 180906, October 5, 2010) clarified 
that dual citizens may qualify provided they 
renounce their foreign allegiance and fulfill all 
other Bar admission requirements. 
 
c. Good Moral Character 
 
Applicants for admission to the Bar must not 
only possess the requisite educational 
qualifications and pass the Bar Examinations 
but also demonstrate fitness to engage in the 
practice of law by exhibiting unwavering 
good moral character. This principle reflects 
the recognition that lawyers are officers of 
the court, tasked with upholding justice and 
public trust in the legal profession. 
 


<!-- PAGE 351 -->

 
 
339 
In Narag v. Narag (B.M. No. 1157, July 25, 
2006), the Court held that acts reflecting 
dishonesty or moral turpitude disqualify an 
applicant, as lawyers are expected to 
embody integrity and moral uprightness. 
 
d. Bar Examinations 
 
The bar examination's significance extends 
beyond mere academic performance—it 
assesses whether the examinee possesses 
the qualities of integrity, critical thinking, and 
dedication 
necessary 
to 
uphold 
the 
Constitution, laws, and justice system.  
 
The examination covers eight core legal 
subjects 
 
Political Law, Labor Law, Civil Law, Taxation

The Bar examination is not simply a 
qualification test but a safeguard to protect 
the legal profession's integrity and the

3. Continuing Requirements for 
Membership in the Bar 
 
The 
Supreme 
Court 
has 
consistently 
emphasized that good moral character is not 
merely a prerequisite for admission but a 
continuing requirement for lawyers, as they 
serve as officers of the court and custodians 
of public trust. In In Re: Almacen (G.R. No. 
L-27654, February 18, 1970), the Court 
declared that a lawyer must remain “a model 
of honor, integrity, and fair dealing” to uphold 
the legal profession's dignity and the public's 
confidence. 
 
Adherence to rigid standards of mental 
fitness, maintaining the highest degree of 
morality, faithful observance of the rules of 
the 
legal 
profession, 
compliance 
with 
mandatory continuing legal education, and 
payment of membership fees to the 
Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) are 
necessary for membership in good standing 
in the bar and for enjoying the privilege to 
practice law.

a. Mandatory Continuing Legal 
Education (MCLE) – CPRA, Canon III, 
Sec. 24; Canon IV, Sec. 8 
 
 
Active involvement in legal education 
 
A lawyer shall keep abreast of legal 
developments, participate in continuing legal 
education programs, and support efforts to 
achieve standards of excellence in law 
schools as well as in the practical training of 
law students. (Sec. 24, Canon III) 
 
Lifelong learning 
 
A competent lawyer engages in lifelong 
learning through the continued development 
of professional skills. (Sec. 8, Canon IV) 
 
Mandatory Continuing Legal Education 
[MCLE] Program 
 
A program which requires lawyers to show 
proof of having undertaken improvement in 
their knowledge as a precondition for 
renewing their license to practice. 
 
Purpose 
 
Continuing legal education is required of 
members of the IBP to: 
 
a. Ensure that throughout their career, they 
keep abreast with law and jurisprudence; 
b. Maintain the ethics of the profession; and 
c. Enhance the standards of the practice of 
law [Sec. 1, Rule 1, B.M. No. 850] 
 
 
 
 
Requirements 
 
Members of the IBP shall complete, every 
three years, at least 36 hours of continuing 
legal education activities approved by the 
MCLE Committee, viz: 
 
 Legal Ethics – 6 hours 
 Trial and Pre-trial Skills – 4 hours 
 Alternative Dispute Resolution – 5 
hours 
 Updates on substantive and procedural 
laws and jurisprudence – 9 hours 
 International law and International 
Conventions – 2 hours 
 Legal writing and oral advocacy – 4 
hours 
 Other MCLE prescribed subjects – 6 
hours 
 
Compliance 
 
Lawyers, not otherwise exempted, are 
required 
to 
complete 
their 
MCLE 
requirements every three (3) years and 
within the compliance periods set by the 
Rules. 
 
Failure to comply 
 
a. A member who, for whatever reason, is in 
non-compliance at the end of the compliance 
period shall pay a non-compliance fee. 
 
b. Any member who fails to satisfactorily 
comply shall be listed as a delinquent 
member by the IBP Board of Governors upon 
the 
recommendation 
of 
the 
MCLE 
Committee, in which case, Rule 139-A, Rules 
of Court, governing the IBP, shall apply. 
[Sec. 1 and 2, Rule 13, B.M. No. 850]

Representatives;

Imposition of Professional Tax 
 
The 
province 
may 
levy 
an 
annual 
professional tax on each person engaged in 
the exercise or practice of his profession 
requiring government examination at such

Where to pay professional tax 
 
Every person legally authorized to practice 
his profession shall pay the professional tax 
to the province where he practices his 
profession or where he maintains his 
principal office in case he practices his 
profession in several places: Provided, 
however, That such person who has paid the 
corresponding professional tax shall be 
entitled to practice his profession in any part 
of the Philippines without being subjected to 
any other national or local tax, license, or fee 
for the practice of such profession. 
 
When to pay 
 
The professional tax shall be payable 
annually, on or before the thirty-first (31st) 
day of January. Any person first beginning to 
practice a profession after the month of 
January must, however, pay the full tax 
before engaging therein. A line of profession 
does not become exempt even if conducted 
with some other profession for which the tax 
has been paid. Professionals exclusively 
employed in the government shall be exempt 
from the payment of this tax. 
 
Reportorial requirements

shall write in deeds, receipts, prescriptions, 
reports, books of account, plans and 
designs, surveys and maps, as the case may 
be, the number of the official receipt issued

d. Legal Aid – CPRA, Canon III, Sec. 25; 
A.M. No. 22-11-01-SC (Rules on Unified 
Legal Aid Service) 
 
 
SECTION 25. Support for legal internship, 
apprenticeship, and training. To prepare 
the next generation of lawyers for ethical 
practice, 
lawyers 
shall 
support 
legal 
internship and apprenticeship programs and 
accept law students for training. 
 
The lawyer shall treat the apprentices as 
junior colleagues and future counsels, and 
shall conscientiously supervise them. 
 
Rules on Unified Legal Aid Service 
(ULAS) 
 
 
The Rules on Unified Legal Aid Service 
(ULAS) institutionalize a unified, nationwide 
system for mandatory pro bono legal aid 
by members of the Philippine Bar, grounded 
on the constitutional mandate of free access 
to courts and adequate legal assistance for 
the underprivileged. The Rules proceed from 
the principle that the practice of law is 
imbued with public interest and that 
membership in the Bar is a privilege 
burdened with conditions, one of which is the 
duty to render legal aid. 
 
ULAS applies to Covered Lawyers, defined 
as members of the Philippine Bar whose IBP 
membership is not terminated, who are not 
retired, and who are not expressly excluded 
by the Rules.  
 
Rendering Pro Bono Legal Aid Services is 
mandatory for Covered Lawyers and covers 
acts involving the application of law, legal 
procedure, or legal knowledge, rendered free 
of charge to Qualified Beneficiaries. These 
services include representation in courts and 
quasi-judicial bodies, legal counseling and 
document drafting, developmental legal 
assistance, participation in accredited legal 
outreach programs and legal missions, 
supervision of law student practitioners 
under Rule 138-A, and other legal services 
as may be authorized by the Supreme Court. 
 
A Qualified Beneficiary includes a person 
for whom a counsel de officio has been 
appointed, as well as indigent litigants under 
the Rules of Court or persons who otherwise 
lack sufficient means to afford adequate legal 


<!-- PAGE 355 -->

 
 
343 
services, 
including 
Overseas 
Filipino 
Workers and migrant workers. Determination 
of qualification requires the execution of an 
affidavit by the beneficiary and the issuance 
by the lawyer of a certification under the 
Lawyer’s Oath, subject to prudence and 
verification. 
 
Each 
Compliance 
Period 
spans 
36 
months, beginning January 1, 2025, and 
Covered Lawyers are required to render a 
minimum of 60 hours of pro bono legal aid 
services per compliance period, subject to 
specific rules on aggregation, exemptions, 
and alternatives. Lawyers who already 
render free legal aid by the nature of their 
work, such as those in NGOs, IBP legal aid 
offices, or as supervising lawyers of law 
student practitioners, may credit such 
services toward compliance. 
 
The Rules allow Registered Organizations, 
including private law firms, to aggregate the 
creditable pro bono hours of their Covered 
Lawyers, provided a prior written election to 
aggregate is filed with the ULAS Board. 
Notwithstanding aggregation, each lawyer 
must personally render pro bono services 
equivalent to at least 25% of the required 
minimum hours. 
 
ULAS introduces an option to give a 
financial contribution to the ULAS Fund in 
lieu of actual service, subject to strict 
limitations. A Covered Lawyer or Registered 
Organization 
may 
substitute 
financial 
contribution for up to 50% of the required 
hours, while Philippine Lawyers Based 
Abroad may opt to contribute financially in 
lieu of rendering 100% of the required hours. 
Financial contribution never results in a total 
exemption from service unless expressly 
allowed by the Rules. 
 
Compliance with ULAS carries incentives, 
including the grant of 15 MCLE units per 
compliance period for lawyers who complete 
the required minimum hours. Other possible 
incentives include subsidies for expenses 
incurred in rendering legal aid and additional 
benefits as may be approved by the 
Supreme Court. 
 
Attorney’s fees awarded in successful pro 
bono litigation accrue to the ULAS Fund, 
and a reasonable portion of the beneficiary’s 
recovery, not exceeding ten percent and 
excluding actual damages, may likewise be 
contributed to the Fund if agreed to in writing. 
Certifications of indigency issued under 
ULAS authorize exemption from docket and 
other lawful fees, subject to challenge and 
verification by the court. 
 
The Rules impose strict reporting and 
accountability 
requirements. 
Covered 
Lawyers must submit a Compliance Report 
within one month after the end of the 
compliance period, detailing full or partial 
compliance, 
exclusion, 
or 
aggregation. 
Failure to comply constitutes noncompliance 
and triggers a 60-day grace period to cure 
deficiencies. 
 
Persistent 
noncompliance 
results 
in 
administrative consequences, including 
the imposition of fines, listing as a delinquent 
IBP member, and ineligibility for a Certificate 
of Good Standing. These penalties are 
without prejudice to further sanctions and do 
not excuse the lawyer from eventually 
completing the required minimum hours, 
which are carried over to the next compliance 
period. 
 
Implementation of ULAS is entrusted to the 
ULAS Board, composed of a Supreme Court 
Justice as Chairperson, ex officio members 
from the IBP, MCLE Governing Board, and 
Philippine Association of Law Schools, and 
representatives from private practitioners 
across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. The 
ULAS Board administers the Rules, accredits 
outreach programs, monitors compliance, 
manages the ULAS Fund, and issues 
implementing guidelines, subject to Supreme 
Court approval.

ii. Paralegals – CPRA, Canon II, Secs. 34-
35 
 
Section 34. Paralegal services; lawyer’s 
responsibility. A paralegal is one who 
performs tasks that require familiarity with 
legal concepts, employed or retained by a 
lawyer, law office, corporation, governmental 
agency, or other entity for non-diagnostic and 
non-advisory work in relation to legal matters 
delegated by such lawyer, law office, 
corporation, governmental agency, or other 
entity. 
A lawyer must direct or supervise a paralegal 
in the performance of the latter’s delegated 
duties. 
The lawyer’s duty of confidentiality shall also 
extend to the services rendered by the 
paralegal, who is equally bound to keep the 
privilege. 
Section 35. Non-delegable legal tasks. A 
lawyer shall not delegate to or permit a non-
lawyer, including a paralegal, to: 
 
(a) accept cases on behalf of the lawyer; 
(b) give legal advice or opinion; 
(c) act independently without the lawyer’s 
supervision or direction; 
(d) to hold himself or herself out as a 
lawyer, or be named in association with 
a lawyer in any pleading or submission 
to any court, tribunal, or other 
government agency;

346 
(e) appear in any court, tribunal, or other 
government agency, or actively 
participate in formal legal proceedings 
on behalf of a client, except when 
allowed by the law or rules; 
(f) conduct negotiations with third parties 
unless allowed in administrative 
agencies, without a lawyer’s supervision 
or direction; 
(g) sign correspondence containing a legal 
opinion; 
(h) perform any of the duties that only 
lawyers may undertake. 
 
These provisions shall not apply to law 
student practitioners under Rule 138-A of the 
Rules of Court.

(a) Cadastral Proceedings – Act No. 
2259, Sec. 9 
 
Under Act No. 2259, non-lawyers are 
allowed to appear in cadastral proceedings 
when representing their own interests.  
 
Cadastral proceedings are administrative in 
character but are conducted in court to 
determine the rightful ownership of lands 
subject to survey. These cases often involve 
ordinary individuals, many of whom are 
landowners or claimants with limited financial 
resources 
and 
no 
access 
to 
legal 
representation. To ensure inclusivity and 
fairness, the law allows non-lawyers to 
appear and advocate for their claims, as the 
primary purpose of such proceedings is to 
streamline land titling and resolve ownership 
disputes expeditiously.

of

Relations

bodies.  
 
(1) Non-lawyers may appear before the 
Commission or any Labor Arbiter only: 
 
1. If they represent themselves; or  
2. If they represent their organization 
or members thereof. 
 
(2) No attorney’s fees, negotiation fees or

Republic Act No. 6657 (Comprehensive

No. 9700, allows non-lawyers, specifically 
farmers, farmworkers, or landowners, to

Agrarian 
Reform 
Adjudication 
Board 
(DARAB).  
The DAR is hereby vested with primary 
jurisdiction to determine and adjudicate

exclusive original jurisdiction over all matters 
involving the implementation of agrarian

It shall not be bound by technical rules of

controversies in a most expeditious manner, 
employing all reasonable means to ascertain 
the facts of every case in accordance with 
justice and equity and the merits of the case.

Toward this end, it shall adopt a uniform rule

(d) Barangay Conciliation – R.A. No. 
7160, Sec. 415 
 
Appearance of Parties in Person 
 
In 
all 
katarungang 
pambarangay 
proceedings, the parties must appear in 
person without the assistance of counsel 
or representative, except for minors and 
incompetents who may be assisted by 
their next-of-kin who are not lawyers. 
 
Barangay conciliation proceedings under the 
Katarungang Pambarangay law prohibit 
lawyers from appearing as counsel. This 
ensures that the process remains simple, 
accessible, and non-adversarial, allowing 
parties to focus on resolving disputes 
amicably without the technicalities often 
associated with formal legal representation. 
However, lawyers may participate as parties 
to the dispute if they are directly involved.  
 
In Paat v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 
111107, January 10, 1997), the Supreme 
Court reiterated the non-litigious nature of 
barangay conciliation because the presence 
of lawyers may defeat its purpose of 
fostering 
community-based 
dispute 
resolution. 
 
(e) Cases under Expedited Procedure 
– A.M. No. 08-8-7-SC, Secs. 12 and 22 
 
Note: Sections 12 and 22 of A.M. No. 08-8-7-SC 
(as provided for under the 2026 Syllabus) do not 
identify cases under expedited procedure.  
 
They merely govern procedural matters within 
Small Claims cases, specifically the effect of 
failure to file a response (Sec. 12) and the 
procedure when Judicial Dispute Resolution fails 
(Sec. 22).  
 
These provisions concern case disposition, not 
the scope of expedited proceedings. 
 
Cases under Expedited Procedure 
 
Cases under expedited procedure are those 
governed by special rules designed to secure 
the speedy, inexpensive, and simplified 
disposition of actions, with limited pleadings, 
summary hearings, and strict timelines. 
 


<!-- PAGE 360 -->

 
 
348 
1. Small Claims Cases 
 
These are civil cases involving purely money 
claims that fall within the jurisdictional 
amount prescribed by the Supreme Court. 
Proceedings are summary in nature, formal 
pleadings are dispensed with, and the case 
is resolved in a single hearing, subject to the 
rules on response, default, and Judicial 
Dispute Resolution. 
 
2. Cases under the Revised Rule on 
Summary Procedure 
 
These include forcible entry and unlawful 
detainer cases, regardless of the amount of 
damages, as well as other civil cases where 
the claim does not exceed the amount fixed 
by the Rule. The procedure limits pleadings 
and motions, prohibits dilatory remedies, and 
requires 
prompt 
resolution 
based 
on 
affidavits and position papers. 
 
3. Other Actions Specifically Placed 
Under Summary or Expedited Rules by 
Law or Supreme Court Issuances 
 
Certain actions are governed by special rules 
that adopt abbreviated proceedings and 
fixed periods, such as election-related 
disputes, administrative or quasi-judicial 
cases, and other proceedings expressly 
declared by law or by the Supreme Court to 
be summary or expeditious in character. 
 
 
(f) Arbitration – R.A. No. 9285, Sec. 
22; R.A. No. 876, Sec. 12 
 
Sec. 
25. 
Legal 
Representation 
in 
International Arbitration. In international 
arbitration conducted in the Philippines, a 
party may be presented by any person of his

unless admitted to the practice of law in the 
Philippines, shall not be authorized to appear

Section 12. Procedure by arbitrators. 
Subject to the terms of the submission or 
contract, if any are specified therein, are 
arbitrators selected as prescribed herein 
must, within five days after appointment if the 
parties to the controversy reside within the 
same city or province, or within fifteen days 
after appointment if the parties reside in 
different provinces, set a time and place for 
the hearing of the matters submitted to them, 
and must cause notice thereof to be given to 
each of the parties.  
 
The hearing can be postponed or adjourned 
by the arbitrators only by agreement of the 
parties; otherwise, adjournment may be 
ordered by the arbitrators upon their own 
motion only at the hearing and for good and 
sufficient cause. No adjournment shall 
extend the hearing beyond the day fixed in 
the submission or contract for rendering the 
award, unless the time so fixed is extended 
by the written agreement of the parties to the 
submission or contract or their attorneys, or 
unless the parties have continued with the 
arbitration 
without 
objection 
to 
such 
adjournment. 
The hearing may proceed in the absence of 
any party who, after due notice, fails to be 
present at such hearing or fails to obtain an 
adjournment thereof. An award shall not be 
made solely on the default of a party. The 
arbitrators shall require the other party to 
submit such evidence as they may require for 
making an award. 
No one other than a party to said arbitration, 
or a person in the regular employ of such 
party duly authorized in writing by said party, 
or a practicing attorney-at-law, shall be 
permitted by the arbitrators to represent 


<!-- PAGE 361 -->

 
 
349 
before him or them any party to the 
arbitration. 
Any 
party 
desiring 
to 
be 
represented by counsel shall notify the other 
party or parties of such intention at least five 
days prior to the hearing. 
The arbitrators shall arrange for the taking of 
a stenographic record of the testimony when 
such a record is requested by one or more 
parties, and when payment of the cost 
thereof is assumed by such party or parties. 
Persons having a direct interest in the 
controversy which is the subject of arbitration 
shall have the right to attend any hearing; but 
the attendance of any other person shall be 
at the discretion of the arbitrators. 
 
c. Members of the Bar Prohibited from 
Private Practice 
 
i. President, Vice-President, Members of 
the 
Cabinet, 
their 
Deputies 
and 
Assistants 
 
Article 
VII, 
Section 13 
of the 
1987 
Constitution prohibits the President, Vice-
President, Members of the Cabinet, and their 
deputies or assistants from engaging in any 
other profession, including the private 
practice of law, during their tenure in office. 
 
ii. Senators and Members of the House 
of Representatives 
 
Article VI, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution 
prohibits Senators and Members of the 
House of Representatives from personally 
appearing as counsel before any court of 
justice, electoral tribunal, quasi-judicial body, 
or administrative agency during their term. 
 
They are not absolutely prohibited from 
practicing law, but the Constitution bars them 
from personal appearance as counsel. 
 
iii. Members of the Constitutional 
Commissions 
 
Article IX-A, Section 2 of the 1987 
Constitution prohibits Members of the 
Constitutional Commissions, namely the 
Commission on Elections, Civil Service 
Commission, and Commission on Audit, from 
engaging in the practice of any profession, 
including law, during their tenure. 
 
iv. Ombudsman and their Deputies 
 
Article XI, Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution 
prohibits the Ombudsman and his or her 
Deputies from engaging in any other 
profession or occupation, including the 
private practice of law, during their term of 
office. 
 
v. Justices, Judges, and Court Employees 
 
Under the Code of Judicial Conduct and the 
Rules of Court, Justices, Judges, and court 
personnel are prohibited from engaging in 
the practice of law. This prohibition applies 
throughout their incumbency and extends to 
acts that may constitute indirect practice. 
 
vi. Governors and Mayors – R.A. No. 
7160, Sec. 90(a) 
 
Section 90(a) of the Local Government Code 
(R.A. No. 7160) prohibits governors, city 
mayors, 
and 
municipal 
mayors 
from 
engaging in the private practice of any 
profession, including law, during their tenure. 
 
vii. Government Officials and Employees 
– R.A. No. 6713, Sec. 7(b)(2) in relation to 
Office of the President Memorandum 
Circular No. 17, s. 1986 and Rule XVIII, 
Sec. 12 of the Revised Civil Service Rules 
 
Section 7(b)(2) of R.A. No. 6713 prohibits 
public officials and employees from engaging 
in the private practice of their profession 
unless authorized by law and permitted 
by the head of the agency, provided that 
such practice does not conflict with official 
functions. 
 


<!-- PAGE 362 -->

 
 
350 
Section 7(b)(2) 
 
Prohibited Acts and Transactions 
(Public Officials and Employes) 
 
Xxx Engage in the private practice of their 
profession unless authorized by the 
Constitution or by law, provided that such 
practice will not conflict or tend to conflict 
with their official functions. 
 
Office 
of 
the 
President 
Memorandum 
Circular No. 17 (s. 1986) and the Revised 
Civil Service Rules reiterate this rule and 
require prior written authority before any 
private practice may be allowed. 
 
d. Members of the Bar with Limited 
Legal Practice 
 
i. Vice-Governors, Vice-Mayors, and 
Members of Local Legislative Bodies – 
R.A. No. 7160 
 
Vice-governors, vice-mayors, and members 
of the sanggunian may practice their 
professions, engage in any occupation, or 
teach in schools except during session 
hours: Provided, That they shall not engage 
in the practice of law or any other profession 
in any case where the local government unit 
of which they are officials is a party. 
 
ii. Government Lawyers 
 
1. Public Attorneys. Lawyers of the Public 
Attorney’s Office are prohibited from 
engaging in private law practice. Their 
functions are limited to representation of 
indigent litigants as provided by law. 
2. Prosecutors (Fiscals). Provincial, city, 
and assistant prosecutors are prohibited 
from engaging in private practice, as their 
duties require full-time devotion to the 
prosecution of criminal actions in behalf of 
the State. 
3. Solicitor General and OSG Lawyers. 
Lawyers of the Office of the Solicitor 
General are prohibited from engaging in 
private practice. They are mandated to 
represent the Government, its agencies, and 
instrumentalities in all legal proceedings. 
4. Government Corporate Counsel and 
Agency Lawyers. Lawyers employed as 
legal officers, counsels, or attorneys in 
government agencies, government-owned or 
controlled corporations, and government 
financial institutions are generally prohibited 
from engaging in private practice unless 
expressly authorized by law or by the head of 
the agency. 
5. Local Government Legal Officers. City, 
provincial, or municipal legal officers are 
prohibited from engaging in private practice 
during their incumbency, as their functions 
require exclusive legal representation of the 
local government unit. 
(a) With Authority to Engage in Limited 
Law Practice 
 
As a rule, government lawyers are 
prohibited from engaging in private 
practice. Limited practice is allowed only 
when expressly authorized by law or 
by the head of the agency, and only 
when such practice does not conflict with 
official duties. In the absence of express 
authority, engagement in private law 
practice constitutes an administrative 
offense. 
 
(b) Separated from the Service – R.A. 
No. 6713 
 


<!-- PAGE 363 -->

 
 
351 
Prohibitions on outside employment and 
related activities continue to apply for one 
(1) year after resignation, retirement, or 
separation from public office.  
 
Thus, a former public official or employee 
who is a member of the Bar remains 
prohibited, within one year from separation, 
from owning, controlling, managing, or 
accepting employment in a private enterprise 
regulated, supervised, or licensed by his 
former office.  
 
Although the prohibition on private practice 
under Section 7(b)(2) does not automatically 
extend after separation, the law expressly 
provides that the professional cannot 
practice his profession in connection with 
any matter before the office he used to be 
with, and in such case, the one-year 
prohibition 
likewise 
applies, 
thereby 
limiting the scope of legal practice of a 
separated government lawyer. 
 
iii. Retired Judges and Justices – R.A. 
No. 910, as amended 
 
Retired 
judges 
and 
justices 
who 
receive 
retirement benefits under R.A. No. 910 are not 
absolutely prohibited from the practice of law. 
Their authority to practice is subject to statutory 
and ethical limitations. 
They are prohibited from appearing as 
counsel in any case or proceeding over which 
they previously exercised judicial authority, or 
in matters closely connected with their former 
official functions. 
They are likewise disqualified from appearing 
before the court or tribunal where they 
previously served, within the period and under 
the conditions prescribed by law and judicial 
ethics, to avoid impropriety and undue influence 
arising from prior judicial office. 
Outside these limitations, retired judges and 
justices may engage in the practice of law, 
provided that such practice does not violate the 
Code 
of 
Professional 
Responsibility 
and 
Accountability or other applicable ethical rules. 
iv. In Small Claims and Katarungang 
Pambarangay 
 
 
Prohibition of lawyers to appear  
 
The prohibition against lawyers to participate 
in small claims cases does not preclude 
legal advice or consultation outside the 
courtroom. 
Parties 
may 
still 
seek 
preliminary guidance from lawyers prior to 
filing or responding to claims, but the 
courtroom dynamic remains strictly between 
the 
parties 
and 
the 
presiding 
judge.

e. Foreign Lawyers – CPRA, Canon III, 
Sec. 33 
 
Foreign lawyers cannot, directly or 
indirectly, 
practice

in

5. Privileges of a Lawyer 
 
The privileges of a lawyer are those rights 
and immunities granted by law and 


<!-- PAGE 364 -->

 
 
352 
jurisprudence to enable the effective 
performance of legal duties as an officer of 
the court. These privileges are not absolute 
and are always subject to law, ethics, and 
judicial control. 
 
a. 
Right 
of 
Appearance 
and 
Representation 
 
A lawyer duly admitted to the Bar has the 
right to appear and represent parties before 
courts, 
quasi-judicial 
bodies, 
and 
administrative 
agencies, 
subject 
to 
applicable rules. This right arises from 
admission to the Bar under Rule 138 of the 
Rules of Court and is exercised under the 
supervision of the courts. 
 
b. Right to Reasonable Compensation 
 
A lawyer is entitled to just and reasonable 
compensation for legal services rendered. 
This right includes the enforcement of 
attorney’s fees and the assertion of an 
attorney’s 
lien, 
subject 
to 
judicial 
determination 
of 
reasonableness 
and 
compliance with ethical standards. 
 
c. Exemption from Arrest in Certain Cases 
 
Under Section 11, Rule 138 of the Rules of 
Court, a lawyer is exempt from arrest in civil 
cases while actually engaged in court duties 
or going to and returning from court. This 
privilege does not apply to criminal cases. 
 
d. Independence in the Exercise of 
Professional Judgment 
 
A lawyer has the privilege to exercise 
independent 
professional 
judgment 
in 
representing a client, consistent with law and 
ethics. This independence is required to 
ensure fidelity to the client’s cause without 
improper interference. 
 
e. Status as an Officer of the Court 
 
A lawyer is an officer of the court and, as 
such, is bound to assist in the administration 
of justice. This status accords the lawyer the 
right to rely on judicial processes and to be 
heard, but it does not create a presumption 
of correctness or immunity from discipline. 
 
f. Right to Respect and Courtesy 
 
A lawyer is entitled to respect and courtesy 
from courts, judicial officers, and litigants in 
the performance of professional duties. This 
privilege 
exists 
to 
ensure 
orderly 
proceedings 
and 
does 
not 
excuse 
misconduct or contemptuous behavior. 
 
g. 
Protection 
Against 
Unauthorized 
Practice of Law 
 
Only members of the Philippine Bar are 
authorized to practice law. Lawyers are 
entitled 
to 
protection 
against 
the 
unauthorized practice of law, which is 
regulated under Rule 138 of the Rules of 
Court and sanctioned by law. 
 
 
6. Unauthorized Practice of Law 
 
a. Penalties 
 
The 
unauthorized 
practice 
of 
law 
is 
prohibited and punishable to protect the 
public and preserve the integrity of the legal 
profession. Penalties may arise from statute, 
court rules, and the inherent contempt power 
of the courts. 
1. Criminal Liability. Under Rule 138 of the 
Rules of Court and related penal laws, a 
person 
who 
practices 
law 
without 
authority may be held criminally liable. 
When the unauthorized practice involves 
deceit, false representation, or the use of 
another’s name or credentials, criminal 
prosecution may lie under the Revised 
Penal Code or special laws. 
2. Contempt 
of 
Court. 
Unauthorized 
practice of law constitutes direct or 
indirect contempt, as it obstructs the 
administration of justice and usurps a 
privilege reserved by law to members of 
the Bar. Courts may summarily punish 


<!-- PAGE 365 -->

 
 
353 
the 
offender 
through 
fines 
or 
imprisonment. 
3. Injunction 
and 
Cease-and-Desist 
Orders. Courts may enjoin individuals or 
entities from continuing the unauthorized 
practice of law. Injunctive relief may be 
issued motu proprio or upon complaint of 
the Integrated Bar or an aggrieved party. 
4. Administrative Sanctions (for Lawyers 
and 
Public 
Officers) 
If committed by a lawyer not authorized 
to practice, or by a public officer 
prohibited from private practice, the act 
constitutes administrative misconduct, 
punishable by suspension or disbarment, 
without prejudice to criminal or contempt 
proceedings. 
5. Nullity 
of 
Acts 
Performed. 
Acts 
constituting 
the 
unauthorized 
practice of law do not confer professional 
rights and may be declared void or 
without legal effect, particularly when 
public interest or judicial proceedings are 
affected. 
 
7. Duties and Responsibilities of 
Lawyers – CPRA 
 
 
The Code of Professional Responsibility and 
Accountability (CPRA), promulgated under 
A.M. No. 22-09-01-SC seeks to promote 
integrity, competence, and accountability 
within the legal profession to protect public 
trust and uphold the rule of law.  
 
Lawyers, as officers of the court, are required 
to demonstrate professionalism, honesty, 
and ethical conduct in their dealings with 
clients, colleagues, and the courts. 
 
 
 
 
a. General Provisions 
 
i. Integrity as Central Principle – 
Preamble 
 
An ethical lawyer is a lawyer possessed of 
integrity. Integrity is the sum total of all the 
ethical values that every lawyer must 
embody and exhibit. A lawyer with integrity, 
therefore, acts with independence, propriety, 
fidelity, competence and diligence, equality 
and accountability. 
Failure to abide by the Code results in 
sanctions. 
 
ii. Applicability of CPRA – Sec. 1 
 
This CPRA shall apply to all members of the 
Philippine Bar in the practice of law, whether 
in private practice, government service, the 
judiciary, or the academe. 
 
iii. Repealing Clause – Sec. 2 
 
All provisions of the Code of Professional 
Responsibility of 1988 and other rules, 
issuances, or jurisprudence inconsistent with 
this CPRA are hereby repealed or modified 
accordingly 
 
iv. Effectivity Date – Sec. 3 
 
This CPRA shall take effect fifteen (15) 
calendar days after its publication in the 
Official Gazette or in a newspaper of general 
circulation. 
 
b. Independence – Canon I 
 
i. Concept – Introduction and Sec. 1 
 
The independence of a lawyer in the 
discharge of professional duties without any 
improper influence, restriction, pressure, 
or interference, direct or indirect, ensures 
effective 
legal 
representation 
and 
is 
ultimately imperative for the rule of law. 
 


<!-- PAGE 366 -->

 
 
354 
A 
lawyer 
shall 
make 
legal 
services 
accessible in an efficient and effective 
manner. In performing this duty, a lawyer 
shall maintain independence, act with 
integrity, and at all times ensure the 
efficient and effective delivery of justice. 
 
ii. Accessible, Efficient, and Effective 
Legal Service 
 
A 
lawyer 
shall 
make 
legal 
services 
accessible in an efficient and effective 
manner. In performing this duty, a lawyer 
shall maintain independence, act with 
integrity, and at all times ensure the efficient 
and effective delivery of justice. 
 
iii. Merit-based Legal Practice 
 
A lawyer shall rely solely on the merits of a 
cause and not exert, or give the appearance 
of, any influence on, nor undermine the 
authority of, the court, tribunal or other 
government agency, or its proceedings. 
 
iv. Avoiding Improper Considerations 
and External Influence 
 
A lawyer shall not, in advocating a client’s 
cause, be influenced by dishonest or immoral 
considerations, 
external 
influences, 
or 
pressure. 
 
v. 
Non-interference 
in 
Courts 
or 
Tribunals 
 
Unless authorized by law or a court, a lawyer 
shall not assist or cause a branch, agency, 
office or officer of the government to interfere 
in any matter before any court, tribunal, or 
other government agency. 
 
vi. Discretion in Procedure and Strategy 
 
(a) Client’s Decision to Settle Case 
 
A lawyer shall not allow the client to dictate 
or determine the procedure in handling the 
case. Nevertheless, a lawyer shall respect 
the client’s decision to settle or compromise 
the case after explaining its consequences to 
the client. 
 
 
c. Propriety – Canon II 
 
 
i. Concept – Introduction 
 
A lawyer shall, at all times, act with propriety 
and maintain the appearance of propriety in 
personal and professional dealings, observe 
honesty, respect and courtesy, and uphold 
the dignity of the legal profession consistent 
with the highest standards of ethical 
behavior. 
 
ii. Proper and Dignified Conduct – Secs. 
1 and 2 
 
Section 1. Proper conduct.  A lawyer shall 
not engage in Unlawful, Dishonest, Immoral, 
or Deceitful conduct. 
 
 
Section 2. Dignified conduct.  A lawyer 
shall respect the law, the courts, tribunals, 
and other government agencies, their 
officials, employees, and processes, and act 
with courtesy, civility, fairness, and candor 
towards fellow members of the bar. 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 367 -->

 
 
355 
iii. Dignified, Gender-fair, Child- and 
Culturally-sensitive Language – Sec. 4 
 
A lawyer shall use only dignified, gender-fair, 
child- and culturally-sensitive language in all 
personal and professional dealings. 
 
To this end, a lawyer shall not use language 
which is abusive, intemperate, offensive or 
otherwise improper, oral or written, and 
whether 
made 
through 
traditional 
or 
electronic means, including all forms or types 
of mass or social media. 
 
iv. Correcting Misrepresentations in 
Applications for Admission to the Bar – 
Sec. 11 
 
A 
lawyer 
shall 
not 
make 
false 
representations or statements. A lawyer shall 
be liable for any material damage caused by 
such false representations or statements. 
 
A lawyer shall not, in demand letters or other 
similar 
correspondence, 
make 
false 
representations or statements, or impute 
civil, criminal, or administrative liability, 
without factual or legal basis. 
 
A lawyer shall correct false or inaccurate 
statements and information made in relation 
to an application for admission to the bar, any 
pleading, or any other document required by 
or submitted to the court, tribunal or agency, 
as soon as its falsity or inaccuracy is 
discovered or made known to him or her. 
 
v. Reporting Dishonest, Deceitful, or 
Misleading Conduct – Sec. 12 
 
A lawyer shall immediately inform a court, 
tribunal, or other government agency of any 
dishonest, deceitful or misleading conduct 
related to a matter being handled by said 
lawyer before such court, tribunal, or other 
government agency. 
 
 
 
A lawyer shall also report to the appropriate 
authority any transaction or unlawful activity 
that is required to be reported under relevant 
laws, including the submission of covered 
and suspicious transactions under regulatory 
laws, such as those concerning anti-money 
laundering.  
 
When disclosing or reporting the foregoing 
information to the appropriate court, tribunal, 
or other government agency, the lawyer shall 
not be deemed to have violated the lawyer’s 
duty of confidentiality. Any such information 
shall be treated with strict confidentiality. 
 
 
A baseless report shall be subject to civil, 
criminal, or administrative action. 
 
vi. Disclosure of Relationship or 
Connection – Sec. 20 
 
A lawyer shall, at the first available 
opportunity, formally disclose on record the 
lawyer’s relationship or connection with the 
presiding officer of any court, tribunal, or 
other government agency, or any of its 
personnel, 
or 
the 
lawyer’s 
partners, 
associates, or clients, that may serve as a 
ground for mandatory inhibition in any 
pending proceeding before such court, 
tribunal, or other government agency. 
 
vii. Avoiding Plagiarism and 
Misrepresentation of Legal Authorities 
– Sec. 8 
 
A lawyer shall not misquote, misrepresent, or 
mislead the court as to the existence or the 
contents of any document, argument, 


<!-- PAGE 368 -->

 
 
356 
evidence, law, or other legal authority, or 
pass off as one’s own the ideas or words of 
another, or assert as a fact that which has not 
been proven. 
 
viii. Non-solicitation and Advertisement 
– Sec. 17 
 
 
A lawyer shall not, directly or indirectly, 
solicit, or appear to solicit, legal business. 
 
A lawyer shall not, directly or indirectly, 
advertise legal services on any platform or 
media except with the use of dignified, 
verifiable, and factual information, including 
biographical data, contact details, fields of 
practice, services offered, and the like, so as 
to allow a potential client to make an 
informed choice. In no case shall the 
permissible advertisement be self-laudatory. 
 
A lawyer, law firm, or any of their 
representatives shall not pay or give any 
benefit or consideration to any media 
practitioner, award-giving body, professional 
organization, or personality, in anticipation 
of, or in return for, publicity or recognition, to 
attract legal representation, service, or 
retainership. 
 
ix. Sub Judice Rule – Sec. 19 
 
A lawyer shall not use any forum or medium 
to comment or publicize opinion pertaining to 
a pending proceeding before any court,

cause 
a 
pre-judgment, 
or 
(b) sway public perception so as to 
impede, 
obstruct, 
or 
influence 
the 
decision of such court, tribunal, or other 
government agency, or which tends to 
tarnish the court’s or tribunal’s integrity, 
or 
(c) impute improper motives against any 
of 
its 
members, 
or 
(d) create a widespread perception of 
guilt 
or 
innocence 
before 
a 
final

x. Avoiding Gifts and Donations to 
Courts and Government Agencies – Sec. 
21 
 
A lawyer shall not directly or indirectly give

or government agency, or any of its officers 
and personnel. 
 
 
xi. Avoiding Abuse of the Right to Sue 
and of Court Processes – Sec. 23; Canon 
III, Sec. 7 
 
A lawyer shall observe formal decorum 
before all courts, tribunals, and other

A lawyer’s attire shall be consistent with the

person’s sexual orientation, gender identity, 
and gender expression.

encroach 
upon 
or

This 
includes

Section 36. Responsible use. A lawyer 
shall have the duty to understand the

Section 37. Online posts. A lawyer shall

Section 38. Non-posting of false or

Section 39. Prohibition against fraudulent 
accounts. A 
lawyer 
shall 
not 
create,

Section 40. Non-disclosure of privileged

lawyer shall not reveal, directly or indirectly,

course 
of, 
or 
emanating 
from, 
the 
representation, except when allowed by law 
or the CPRA. 
 
Section 41. Duty to safeguard client 
confidences in social media. A lawyer, 
who uses a social media account to

relation 
to 
client 
confidences 
and 
information, shall exert efforts to prevent the

use of, or unauthorized access to, such an

Section 42. Prohibition against influence 
through social media. A lawyer shall not

43. Legal 
information; 
legal

d. Fidelity – Canon III 
 
i. CONCEPT – Introduction and Sec. 2 
 
Fidelity pertains to a lawyer’s duty to uphold 
the Constitution and the laws of the land, to 
assist in the administration of justice as an 
officer of the court, and to advance or defend 
a client’s cause, with full devotion, genuine 
interest, and zeal in the pursuit of truth and 
justice. 
 
A lawyer shall uphold the constitution, obey 
the laws of the land, promote respect for laws 
and legal processes, safeguard human 
rights, and at all times advance the honor 
and integrity of the legal profession. 
 
As an officer of the court, a lawyer shall 
uphold the rule of law and conscientiously 
assist 
in 
the 
speedy 
and 
efficient 
administration of justice. 
 
As an advocate, a lawyer shall represent the 
client with fidelity and zeal within the bounds 
of the law and the CPRA. 
 
 
 
ii. Lawyer-Client Relationship 
 
(a) Definition 
 
A lawyer-client relationship is of the 
highest fiduciary character.  
 
 
 
As a trust relation, it is essential that the 
engagement is founded on the confidence 
reposed by the client on the lawyer. 
Therefore, a lawyer-client relationship shall 
arise when the client consciously, voluntarily 
and in good faith vests a lawyer with the 
client’s confidence for the purpose of 
rendering legal services such as providing 
legal advice or representation, and the 
lawyer, whether expressly or impliedly, 
agrees to render such services. 
 
(b) Duty of Representation 
 
(1) Authority of Lawyer to Bind 
Client – Sec. 4 
 
A lawyer can bind a client in a legal 
engagement only when so authorized 
through a written agreement. 
 
The lawyer, however, cannot compromise a 
client’s litigation, or receive anything in 
discharge of a client’s claim, without a 
special power of attorney for such purpose. 
 
(c) Fiduciary Duty – Sec. 6 
 
A lawyer shall be mindful of the trust and 
confidence reposed by the client. 
 
To this end, a lawyer shall not abuse or 
exploit the relationship with a client. 
 
(1) Encouragement and Settlement 


<!-- PAGE 371 -->

 
 
359 
A lawyer shall encourage the client to avoid, 
end or settle a controversy, whether pending 
or not, in order to reach a settlement or a 
compromise 
if 
the 
matter 
can 
be 
compromised under the law and will admit of 
a fair settlement. 
 
To this end, the lawyer shall actively assist 
the parties and the court, tribunal, or other 
government agency to effect mediation 
and/or dispute resolution. 
 
(2) Rectification of Fraud 
A lawyer who receives information that a 
client 
has, 
in 
the 
course 
of 
the 
representation, perpetrated a fraud in 
relation to any matter subject of the 
representation before a court, tribunal, or 
other government agency, or against any 
officer thereof, shall promptly call upon the 
client to rectify the same. Such fraudulent act 
on the part of the client shall be a ground for 
the termination by the lawyer of the 
engagement. 
 
(d) Lawyer’s Right to Compensation  
 
(1) Attorney’s Fees – Secs. 41-48  
 
Section 41. Fair and reasonable fees. 
A lawyer shall charge only fair and 
reasonable fees. 
 
Attorney’s fees shall be deemed fair and 
reasonable if determined based on the 
following factors:  
 
(a) The time spent and the extent of the 
service 
rendered 
or 
required; 
 
(b) The novelty and difficulty of the issues 
involved; 
 
(c) The skill or expertise of the lawyer, 
including the level of study and experience 
required 
for 
the 
engagement; 
 
(d) 
The 
probability 
of 
losing 
other 
engagements as a result of acceptance of 
the 
case; 
 
(e) The customary charges for similar 
services and the recommended schedule of 
fees, which the IBP chapter shall provide; 
 
(f) The quantitative or qualitative value of the 
client’s interest in the engagement, or the 
benefits resulting to the client from the 
service; 
 
(g) 
The 
contingency 
or 
certainty 
of 
compensation; 
 
(h) The character of the engagement, 
whether limited, seasonal, or otherwise; and 
 
(i) Other analogous factors.  
 
Section 42. Division of fees upon referral. 
A lawyer shall, in case of referral of legal 
services in favor of another lawyer with the 
written informed consent of the client, be 
entitled to a division of fees in proportion to 
the work performed and responsibility 
assumed. 
 
Where a lawyer undertakes to complete 
unfinished legal business of a deceased 
lawyer, a division or sharing of fees is 
allowed with the deceased lawyer’s legal 
heirs or estate. 
 
Section 43. Non-sharing of fees with non-
lawyers. A lawyer shall not share, split, or 
divide or stipulate to divide, directly or 
indirectly, a fee for legal services with 
persons or organizations not licensed or 
authorized to practice law. 
 
Section 44. Payment of compensation by 
third party. A lawyer shall not receive any 
fee, reward, costs, commission, interest, 
rebate or forwarding allowance or other 
compensation from anyone other than the 
client, except upon the written informed 
consent of such client. 
Receipt of compensation from someone 
other than the client must not interfere with 


<!-- PAGE 372 -->

 
 
360 
the lawyer’s independence, professional 
judgment, or the lawyer-client relationship. 
Neither 
should 
information 
relating 
to 
representation of a client be disclosed in 
violation 
of 
the 
rule 
on 
privileged 
communication. 
 
Section 45. Prompt payment of legal fees. 
A lawyer is entitled to prompt payment from 
the client of attorney’s fees. 
 
Absent an express agreement as to 
professional fees, a lawyer is entitled to be 
paid 
reasonable 
attorney’s 
fees 
in 
accordance with Canon III, Section 41. 
 
Section 46. Controversy over legal fees. 
A lawyer shall avoid any controversy with a 
client concerning fees for legal services and 
shall resort to judicial action solely to prevent 
imposition, injustice or fraud. 
 
Section 48. Compensation for counsel de 
oficio. Subject to availability of funds as may 
be provided by law, the court may, in its 
discretion, order a lawyer engaged as 
counsel de oficio to be compensated in such 
sum as the court may fix following Canon III, 
Section 41, provided that it is not covered by 
the provision on Limited Legal Services. 
 
(2) Attorney’s Lien – Sec. 47 
 
Section 47. Enforcement of attorney’s 
lien. In case of non-payment of attorney’s 
fees, a lawyer may resort to the enforcement 
of the attorney’s lien under Canon III, Section 
54, by filing a Notice of Enforcement of 
Attorney’s Lien with the court, tribunal, or 
other government agency of origin where the 
action or proceeding the lawyer rendered 
service for is pending, without prejudice to 
other remedies under the law or the Rules of 
Court. The Notice shall be accompanied by 
proof of the services rendered, and served 
on the client. The court, tribunal, or other 
government agency, after hearing, shall 
determine the lawyer’s entitlement to the 
claimed fees. 
 
The enforcement of an attorney’s lien shall 
be treated as an independent claim and shall 
in no instance delay the resolution of the 
main case. The resolution of the lawyer’s 
claim may be included in the main judgment 
or in a separate partial judgment. In the case 
of a partial judgment, the same shall be 
subject of appeal. 
 
An appeal in the main case shall not stay the 
execution of the lawyer’s lien. In the 
execution of the judgment in the main case, 
the court shall give due consideration to the 
pending claim of the lawyer. 
 
If the claim for attorney’s lien arises after a 
decision has been rendered by the court, 
tribunal, or other government agency of 
origin on the action or proceeding, the claim 
for the enforcement of the lien shall be by an 
independent action. 
 
(e) Management of Client Resources  
 
(1) Lending and Borrowing – Sec. 52  
 
During the existence of the lawyer-client 
relationship, a lawyer shall not lend money to 
a client, except under urgent and justifiable 
circumstances. Advances for professional 
fees and necessary expenses in a legal 
matter the lawyer is handling for a client shall 
not be covered by this rule. 
 
Neither shall a lawyer borrow money from a 
client during the existence of the lawyer-
client 
relationship, 
unless 
the 
client’s 
interests are fully protected by the nature of 
the case, or by independent advice. This rule 
does not apply to standard commercial 
transactions for products or services that the 
client offers to the public in general, or where 
the lawyer and the client have an existing or 
prior business relationship, or where there is 
a contract between the lawyer and the client. 
 
A lawyer is strictly prohibited from borrowing 
money from a client during the existence 
of 
the 
lawyer-client 
relationship,

361 
regardless of subsequent payment or 
settlement of the loan, unless the client’s 
interests are fully protected by the nature of 
the case or by independent advice. The 
prohibition applies once legal advice or 
assistance is sought and accepted, as the 
fiduciary nature of the relationship demands 
utmost trust and prevents undue influence or 
exploitation. Payment of the debt does not 
erase the ethical violation, and borrowing 
money from a client constitutes professional 
misconduct and warrants a disciplinary 
sanction. (★Babe Mae Villafuerte v. Atty. 
Cezar R. Tajanlangit, A.C. No. 7619, 
December 6, 2023, as penned by J. 
Gaerlan)

A lawyer shall not acquire, directly or

(3) Accounting and Management of 
Funds – Secs. 49 and 50 
 
A lawyer, during the existence of the lawyer- 
client relationship, shall account for and 
prepare an inventory of any fund or property 
belonging to the client, whether received 
from the latter or from a third person, 
immediately upon such receipt. 
 
When funds are entrusted to a lawyer by a 
client for a specific purpose, the lawyer shall 
use such funds only for the client’s declared 
purpose. Any unused amount of the 
entrusted funds shall be promptly returned to 
the client upon accomplishment of the stated 
purpose or the client’s demand. 
 
A lawyer shall keep the funds of the clients 
separate and apart from his or her own and 
those of others kept by the lawyer.

(f) Keeping Client Confidences – Secs. 
27-30 
 
Section 27. Confidentiality of privileged 
communication. A lawyer shall maintain the 
confidences of the client, and shall respect 
data privacy laws. The duty of confidentiality 
shall continue even after the termination of 
the lawyer- client engagement. 
 
Section 28. Protecting client 
confidences.  
 
A lawyer shall not reveal the confidences of 
the client, including data from the client’s 
files, except; 
 
(a) When a written informed consent is 
obtained from the client; 
 
(b) When required by law, such as anti-
money laundering statutes, or the 
Rules of Court; 
(c) To the extent necessary, to collect the 
lawyer’s fees; 
 
(d) In defense of the lawyer, or the 
lawyer’s employees or associates; or 
(e)   By judicial order (only if material)

Section 29. Duty of confidentiality by 
former lawyers of a law firm. A lawyer shall 
continue to be bound by the rule on 
confidentiality pertaining to clients of his or 
her previous law office or law firm. 
 
Section 30. Duty of confidentiality of 
members of a law firm. A lawyer may 
disclose the legal matters entrusted by a 
client of the firm to the partners and 
associates, as well as paralegals, legal 
assistants, law clerks, legal researchers, law 
interns, and other non-legal staff, who are or 
will be involved in the handling of the client’s 
account, unless expressly prohibited by the 
client. 
 
 
A lawyer directly entrusted with a client’s 
confidences 
shall 
adopt 
necessary 
measures to prevent other members of the 
law firm, both legal and non-legal, to whom 
the client’s confidences have been shared, 
from disclosing or using them, without the 
written informed consent of the client. 
 
(g) Duty to Provide Regular Updates – 
Canon IV, Sec. 6 
 
A lawyer shall regularly inform the client of 
the status and the result of the matter 
undertaken, and any action in connection 
thereto, 
and 
shall 
respond 
within 
a 
reasonable time to the client’s request for 
information.

(h) Termination – Secs. 53-56 
 
(1) By the Lawyer 
 
A lawyer shall terminate the lawyer- client 
engagement only for good cause and upon 
written notice, in any of the following cases: 
 
(a) When the client pursues an illegal or 
immoral course of conduct in connection with 
the 
engagement; 
 
(b) When the client insists that the lawyer 
pursue conduct that is violative of these 
Canons 
and 
rules; 
 
(c) When the lawyer’s inability to work with a 
co-counsel will not promote the best interest 
of 
the 
client; 
 
(d) When the moral predisposition or the 
mental or physical condition of the lawyer 
renders 
it 
difficult 
to 
carry 
out 
the 
engagement 
effectively; 
 
(e) When the client deliberately fails to pay 
the fees for the lawyer’s services, fails to 
comply with the retainer agreement, or can 
no longer be found despite diligent efforts; 
 
(f) When the lawyer is elected or appointed 
to 
public 
office; 
 
(g) Other similar cases. 
 
(2) By the Client 
 
The lawyer-client engagement may be 
terminated by the client at any time upon loss 
of trust and confidence. 
 
The termination of the engagement shall not 
relieve the client from full payment of all 
professional fees due to the lawyer. If the 
engagement has been reduced to writing, the 
lawyer shall be entitled to recover from the 
client the full compensation stipulated, 
unless found by the court, tribunal or other 
government agency to be unconscionable or 
unreasonable under Canon III, Section 41 of 
the CPRA.

For the payment of the compensation, the 
lawyer shall have a charging lien upon all 
judgments for the payment of money, and 
executions issued in pursuance of such 
judgment, rendered in the case where the 
lawyer’s services had been retained by the 
client. 
 
(3) By Death of Either Party 
 
The death of the lawyer or client shall 
terminate the lawyer-client relationship. The 
death of such lawyer shall not extinguish the 
lawyer-client engagement between the law 
firm and the client handled by such law firm. 
 
(4) Accounting and Turnover of 
Funds 
 
 
A lawyer who is discharged from or 
terminates the engagement shall, subject to 
an attorney’s lien, immediately render a full 
account of and turn over all documents, 
evidence, funds, and properties belonging to 
the client. 
 
The lawyer shall cooperate with the chosen 
successor in the orderly transfer of the legal 
matter, including all information necessary 
for the efficient handling of the client’s 
representation. 
 
A lawyer shall have a lien upon the funds, 
documents, and papers of the client which 
have lawfully come into his or her possession 
and may retain the same until the fair and 
reasonable fees and disbursements have 
been paid, and may apply such funds to the 
satisfaction thereof. 
 
iii. Conflict of Interest – Secs. 13-22 
 
The CPRA strictly prohibits lawyers from 
representing conflicting interests without the 
informed consent of all parties. This rule 
safeguards the lawyer’s independence and 
ensures the integrity of their representation. 
 
Conflict of interest 
 
A lawyer shall not represent conflicting 
interests 
except 
by 
written informed 
consent of all concerned given after a full 
disclosure of the facts. 
 
 
Relevant Jurisprudence 
 
A lawyer-client relationship existed between 
Edna and respondent when he prepared the 
SPA upon her request. Respondent later 
appeared as counsel for Petronila in both the 
civil and criminal cases where the core 
factual issue was Edna’s execution and the 
validity of the very SPA he prepared and 
notarized. 
In 
representing 
Petronila, 
respondent was placed in a position where 
his duty to one client required him to oppose 
the interest of his former client, and where he 
could use information obtained in the prior 
engagement. Respondent’s representation 
of Edna at the SPA’s preparation, followed by 
his representation of Petronila in litigations 
attacking or defending that SPA, squarely fell 
within the prohibition against conflicting 
interests. No written informed consent of 
both clients was shown. This constituted 
an intentional violation of the conflict-of-
interest rule and warranted disciplinary 
sanction 


<!-- PAGE 377 -->

 
 
365 
 
(★Edna Tan Malapit v. Rogelio M. Watin, 
A.C. NO. 11777, October 1, 2024, as 
penned by J. Gaerlan) 
 
There is conflict of interest when a lawyer 
represents inconsistent or opposing interests 
of two or more persons. The test is whether 
in behalf of one client, it is the lawyer’s duty 
to fight for an issue or claim, but which is his 
or her duty to oppose for the other client. 
 
Prohibition against conflict- of-interest 
representation; current clients 
 
In relation to current clients, the following 
rules shall be observed: 
 
(a) A lawyer shall not enter into a business 
transaction with a client or knowingly acquire 
an ownership, possessory, security, or other 
pecuniary interest adverse to a client unless: 
 
(1) it is shown that the transaction and 
terms on which the lawyer acquires the 
interest are fair and reasonable to the 
client and are fully disclosed and 
transmitted in writing in a manner that can 
be reasonably understood by the client; 
 
(2) the client is advised in writing of the 
desirability of seeking, and is given a 
reasonable opportunity to seek, the 
advice of another independent lawyer on 
the transaction; and 
 
(3) the client gives written informed 
consent to the essential terms of the 
transaction and the lawyer’s role in the 
transaction, including whether the lawyer 
is 
representing 
the 
client 
in 
the 
transaction. 
(b) A lawyer shall not use confidential 
information relating to representation of a 
client without the client’s written informed 
consent, except as permitted or required by 
law or the CPRA. 
 
(c) A lawyer shall not, by undue influence, 
acquire any substantial gift from a client, 
including a testamentary gift, or prepare on 
behalf of a client an instrument giving the 
lawyer such gift, directly or indirectly. 
 
(d) Unless with the written informed consent 
of the client and subject to the application of 
the sub judice rule, a lawyer shall not make 
or negotiate an agreement giving the lawyer 
literary or media rights to a portrayal or 
account based in substantial part on 
information relating to the representation. 
 
(e) A lawyer shall not accept compensation 
for representing a client from any person 
other than the client, unless: 
 
(1) the client gives written informed 
consent; 
 
(2) there is no interference with the 
lawyer’s independence or professional 
judgment or with the lawyer-client 
relationship; or 
 
(3) the information relating to 
representation of a client is protected as 
required by the rule on privileged 
communication.  
 
(f) A lawyer, who represents two or more 
clients in the same case, in case there is a 
settlement or plea-bargaining, shall disclose 
to all the clients the existence and nature of 
all the claims or pleas involved and the 
participation of each client in the settlement 
or plea-bargaining. 
 
(g) A lawyer shall avoid testifying in behalf 
of the client, except:

When a lawyer joins a law firm, it shall be the

Corporate lawyers; conflict of interest 
 
In relation to organizational clients, a lawyer 
who represents a corporation or any 
organization does not, by virtue of such 
representation, necessarily represent any 
constituent or affiliated organization, such as 
a parent or subsidiary. 
 
A lawyer for a corporation or other

Legal services organization; conflict of 
interest 
 
A legal services organization is any private 
organization, including a legal aid clinic, 
partnership, association, or corporation, 
whose primary purpose is to provide free 
legal services. 
 
A lawyer-client relationship shall arise only 
between the client and the handling lawyers 
of the legal services organization. All the 
lawyers of the legal services organization 
who participated in the handling of a legal 
matter shall be covered by the rule on conflict 
of interest and confidentiality. 
 
Lawyers in government service; conflict 
of interest 
 
A lawyer currently serving in the government 
shall not practice law privately, unless 
otherwise authorized by the Constitution, the 
law or applicable Civil Service rules and 
regulations. If allowed, private practice shall 
be upon the express authority of the lawyer’s 
superior, for a stated specified purpose or 
engagement, and only during an approved 
leave of absence. However, the lawyer shall 
not represent an interest adverse to the 
government. 
 
Public Attorney’s Office; conflict of 
interest 
 
The Public Attorney’s Office is the primary 
legal aid service office of the government. In 
the pursuit of its mandate under its charter, 
the Public Attorney’s Office shall ensure 
ready access to its services by the 
marginalized sectors of society in a manner 
that takes into consideration the avoidance of 
potential conflict of interest situations which 
will 
leave 
these 
marginalized 
parties 
unassisted by counsel. 
 
A conflict of interest of any of the lawyers of 
the Public Attorney’s Office incident to 
services rendered for the Office shall be 
imputed only to the said lawyer and the 
lawyer’s direct supervisor. Such conflict of 
interest shall not disqualify the rest of the 
lawyers from the Public Attorney’s Office 
from representing the affected client, upon 
full disclosure to the latter and written 
informed consent.

officio, unless prohibited by law, or the 
applicable 
Civil 
Service 
rules 
and 
regulations, or when there is a conflict of 
interest with government. 
 
Section 37. Duty of confidentiality in 
Limited Legal Services. A lawyer who 
provides Limited Legal Services must protect 
the client’s private confidences to the same 
extent as if engaged under regular terms. 
 
Section 38. Termination of Limited Legal 
Services. Unless governed by Canon III, 
Section 36, a lawyer must cease to provide 
Limited Legal Services to a client when the 
lawyer becomes aware that there may be an 
actual or potential conflict of interest, except 
with the written informed consent of the 
client.

370 
In all cases, the Limited Legal Services 
terminates upon the completion of such

Section 39. Limited Legal Services of law 
student practitioners. The Limited Legal 
Services 
rendered 
by 
a 
law
