under 
the 
Clinical 
Legal 
Education Program shall be governed by the 
CPRA. 
 
Section 40. Accountability of legal clinic 
director and supervising lawyer. A law 
student clinic director and supervising 
lawyer, under Rule 138-A of the Rules of 
Court shall provide meaningful training to law 
students. They shall assume responsibility 
for any work performed by the law student 
while under their supervision and shall 
comply with all the laws, rules, and 
guidelines 
pertaining 
to 
Law 
Student 
Practice. 
 
e. Competence and Diligence – Canon IV 
 
i. General Duty of Competence – Sec. 1; 
Sec. 2, first sentence 
 
A lawyer professionally handling a client’s 
cause shall, to the best of his or her ability, 
observe 
competence, 
diligence, 
commitment, and skill consistent with the 
fiduciary 
nature 
of 
the 
lawyer-client 
relationship, regardless of the nature of the 
legal matter or issues involved, and whether 
for a fee or pro bono. 
 
Section 
1. Competent, 
efficient 
and 
conscientious 
service. A 
lawyer 
shall 
provide legal service that is competent, 
efficient, and conscientious. A lawyer shall 
be thorough in research, preparation, and 
application of the legal knowledge and skills 
necessary for an engagement. 
 
 
 
ii. Collaboration with other Counsel – 
Sec. 2 
 
 
Section 2. Undertaking legal services; 
collaborating counsel.  A lawyer shall only 
undertake legal services he or she can 
deliver. 
 
With the prior written consent of the client, a 
lawyer may secure the services of a 
collaborating counsel. 
 
iii. Avoidance of Delay – Sec. 3, first 
sentence; Secs. 4 and 7 
 
Section 4. Diligence in all undertakings. A 
lawyer 
shall 
observe 
diligence 
in 
all 
professional undertakings, and shall not 
cause or occasion delay in any legal matter 
before any court, tribunal, or other agency. 
 
A lawyer shall appear for trial adequately 
familiar with the law, the facts of the case, 
and the evidence to be presented. A lawyer 
shall also be ready with the object and 
documentary evidence, as well as the judicial 
affidavits of the witnesses, when required by 
the rules or the court. 
 
Section 7. Extension of time to file. A 
lawyer shall avoid asking for an extension of 
time to file any pleading, motion, or other 
court submission, except when allowed by 
the Rules of Court or for good cause. 
 
When an extension is obtained, the lawyer 
shall not let the period lapse without 
submitting the pleading, motion, or other 
court submission, except upon the client’s 
decision not to pursue the case any further or 
for other justifiable cause.

A lawyer shall diligently and seasonably act

lawyer

in

v. Responding to Inquiries – Sec. 5 
 
A lawyer shall, after reasonable inquiry,

A lawyer shall explain the viable options to

Section 9. Practice of law concurrent with

The practice of another profession or

Section 10. Non-legal activities. A lawyer

f. Equality – Canon V 
 
Every lawyer shall adhere to the principle of 
equality and hold firmly the belief that every 
person, regardless of nationality or ethnicity, 
color, sexual orientation or gender identity, 
religion, disability, age, marital status, social 
or 
economic 
status, 
and 
other 
like 
circumstances, has the fundamental right to 
equal treatment and representation. 
 
As such, the lawyer shall accord equal 
respect, attention, dedication and zeal in 
advancing the client’s cause, regardless of 
personal opinion, religious or political beliefs 
pertaining on the personal circumstances of 
the client, except for justifiable reasons. 
 
i. Non-discrimination – Secs. 1 and 4 
 
Section 1. Non-discrimination. A lawyer 
shall not decline to represent a person solely 
on account of the latter’s nationality or 
ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender 
identity, religion, disability, age, marital 
status, social or economic status, political 
beliefs, or such lawyer’s or the public’s 
opinion regarding the guilt of said person, 
except for justifiable reasons. 
 
Section 4. Standard of service. A lawyer 
shall observe the same standard of service 
for all clients, regardless of remuneration, 
except for the higher standard required for 
representation of vulnerable persons. 
 
ii. Higher Standard of Service to 
Vulnerable Persons – Sec. 2 
 
Section 
2. Treatment 
of 
vulnerable 
persons. In dealing with a client who 
belongs to a vulnerable sector, a lawyer shall 
be mindful and sensitive of, and consider the

applicable laws and rules. 
 
The lawyer shall observe a higher standard 
of service suited to the particular needs of the 
vulnerable person and shall assert such

372 
person’s right to meaningful access to

A vulnerable person is a person who is at a

those 
who 
are 
socio-economically 
disadvantaged, those who belong to racial or

8. Discipline and Disbarment of Lawyers 
– CPRA, Canon VI 
 
 
By taking the Lawyer’s Oath, a lawyer 
becomes a guardian of the law and an 
administrator of justice. As such, the lawyer 
shall observe the highest degree of morality, 
adhere to rigid standards of mental fitness, 
and faithfully comply with the rules of the 
legal profession. 
 
Failure to honor this covenant makes the 
lawyer unfit to continue in the practice of law 
and accountable to society, the courts, the 
legal profession, and the client. 
 
a. Nature of Bar Discipline Proceedings 
 
i. Non-penal; Public Welfare Measure 
 
Bar disciplinary proceedings are not penal 
in character. They are instituted not to 
punish the lawyer, but to protect the public, 
preserve the integrity of the legal 
profession, and maintain the orderly 
administration of justice. 
 
Under Canon VI (Accountability) of the 
CPRA, disciplinary proceedings against 
lawyers are confidential in character and 
summary 
in 
nature. 
This 
character 
underscores that such proceedings are sui 
generis, distinct from criminal or civil actions, 
and are governed by the Supreme Court’s 
constitutional power to regulate the practice 
of law. 
 
The objective of bar discipline is public 
welfare, not private redress. Thus, the 
outcome of disciplinary proceedings does 
not depend on the will of the complainant. 
Desistance, 
settlement, 
compromise, 
restitution, withdrawal of charges, or failure 
of the complainant to prosecute does not 
terminate or interrupt the investigation, as the 
matter involves the fitness of the lawyer to 
remain a member of the Bar  
 
Because bar discipline is a public welfare 
measure, proceedings may be initiated motu 
proprio by the Supreme Court, and sanctions 
imposed are directed toward protecting 
society, the courts, the profession, and 
clients, rather than vindicating private rights. 
 
Disciplinary proceedings against lawyers 
shall be confidential in character and 
summary in nature. Nonetheless, the final 


<!-- PAGE 385 -->

 
 
373 
order of the Supreme Court shall be 
published like its decisions in other cases. 
 
ii. Not Subject to Desistance or 
Compromise – Sec. 16 
 
Section 16. Irrelevance of desistance, 
settlement, 
compromise, 
restitution, 
withdrawal, or failure to prosecute.  No 
investigation 
shall 
be 
interrupted 
or 
terminated by reason of the desistance, 
settlement, 
compromise, 
restitution, 
withdrawal of the charges, or failure of the 
complainant to prosecute the same. 
 
b. Institution of Bar Discipline 
Proceedings – Secs. 2, 3, and 30 
 
Section 2. How instituted.  Proceedings for 
the disbarment, suspension, or discipline of 
lawyers may be commenced by the Supreme 
Court on its own initiative, or upon the filing 
of a verified complaint by the Board of 
Governors of the Integrated Bar of the 
Philippines (IBP), or by any person, before 
the Supreme Court or the IBP. However, a 
verified complaint against a government 
lawyer which seeks to discipline such lawyer 
as a member of the Bar shall only be filed in 
the Supreme Court. 
 
A verified complaint filed with the Supreme 
Court may be referred to the IBP for 
investigation, report and recommendation, 
except when filed directly by the IBP, in 
which case, the verified complaint shall be 
referred to the Office of the Bar Confidant or 
such fact-finding body as may be designated. 
 
Section 3. Contents of the complaint.  The 
complaint shall be verified. It shall state 
clearly and concisely the acts or omissions 
complained of and shall be supported by 
judicial affidavits of the witnesses and such 
other documents in support thereof. 
 
If the verified complaint is filed before the 
IBP, six (6) copies thereof shall be filed with 
the Secretary of the IBP or the Secretary of 
any of its chapters, who shall forthwith 
transmit the same to the IBP Board of 
Governors. 
 
i. Against Government Lawyers – Sec. 6 
 
When a complaint is filed against a 
government 
lawyer, 
the 
Investigating 
Commissioner shall determine, within five 
days from assignment by raffle, whether the 
concerned agency, the Ombudsman, or the 
Supreme Court has jurisdiction. If the 
allegations in the complaint touch upon the 
lawyer’s continuing obligations under the 
CPRA or if the allegations, assuming them to 
be true, make the lawyer unfit to practice the 
profession, 
then 
the 
Investigating 
Commissioner shall proceed with the case. 
Otherwise, the Investigating Commissioner 
shall recommend that the complaint be 
dismissed. 
 
ii. Against Members of the Judiciary – 
Sec. 2 
 
Complaints for disbarment, suspension and 
discipline filed against incumbent Justices of 
the Court of Appeals, Sandiganbayan, Court 
of Tax Appeals and judges of lower courts, or 
against lawyers in the judicial service, 
whether they are charged singly or jointly 
with other respondents, and whether such 
complaint deals with acts unrelated to the 
discharge of their official functions, shall be 
forwarded by the IBP to the Supreme Court 
for appropriate disposition under Rule 140, 
as amended.

Serious offenses. Serious offenses include:

Section 36. Assisting in the commission

d. Preventive Suspension – Sec. 31 
 
After receipt of respondent’s answer or lapse 
of the period therefor, the Supreme Court, on 
its 
own 
initiative, 
or 
upon 
the

30, may suspend a lawyer from the practice

law

e. Quantum and Burden of Proof – Sec. 
32 
 
In administrative disciplinary cases, the 
complainant has the burden of proof to 
establish with substantial evidence the 
allegations 
against 
the 
respondent. 
Substantial evidence is that amount of 
relevant evidence which a reasonable mind 
might accept as adequate to justify a 
conclusion. 
 
f. Executory Nature of Decision or 
Resolution – Sec. 43 
 
The decision or resolution pronouncing the 
respondent’s 
administrative 
liability 
is 
immediately executory. The copies of the

the Office of the Bar Confidant, the 
Integrated Bar of the Philippines National 
Office and local chapter to which the 
respondent belongs, and the Office of the

g. Sworn Statement After Service of 
Suspension – Secs. 45 and 46 
 
Section 45. Sworn statement after service 
of suspension.  
 
Upon the expiration of the period of 
suspension from the practice of law, the 
lawyer shall file a Sworn Statement with the 
Supreme Court, through the Office of the Bar 
Confidant, to show that the petitioner, during 
the period of suspension: 
 
(a) has not appeared before any court, 
tribunal or other government agency, 
whether in respect of current, former or 
prospective 
clients; 
(b) has not signed or filed any pleading or 
other 
court 
submission; 
(c) has duly informed his or her clients,

service organization of which he or she is

377 
a member, regarding the suspension; 
and 
(d) has not otherwise performed any act, 
directly or indirectly, that amounts to the 
practice of law. 
 
The Sworn Statement shall state the date of 
the lawyer’s receipt of the order, decision or 
resolution 
imposing 
the 
penalty 
of 
suspension, as well as a list of the lawyer’s 
engagements affected by the suspension, 
indicating the relevant court, tribunal or other 
government agency, if any. 
 
Copies of the Sworn Statement shall be 
furnished to the Local Chapter of the IBP, to

suspended lawyer has pending cases 
handled by him or her, and/or where he or 
she has appeared as counsel. 
 
Section 46. Resumption of practice of 
law. The 
Sworn 
Statement 
shall 
be 
considered as proof of the suspended 
lawyer’s compliance with the order of 
suspension. Such lawyer shall be allowed to 
resume the practice of law upon the filing of 
the Sworn Statement before the Supreme 
Court. 
 
However, any false statement in the Sworn 
Statement shall be a ground for a complaint 
for disbarment. 
 
Within five (5) days from the filing of the 
Sworn Statement and the Office of the Bar 
Confidant determines that there is a false 
statement stated therein, it shall refer the 
same to the Court for its immediate action. 
 
h. Clemency – Secs. 47-51 
 
Section 47. Reinstatement in the Roll of 
Attorneys. A lawyer who has been disbarred 
may file a verified petition for judicial 
clemency after five years from the receipt of 
the order, decision, resolution of disbarment. 
 
Section 
48. Petition 
for 
judicial 
clemency. The verified petition for judicial 
clemency shall allege the following: 
 
(a) that the verified petition was filed after 
five years from the receipt of the order, 
decision, or resolution of disbarment; 
 
(b) that the disbarred lawyer has fully 
complied with the terms and conditions of 
all prior disciplinary orders, including 
orders for restitution; 
 
(c) that he or she recognizes the 
wrongfulness and seriousness of the 
misconduct for which he or she was 
disbarred by showing positive acts 
evidencing reformation; 
 
(d) that he or she has reconciled, or 
attempted in good faith to reconcile, with 
the wronged private offended party in the 
disbarment case, or if the same is not 
possible, an explanation as to why such 
attempt at reconciliation could not be 
made. 
Where there is no private offended party, 
the plea for clemency must contain a 
public apology; and 
 
(e) notwithstanding the conduct for which 
the disbarred lawyer was disciplined, he 
or she has the requisite good moral 
character and competence. 
 
Any of the following allegations may also be 
made in support of the petition: 
 
(a) that he or she still has productive 
years that can be put to good use if given 
a chance; or 
 
(b) there is a showing of promise (such 
as intellectual aptitude, learning or legal 


<!-- PAGE 390 -->

 
 
378 
acumen 
or 
contribution 
to 
legal 
scholarship and the development of the 
legal system or administrative and other 
relevant skills), as well as potential for 
public service. 
 
Section 49. Action on the petition for 
judicial clemency; prima facie merit. Upon 
receipt of the petition, the Supreme Court 
shall conduct a preliminary evaluation and 
determine if the same has prima facie merit 
based on the criteria. 
 
If the petition has prima facie merit, the 
Supreme Court shall refer the petition to the 
Office of the Bar Confidant or any fact-finding 
body 
the 
Court 
so 
designates 
for 
investigation, report and recommendation. 
 
If the petition fails to show any prima facie 
merit, it shall be denied outright. 
 
Section 50. Investigation by the Office of 
the Bar Confidant or other fact-finding 
body. The Office of the Bar Confidant or any 
other fact-finding body designated shall 
conduct and terminate the investigation and 
submit to the Supreme Court its report and 
recommendation within ninety (90) calendar 
days from receipt of the referral. 
 
Section 51. Decision on the petition for 
judicial 
clemency; 
quantum 
of 
evidence. The Supreme Court shall decide 
the petition on the basis of clear and 
convincing evidence. 
 
 
9. Notarial Practice – A.M. No. 
02-8-13-SC, as amended 
 
 
 
a. Qualifications 
 
a. Must be a citizen of the Philippines; 
b. Must be over twenty-one (21) years 
of age; 
c. Must be a resident in the Philippines 
for at least one (1) year and maintains 
a regular place of work or business in 
the city or province where the 
commission is to be issued; 
d. Must be a member of the Philippine 
Bar in good standing with clearances 
from the Office of the Bar Confidant 
of the Supreme Court and the 
Integrated Bar of the Philippines; and 
e. Must not have been convicted in the 
first instance of any crime involving 
moral turpitude. 
 
b. Term of Office 
 
A person commissioned as notary public 
may perform notarial acts in any place within 
the 
territorial 
jurisdiction 
of 
the 
commissioning court for a period of two (2) 
years commencing the first day of January of 
the year in which the commissioning is made, 
unless earlier revoked or the notary public 
has resigned under these Rules and the 
Rules of Court. 
 
c. Powers and Limitations 
 
A notary public is authorized to perform 
notarial acts such as acknowledgments, 
jurats, oaths, affirmations, and certifications. 
However, their powers are subject to 
limitations, including: 
 
a. Prohibition 
against 
notarizing 
documents in which they have a direct or 
indirect financial or personal interest; 
b. Requirement 
to 
comply 
with 
jurisdictional limits; and 
c. Obligation to ensure that documents 
are properly signed, verified, and free 
from fraudulent representations. 
 
 


<!-- PAGE 391 -->

 
 
379 
 
d. Notarial Register 
 
Rule VI of the 2004 Rules mandates that all 
notarial acts must be recorded in a Notarial 
Register, a formal logbook maintained by the 
notary public. Each entry must include: 
 
a. The nature of the notarial act; 
b. The title or description of the 
document; 
c. The names of the signatories; 
d. Evidence of identity; and 
e. Fees collected. 
The register serves as an essential 
safeguard against fraud and is subject 
to audit and inspection by the court. 
 
e. Jurisdiction and Place of Notarization 
 
A 
notary 
public’s 
commission 
is 
geographically limited to the judicial region 
where they are authorized to practice. 
Notarial acts conducted outside the assigned 
region are invalid and may result in 
administrative penalties. 
 
f. Competent Evidence of Identity 
 
To prevent fraud and forgery, Rule II, Section 
12 requires notaries public to verify the 
identity of signatories using competent 
evidence of identity, which includes: 
 
a. A government-issued ID with a 
photograph and signature; or 
b. The oath or affirmation of a credible 
witness personally known to the notary 
public. 
This provision ensures the authenticity of 
notarized documents and upholds the 
integrity of the notarial process. 
 
g. Sanctions 
 
Violations of the 2004 Rules expose notaries 
public to administrative penalties, including: 
 
a. Suspension or revocation of their 
commission; 
b. Fines; 
c. Suspension from the practice of law; 
or 
d. Disbarment, in severe cases. 
 
These sanctions aim to deter misconduct 
and preserve the public's trust in the notarial 
system. 
 
h. Remote Notarization – A.M. No. 20-
07-04-SC, July 14, 2020 
 
In response to the challenges posed by the 
COVID-19 pandemic, the Supreme Court 
issued the 2020 Interim Rules on Remote 
Notarization 
of 
Paper 
Documents, 
allowing 
notarization to 
be 
conducted 
through videoconferencing technology, 
subject to strict safeguards, including: 
 
 
(a) Personal appearance of the principal 
through videoconferencing technology 
for purposes of identity verification; 
(b) Submission and presentation of the 
paper document to the notary public in 
accordance with the Interim Rules; 
(c) Compliance with the requirements of 
the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, 
suppletorily applied, insofar as they are 
not inconsistent with the Interim Rules; 
and 
(d) Observance of security, record-
keeping, and confidentiality measures 
prescribed under the Interim Rules. 
 
Relevant Jurisprudence 
 
Notarization is not an empty, meaningless, 
routinary act. It is invested with substantive 
public interest. The notarization by a notary 
public converts a private document into a 
public document, making it admissible in 


<!-- PAGE 392 -->

 
 
380 
evidence 
without 
further 
proof 
of 
its 
authenticity.  
 
A notarial document is, by law, entitled to full 
faith and credit upon its face. A notary public 
must observe with utmost care the basic 
requirements in the performance of their 
duties; otherwise, the public’s confidence in 
the integrity of the document would be 
undermined. (★Celia D. Mendoza v. Atty. 
Cesar R. Santiago, A.C. No. 13548, June 
14, 2023, as penned by J. Gaerlan) 
 
B. JUDICIAL ETHICS 
 
1. Sources 
 
a. New Code of Judicial Conduct (NCJC) 
– A.M. No. 03-05-01-SC 
 
The New Code of Judicial Conduct (NCJC) 
governs the ethical standards of judges in the 
Philippine judiciary. It was adopted to replace 
earlier codes and to place Philippine judicial 
ethics within a single, coherent framework. 
The Code sets binding ethical standards built 
around six values: Independence, Integrity, 
Impartiality, 
Propriety, 
Equality, 
and 
Competence and Diligence. These values 
define how judges must decide cases, relate 
to litigants, and conduct themselves in public 
life. 
 
The 
NCJC 
is 
not aspirational. It 
is 
enforceable and serves as a basis for 
administrative discipline, ensuring that the 
judiciary remains credible, independent, and 
worthy of public trust. 
 
b. Bangalore Principles of Judicial 
Conduct 2002 
 
The Bangalore Principles of Judicial 
Conduct (2002) set internationally accepted 
standards for judicial ethics, grounded on the 
right of every person to a fair and public 
hearing before a competent, independent, 
and impartial tribunal. 
They proceed from the premise that a 
credible judiciary is indispensable to the 
rule of law. Without an independent and 
impartial bench, constitutional guarantees 
and human rights cannot be meaningfully 
enforced. 
At the core of the Principles is the need for 
public confidence. Judicial authority rests 
not only on legal correctness but on the 
moral integrity of judges, who are required 
to treat judicial office as a public trust and to 
conduct themselves in a manner that 
sustains confidence in the justice system. 
The Principles identify six fundamental 
values 
that 
govern 
judicial 
conduct: 
Independence, 
Impartiality, 
Integrity, 
Propriety, Equality, and Competence and 
Diligence. These values serve as standards 
for judges and as reference points for 
institutions and the public in evaluating 
judicial behavior. 
The Bangalore Principles do not replace 
domestic rules on judicial discipline. They 
supplement existing laws and ethical 
codes, while recognizing that judges remain 
accountable to independent and impartial 
disciplinary 
mechanisms 
within 
their 
respective legal systems. 
d. Rules of Court 
 
The Rules of Court form a direct source of 
judicial ethics by prescribing standards of 


<!-- PAGE 393 -->

 
 
381 
conduct and discipline for judges in the 
exercise 
of 
judicial 
functions. 
Beyond 
procedural rules, they impose mandatory 
duties and restraints on judges to ensure 
fairness, impartiality, efficiency, and respect 
for due process. 
 
Through provisions on judicial discipline, 
contempt, inhibition, disqualification, and 
administrative accountability, the Rules of 
Court regulate how judges must act in 
relation to parties, lawyers, and court 
personnel. These rules reinforce the principle 
that judicial power must be exercised within 
defined legal and ethical limits. 
 
The ethical obligations found in the Rules of 
Court 
are 
binding 
and 
enforceable. 
Violations give rise to administrative liability, 
independent of criminal or civil responsibility, 
underscoring that judicial ethics is not merely 
aspirational but an integral part of procedural 
law. 
 
2. Principles 
 
a. Independence – NCJC, Canon 1; 1989 
CJC, Canon 1 
 
Judicial independence is a pre-requisite to 
the rule of law and a fundamental guarantee 
of a fair trial. A judge shall therefore uphold 
and exemplify judicial independence in both 
its individual and institutional aspects. 
 
Section 1 
 
Judges shall exercise the judicial function 
independently 
on 
the 
basis 
of 
their 
assessment of the facts and in accordance 
with a conscientious understanding of the 
law, free of any extraneous influence, 
inducement, pressure, threat or interference, 
direct or indirect, from any quarter or for any 
reason. 
 
Section 2 
 
In performing judicial duties, Judges shall be 
independent from judicial colleagues in 
respect of decisions which the judge is 
obliged to make independently. 
 
Section 3 
 
Judges shall refrain from influencing in any 
manner the outcome of litigation or dispute 
pending 
before 
another 
court 
or 
administrative agency. 
 
Section 4 
 
Judges shall not allow family, social, or other 
relationships to influence judicial conduct or 
judgment. The prestige of judicial office shall 
not be used or lent to advance the private 
interests of others, nor convey or permit 
others to convey the impression that they are 
in a special position to influence the judge. 
 
Section 5 
 
Judges shall not only be free from 
inappropriate 
connections 
with, 
and 
influence by, the executive and legislative 
branches of government, but must also 
appear to be free therefrom to a reasonable 
observer. 
 
Section 6 
 
Judges shall be independent in relation to 
society in general and in relation to the 
particular parties to a dispute which he or she 
has to adjudicate. 
 
Section 7 
 
Judges 
shall 
encourage 
and 
uphold 
safeguards for the discharge of judicial duties 
in order to maintain and enhance the 
institutional and operational independence of 
the judiciary. 
 
Section 8 
 
Judges shall exhibit and promote high 
standards of judicial conduct in order to 
reinforce public confidence in the judiciary 
which is fundamental to the maintenance of 
judicial independence. 


<!-- PAGE 394 -->

 
 
382 
b. Integrity – NCJC, Canon 2; 1989 CJC, 
Canon 1, Rules 3.02 to 3.05 
 
Integrity is essential not only to the proper 
discharge of the judicial office but also to the 
personal demeanor of judges. 
 
Section 1 
 
Judges shall ensure that not only is their 
conduct above reproach, but that it is 
perceived to be so in the view of a 
reasonable observer. 
 
Section 2 
 
The behavior and conduct of judges must 
reaffirm the people's faith in the integrity of 
the judiciary. Justice musty not merely be 
done but must also be seen to be done. 
 
Section 3 
 
Judges should take or initiate appropriate 
disciplinary measures against lawyers or 
court personnel for unprofessional conduct 
of which the judge may have become aware. 
 
 
1989 CJC (Code of Judicial Conduct) 
 
RULE 3.02 - In every case, a judge shall 
endeavor diligently to ascertain the facts and 
the applicable law unswayed by partisan 
interests, public opinion or fear of criticism. 
 
RULE 3.05 - A judge shall dispose of the 
court's business promptly and decide cases 
within the required periods. 
 
c. Impartiality – NCJC, Canon 3; 1989 
CJC, Canon 3 
 
Impartiality is essential to the proper 
discharge of the judicial office. It applies not 
only to the decision itself but also to the 
process by which the decision to made. 
 
RULE 3.01 - A judge shall be faithful to the 
law and maintain professional competence. 
RULE 3.02 - In every case, a judge shall 
endeavor diligently to ascertain the facts and 
the applicable law unswayed by partisan 
interests, public opinion or fear of criticism. 
RULE 3.03 - A judge shall maintain order and 
proper decorum in the court. 
RULE 3.04 - A judge should be patient, 
attentive, 
and 
courteous 
to 
lawyers, 
especially the inexperienced, to litigants, 
witnesses, and others appearing before the 
court. A judge should avoid unconsciously 
falling into the attitude of mind that the 
litigants are made for the courts, instead of 
the courts for the litigants. 
d. Propriety – NCJC, Canon 4; 1989 CJC 
Canon 5, Rule 3.03 
 
 
Propriety and the appearance of propriety 
are essential to the performance of all the 
activities of a judge. 
 
i. Conditions to Engage in Business – 
1989 CJC, Canon 5, Rules 5.02 and 5.04 
 
RULE 5.02 - A judge shall refrain from 
financial and business dealing that tend to 
reflect adversely on the court's impartiality, 
interfere with the proper performance of 
judicial activities or increase involvement 
with lawyers or persons likely to come before 
the court. A judge should so manage 
investments and other financial interests as 
to minimize the number of cases giving 
grounds for disqualifications. 
 
RULE 5.04 - A judge or any immediate 
member of the family shall not accept a gift, 
bequest, factor or loan from any one except 
as may be allowed by law. 


<!-- PAGE 395 -->

 
 
383 
ii. Conditions for Teaching – A.M. No. 
13-05-05-SC; OCA Circular No. 218-2019 
 
 
Teaching by Judges A.M. No. 13-05-05-SC 
(Implemented by OCA Circular No. 218-
2019) 
 
Authority to Teach 
 
Judges may engage in teaching only upon 
prior authority from the Supreme Court, 
secured through the Office of the Court 
Administrator. Permission is required to 
ensure that teaching does not impair judicial 
duties or violate ethical standards governing 
judicial conduct. 
 
Coverage of Teaching Activities 
 
The requirement applies to all forms of 
teaching and lecturing. This includes law 
schools, review centers, bar review classes, 
MCLE programs, academic institutions, and 
similar forums. It covers both in-person and 
online instruction, as well as recurring 
lectures, 
symposiums, 
and 
workshops. 
Sporadic guest appearances remain subject 
to ethical scrutiny when they go beyond 
incidental participation. 
 
Compatibility with Judicial Duties 
 
Teaching must not interfere with the 
performance of judicial functions. Judges 
must ensure that court sessions, case 
disposition, research, and decision writing 
are not delayed or compromised by teaching 
commitments. While no fixed numerical limit 
on teaching hours is prescribed, judges may 
be required to disclose schedules to show 
continued compliance with judicial workload 
requirements. 
 
Court Hours and Scheduling 
 
Teaching activities must not conflict with 
official court hours. Judges are prohibited 
from 
teaching 
during 
scheduled 
court 
sessions or official working hours unless 
expressly authorized. Classes are generally 
confined to after office hours or weekends, 
subject to approval by the Supreme Court or 
the OCA. 
 
Avoidance of Conflict of Interest and 
Impropriety 
 
Judges must avoid teaching engagements 
that create actual conflict of interest or the 
appearance of impropriety. This includes 
teaching in institutions closely connected 
with litigants who regularly appear before the 
judge’s court, or engagements that may cast 
doubt on impartiality. Judicial office must not 
be used to attract students, participants, or 
institutional advantage. 
 
Compensation and Dignity of Office 
 
Compensation 
for 
teaching 
must 
be 
reasonable and consistent with standard 
academic rates. Judges may not use 
teaching 
engagements 
for 
commercial 
exploitation, solicitation of business, or 
personal gain inconsistent with the dignity of 
judicial office. 
 
Reporting and Monitoring 
 
Judges are required to disclose teaching 
engagements to the OCA. Disclosure 
includes the institution or organizer, subject 
matter, schedule, number of hours, and 
compensation or allowances. The OCA 
retains authority to monitor compliance and 
assess impact on judicial performance. 
 
 
Sanctions 
 
Failure to obtain authority, make proper 
disclosure, or maintain judicial efficiency due 
to 
teaching 
activities 
constitutes 
administrative misconduct. Sanctions range 


<!-- PAGE 396 -->

 
 
384 
from admonition to suspension or other 
disciplinary penalties, depending on the 
gravity of the violation and its effect on court 
operations. 
 
iii. Purchase of Property in Litigation – 
NCC, Art. 1491(5) 
 
Article 1491, Civil Code. The following 
persons cannot acquire by purchase, even 
at a public or judicial auction, either in 
person or through the mediation of 
another: 
 
xxx (5) Justices, judges, prosecuting 
attorneys, clerks of superior and 
inferior courts, and other officers and 
employees 
connected 
with 
the 
administration of justice, the property 
and rights in litigation or levied upon 
an execution before the court within 
whose jurisdiction or territory they 
exercise their respective functions; 
this prohibition includes the act of 
acquiring by assignment and shall 
apply to lawyers, with respect to the 
property and rights which may be 
the object of any litigation in which 
they may take part by virtue of their 
profession; 
 
e. Equality – NCJC, Canon 5 
 
Ensuring equality of treatment to all before 
the 
courts 
is 
essential 
to 
the 
due 
performance of the judicial office. 
 
Section 1 
 
Judges shall be aware of, and understand, 
diversity in society and differences arising 
from various sources, including but not 
limited to race, color, sex, religion, national 
origin, caste, disability, age, marital status, 
sexual orientation, social and economic 
status and other like causes. 
 
Section 2 
 
Judges shall not, in the performance of 
judicial duties, by words or conduct, manifest 
bias or prejudice towards any person or 
group on irrelevant grounds. 
 
Section 3 
 
Judges shall carry out judicial duties with 
appropriate consideration for all persons, 
such as the parties, witnesses, lawyers, court 
staff 
and 
judicial 
colleagues, 
without 
differentiation on any irrelevant ground, 
immaterial to the proper performance of such 
duties. 
 
Section 4 
 
Judges shall not knowingly permit court staff 
or others subject to his or her influence, 
direction or control to differentiate between 
persons concerned, in a matter before the 
judge on any irrelevant ground. 
 
Section 5 
 
Judges shall require lawyers in proceedings 
before the court to refrain from manifesting, 
by words or conduct, bias or prejudice based 
on irrelevant grounds, except such as are 
legally relevant to an issue in proceedings 
and may be the subject of legitimate 
advocacy. 
 
f. Competence and Diligence – NCJC, 
Canon 6; 1989 CJC, Canon 4, Rules 3.01 
and 3.05 
 
Competence and diligence are prerequisites 
to the due performance of judicial office. 
 
Section 1 
 
The judicial 
duties of 
a judge 
take 
precedence over all other activities. 
 


<!-- PAGE 397 -->

 
 
385 
Section 2 
 
Judges shall devote their professional 
activity to judicial duties, which include not 
only the performance of judicial functions and 
responsibilities in court and the making of 
decisions, but also other tasks relevant to the 
judicial office or the court's operations. 
 
Section 3 
 
Judges shall take reasonable steps to 
maintain and enhance their knowledge, skills 
and personal qualities necessary for the 
proper performance of judicial duties, taking 
advantage for this purpose of the training and 
other facilities which should be made 
available, under judicial control, to judges. 
 
Section 4 
 
Judges shall keep themselves informed 
about relevant developments of international 
law, including international conventions and 
other instruments establishing human rights 
norms. 
 
Section 5 
 
Judges shall perform all judicial duties, 
including the delivery of reserved decisions, 
efficiently, 
fairly 
and 
with 
reasonable 
promptness. 
 
Section 6 
 
Judges shall maintain order and decorum in 
all proceedings before the court and be 
patient, dignified and courteous in relation to 
litigants, witnesses, lawyers and others with 
whom the judge deals in an official capacity. 
Judges shall require similar conduct of legal 
representatives, court staff and others 
subject to their influence, direction or control. 
 
Section 7 
 
Judges shall not engage in conduct 
incompatible with the diligent discharge of 
judicial duties.

3. INHIBITION AND 
DISQUALIFICATION – Rules of 
Court, Rule 137; 1989 CJC, Rules 
3.12 and 3.13 
 
RULE 137 
 
Disqualification of Judicial Officers 
 
Section 1. Disqualification of judges 
 
No judge or judicial officer shall sit in any 
case in which he, or his wife or child, is 
pecuniarily interested as heir, legatee, 
creditor or otherwise, or in which he is related 
to either party within the sixth degree of 
consanguinity or affinity, or to counsel within 
the fourth degree, computed according to the 
rules of the civil law, or in which he has been 
executor, administrator, guardian, trustee or 
counsel, or in which he has been presided in 
any inferior court when his ruling or decision 
is the subject of review, without the written 
consent of all parties in interest, signed by 
them and entered upon the record. 
A judge may, in the exercise of his sound 
discretion, disqualify himself from sitting in a 
case, for just or valid reasons other than 
those mentioned above. 
 
Section 
2. Objection 
that 
judge 
disqualified, how made and effect. If it be 
claimed that an official is disqualified from 
sitting as above provided, the party objecting 
to his competency may, in writing, file with 
the official his objection, stating the grounds 
therefor, and the official shall thereupon 
proceed with the trial, or withdraw therefrom, 
in accordance with his determination of the 


<!-- PAGE 398 -->

 
 
386 
question of his disqualification. His decision 
shall be forthwith made in writing and filed 
with the other papers in the case, but no 
appeal or stay shall be allowed from, or by 
reason of, his decision in favor of his own 
competency, until after final judgment in the 
case.

RULE 3.12. A judge should take no part in a

In every instance the judge shall indicate the

the

and

independently of the judge's participation, all 
agree in writing that the reason for the 
inhibition is immaterial or insubstantial, the 
judge may then participate in the proceeding. 
The agreement, signed by all parties and 
lawyers, shall be incorporated in the record 
of the proceeding.

Impeachment 
is 
the

b. Graft 
and 
Corruption

Engagement in acts of dishonesty or

c. Other High Crimes – Serious 
offenses, including those involving

(b) Dual Nature – Sec. 4; A.M.  No. 02-
9-02-SC 
 
Administrative proceedings against judges 
are dual in character. They are disciplinary, 
because they inquire into the administrative 
liability of a judge for acts or omissions in 
violation of law, rules, or ethical standards.  
 
At the same time, they are imbued with public 
interest, as their primary purpose is to 
protect the integrity of the judiciary and 
preserve public confidence in the courts, 
rather than to vindicate private rights. 
 
Because of this public character, the 
institution 
and 
continuation 
of 
the 
proceedings 
do 
not 
depend 
on 
the 
complainant.  
 
The withdrawal, desistance, settlement, 
or failure to prosecute by the complainant 
does not divest the Supreme Court of 
jurisdiction. The Court may proceed motu 
proprio to determine the fitness of the judge 
to remain in office. 
 
(c) Charges – Secs. 13-16 
 
Administrative charges against members of 
the judiciary are classified according to 
gravity, with each classification carrying 
corresponding sanctions. The classification 
determines both the nature of the offense 
and the range of penalties imposable. 
 
Section 13. Serious Charges 
 
Serious charges refer to grave offenses that 
directly undermine judicial integrity and 
public confidence. These include, among 
others, gross misconduct, corruption, gross 
ignorance of the law, gross neglect of duty, 
partiality, bribery, and conduct prejudicial to 
the best interest of the service when 
attended by bad faith, fraud, or malice. 
Serious charges warrant the most severe 
penalties, including dismissal from the 
service. 
 
Section 14. Less Serious Charges 
 
Less serious charges involve violations that 
do not rise to the level of serious charges but 
still reflect adversely on judicial conduct. 
These include undue delay in rendering a 
decision or order, simple misconduct, simple 
neglect of duty, and violations of judicial rules 
without proof of corrupt intent. Sanctions are 
corrective in nature and proportionate to the 
offense. 
 
Section 15. Light Charges 
 
Light 
charges 
cover 
minor 
infractions 
involving lapses in propriety, decorum, or 
diligence that do not materially affect judicial 
functions. These offenses typically involve 
minor violations of court rules or ethical 


<!-- PAGE 402 -->

 
 
390 
standards and are penalized with the least 
severe administrative sanctions. 
 
Section 16. Effect of Classification 
 
The classification of the charge controls the 
penalty imposable, subject to the presence of 
aggravating or mitigating circumstances. 
Multiple offenses may be considered, and 
penalties may be imposed separately or 
cumulatively, in accordance with the Rules. 
 
(d) Sanctions – Secs. 17-23 
 
Sanctions under Rule 140 are tied directly 
to the classification of charges (Serious, Less 
Serious, Light) and are designed to reflect 
the gravity of the transgression while 
preserving judicial integrity. 
 
Serious 
Charges 
Penalties 
range 
from 
dismissal from service to 
suspension 
or 
fines, 
depending 
on 
the 
specific 
violation 
and 
aggravating/mitigating 
circumstances. 
Examples 
include 
corruption, 
gross 
neglect 
of 
duty, 
bias 
or 
prejudice, gross ignorance of 
the law, and conviction of 
crimes 
involving 
moral 
turpitude. 
Less 
Serious 
Charges 
Sanctions typically consist of 
fines, suspension, or other 
corrective measures. These 
cover offenses such as undue 
delay in decisions, habitual 
tardiness, violation of court 
rules and directives, or simple 
misconduct. 
Light 
Charges 
Penalties commonly involve 
reprimand, admonition, or 
lighter fines, applicable to 
minor 
infractions 
like 
discourtesy 
or 
improper 
conduct that do not materially 
affect judicial functions. 
 
 
 
 
(e) Clemency 
 
 
Clemency in administrative cases against 
members of the judiciary is an act of grace 
that rests exclusively within the discretion of 
the Supreme Court. It is not a right, but a 
matter of judicial policy grounded on equity 
and public interest. 
 
Clemency may be granted only after the 
penalty imposed has been fully served, 
unless 
the 
Supreme 
Court 
provides 
otherwise. It does not erase the fact of 
administrative liability, but merely mitigates 
or relieves the effects of the penalty, such as 
disqualification from reappointment or other 
accessory consequences. 
 
In determining whether to grant clemency, 
the Supreme Court considers the nature and 
gravity of the offense, the length of service, 
the conduct of the respondent before and 
after the infraction, evidence of remorse and 
reformation, and the impact on public 
confidence in the judiciary. Clemency will not 
be granted where it would undermine judicial 
integrity or erode trust in the courts. 
 
Clemency 
does 
not 
expunge 
the 
administrative record of the offense. The 
finding of guilt remains, and the grant of 
clemency does not bar the use of the 
administrative case as a reference in future 
proceedings, where relevant.

purpose of presenting my testimony in connection with the case entitled “Pedro W. Utang 
vs. Juan T. Hingi” (Civil Case No. 2023-456) pending before Branch 45 of the

Q2: What is your relation to the parties involved in this case? 
A2: I am a witness for the plaintiff, Pedro W. Utang, who is my friend and neighbor. 
 
Q3: What do you know about the case?

repeated reminders.

J. MOTIONS 
 
1. TO DISMISS 
 
REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES 
REGIONAL TRIAL COURT 
NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION 
LAS PINAS CITY, BRANCH 143 
 
 
JUAN DELA CRUZ, 
 
 
 
Plaintiff, 
 
               vs.   
 
 
 
 
 
    CIVIL CASE NO. 15 88888 
 
 
 
 
 
for  DAMAGES 
 
 
DIEGO REYES, 
 
                    Defendant, 
 
MOTION TO DISMISS 
 
 
COME NOW, DEFENDANT, by counsel and unto this Honorable Court, most 
respectfully move for the dismissal of the above-captioned case upon the argument: 
 
THAT THE PLAINTIFF HAS NO LEGAL CAPACITY TO SUE; THE COMPLAINT 
FAILED TO STATE A CAUSE OF ACTION; THAT A CONDITION PRECEDENT FOR 
FILING THE CLAIM HAS NOT BEEN COMPLIED WITH. 
 
 
 
DISCUSSION 
 
PLAINTIFF HAS NO LEGAL CAPACITY TO SUE 
 
Sec. 5, Rule 3 of the Rules of Court which pertains to Minor or Incompetent persons 
provides that a minor or person alleged to be incompetent, may sue or be sued, with the 
assistance of his father, mother, guardian, or if he has none, a guardian ad litem. 
 
Plaintiff, being only seventeen years of age has no legal capacity to sue and cannot file 
any case in court without the legal assistance and representation of the people 
mentioned in the above rule. Thus, having no legal capacity, complaint filed by the 
plaintiff has no legal effect. 
  
 
 


<!-- PAGE 426 -->

  
 
 
 
363 
 
 
THE COMPLAINT DOES NOT STATE A CAUSE OF ACTION 
 
 
Section 1, Rule 2 of the Rules of Court provides that every ordinary civil action must 
be based on a cause of action. As defined by the rules, a cause of action is the act or 
omission by which a party violates a right of another. It is the delict or wrongful act or 
omission committed by the defendant in violation of the primary right of the plaintiff. 
 
To be sufficient, a cause of action must appear from the face of the complaint. In the 
case at bar, defendant respectfully submit that the complaint is wanting on this particular 
matter and the test is whether the court can render a valid judgment on the complaint 
based on the facts alleged and the prayer asked for. Indeed, the elementary test for 
failure to state a cause of action is whether the complaint alleges facts which if true would 
justify the relief demanded. Only ultimate facts and not legal conclusions or evidentiary 
facts, which should not be alleged in the complaint in the first place, are considered for 
purposes of applying the test. 
 
Applying this to the complaint, plaintiff failed to state the damages suffered by him which 
would be the reason for filing his case. The plaintiff also failed to establish the existence 
of his right through which was allegedly violated by Mr. Reyes as there was nothing 
mentioned about a contract or stipulation entered into by the parties.  
 
THE CONDITION PRECEDENT OF ENTERING INTO A BARANGAY 
CONCILIATATION PROCEEDINGS BEFORE FILING THE CASE IN COURT HAS 
NOT BEEN COMPLIED WITH. 
 
Section 3, of P.D. 1508 states that disputes between or among persons actually residing 
in the same barangay shall be brought for amicable settlement before the Lupon of said 
barangay. Those involving actual residents of different barangays within the same city or 
municipality shall be brought inn the barangay where the respondent or any of the 
respondents actually resides, at the election of the complainant. However, all disputes 
which involved real property or any interest therein shall be brought in the barangay 
where the real property or any part thereof is situated. 
 
The plaintiff resides at 44 Bauhinia St., Barangay Ginebra, Las Piñas City while the 
defendant resides at 89 Narra St., Barangay Ginebra, Las Piñas City. Since the plaintiff 
and the defendant are residing in the same barangay, it must be settled first in the Lupon 
of the said barangay before filing a complaint to the Court. The plaintiff who has a cause 
of action against the defendant must first comply with the Barangay Captain. Thus, not 
having the conciliation proceedings, complaint filed by the plaintiff is without legal effect.

failure of the plaintiff to state a cause of action..
